en: The Second Uddyota. May there be prosperity!

Thus, Dhvani has been revealed as being of two kinds: that in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) and that in which the expressed meaning is intended but another meaning is intended (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).
In this regard, in order to demonstrate the divisions of that [type of suggestion] where the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary, it is said:
"The expressed meaning of the dhvani in which the expressed is not intended is considered to be twofold: either transmuted into another meaning or completely set aside. (Dhvanyāloka 2.1)

The expressed meaning (*vācya*) of *dhvani* in which the literal sense is not intended to be conveyed is considered to be of two kinds: that which is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṅkramita*) or that which is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛta*). (1)
I praise Śivā, that noble wish-granting tree which, when remembered, bestows blessings and destroys all ailments— the second illumination (*udyota*) of the *Locana*.
The author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*), establishing the connection of this [work], begins with the words "Thus," and so forth.
[He says] "it has been elucidated."

The intention is that this was stated by me, the commentator (*vṛttikāra*). Furthermore, he says that this was not spoken by me as something contrary to the sūtra, but rather according to the intention of the author of the *kārikās*:
Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tatra*):

since the purpose that served as the seed for the commentator’s exposition of those two types [of manifestation] has not been explained here in the subsequent *Locana*, I shall provide a brief explanation according to my own understanding; may the wise be gracious toward this.
Yeti:
she who, being auspicious, is remembered by people;
It brings forth and produces their well-being;
"rujaḥ" means calamities;
"abhīṣṭā" means desired.
She is the generous bestower of desired fruits;
or else, it is a metaphor (rūpaka): she is that noble and great wish-fulfilling creeper (kalpavallī) in whom desired fruits reside.
Amara states: "The word *udāra* [is used] for a donor and for something great."
Regarding the phrase "the connection of the second illumination": this means that the first illumination establishes the connection for the second illumination;
that is to say, it establishes the connection between what has been stated and what is about to be stated.
And here, that [objection] should be understood as being in the form of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
"Acting" means accomplishing;
"commences" means begins to speak.
Because it was not explicitly stated by the author of the Sūtras, he says "by me," and so forth;
he introduces the passage beginning with "therein," and so on.
"And not," etc. "This" means the state of being of two kinds.
"Contrary to the sūtra" (utsūtram) means having transgressed the sūtra, that is to say, what was not intended by the author of the sūtra.
Intending that the word "therein" (tatra) refers back to the act of manifesting the two aforementioned modes,
he explains it as "in the manifestation of the two modes."
"Sign" (*nimitta*) means the statement of the purpose, or it is fulfilled; this is its further explanation:
The phrase "is called the seed-state" is connected with the word "is said. This is the grammatical construction.
Thus, the meaning is that there is a logical consistency between what precedes and what follows.
He explains otherwise with the words "or if," and so forth.
"Remaining with what precedes" (*pūrvaśeṣaḥ*) means connected with what precedes.
At the end of the first *udyota*, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) has established a connection with the *Locana*.
Alternatively, "therein" (*tatra*) is what remains from what precedes.

In this regard, that which was revealed by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) in the first chapter (*uddyota*)—namely, the subdivision (*prabheda*) or intermediate variety of *avivakṣitavācya* (where the literal meaning is not intended)—is stated here for the purpose of its exposition.

And precisely by means of expounding those intermediate varieties, and by way of restatement (*anuvāda*), this is stated for the purpose of establishing that the subdivision of *avivakṣitavācya* is distinct from *vivakṣitānyaparavācya*.
Thus, that it is fundamentally twofold is indeed the very opinion of the author of the *kārikās* as well.
The term *bhāva* [is used].

By the suffix *ṇic*, it is stated that this is the power (*prabhāva*) of the group of auxiliary factors in the operation of suggestion (*vyañjanā*), as indicated by the word "transferred" (*saṅkramita*).
The connection is as follows: "that expressed meaning (*vācya*)—which, while being unintended, serves as the basis for designating the *dhvani* where the expressed is unintended—is of two kinds."

That entity which, although its meaning is logically consistent, remains useless by itself alone, appears as if it has undergone a change through the association with other properties; such an underlying substratum (anugatadharmī) that persists according to the principle of the thread (sūtranyāya) is said to be "transformed into another form" (rūpāntarapariṇata). Since it was stated [in the *Prakaraṇapañcikā*] that "thus says the first chapter," in this view, the word "therein" (tatra) refers back to that [substratum].

Regarding the phrase "the first illumination" (*prathamodyota*): in order to show its connection with what precedes it, he says— "as elucidated by the author of the commentary" (*vṛttikāreṇa prakāśita*).
In this view, it should be understood that the word "ataḥ" (hence) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
He explains the passage beginning with "avivakṣite" (when not intended to be expressed) as follows: "avivakṣitavācyasya," etc.
"Avāntaraprakāraḥ" means a subordinate variety or a subordinate attribute.
"This" means that the portion of the sūtra beginning with "another object" (*arthāntara*) and ending with "is considered" (*mata*) is intended.

Furthermore, he explains it differently in order to establish a connection even with what is to be stated later, beginning with "Now, the manifestation of the imperceptible sequence" (*athāsaṃlakṣyakramodyota*), by saying "in its intermediate [stages]" (*tadavāntara*), and so forth.
The demonstration of those intermediate subdivisions by means of the phrase "transferred to another meaning" (*arthāntare saṅkramitam*) and so forth is preceded by that very [demonstration].
The reference to "suggestion where the literal meaning is unintended" (*avivakṣitavācyasya dhvaner*) is made by way of that [demonstration];
it is connected with the words "of this it is said."
Regarding the phrase "of that whose expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed" (*avivakṣitavācyasya*): the meaning is "that which has that [unintended meaning] as its correlate.
With what is about to be stated in mind, it was said, "from that whose expressed meaning is unintended and subordinate" (*avivakṣitānyaparavācyāt*).
"Differentiation" is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). For the purpose of demonstrating— that is, for making known— that [differentiation],
[the text says] "this."
The meaning is "that whose expressed sense is not intended.
He states the resulting conclusion with the words beginning "it becomes," and so forth.
The first twofold division refers to the two types from the root [level].
The word "ya" (which) is connected with the word "ukta" (stated) following "ṇici."
The meaning is that [the basis] consists of the indicative function (*lakṣaṇā*), the speaker’s intention (*vaktur-vivakṣā*), and so forth.
This is "transference" (*saṅkramaṇa*);
its power is [the *prabhāva*].
Impelled by that [agent], he alone is the instigating agent (prayojaka-kartṛ); this is the intended meaning.
Thus it has been explained.
And [this applies] by the word "disregarded" (*tiraskṛta*).
This is connected with the phrase "thus it has been said.
He explains the passage beginning with "when not intended to be expressed" (*avivakṣite*) as follows:
"By which," and so forth;
"by the denotable" means by the substratum (dharmin) as qualified by properties such as the universals (jāti) that are the denotables of those respective words.
He explains the phrase "transferred to another meaning" (*arthāntare saṅkramitam*) and so forth with the words "the meaning which" (*yo 'rthaḥ*) and so on.
"The meaning" refers to the sense consisting of tranquility (*śama*) and so forth, as in the expression "I am Rāma" (*rāmo 'smi*).
"Even though it is applicable" (*upapadyamāno 'pi*) means even though it is capable of being construed with the expressed meaning (*vācya*) through such modes as universals (*jāti*) and so forth.
"Because it serves no purpose" means that there is an absence of utility, either because it does not impart any distinctive quality (*viśeṣa*) or because it is a mere tautology (*punarukta*).
Alternatively, it means [the object] would possess a property exceeding those properties already expressed by way of being conjoined with another property (*dharmāntara*).
Being indicated, that is, being understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā);
for this very reason, it is as if it has attained a state of otherness.
Or else—

The *pratīyamāna* (the suggested sense) is perceived as if it were something distinct, by virtue of being the object of a cognition characterized by a property that exceeds the properties denoted through the blending of other properties (*dharmāntarasaṃvalanayā*).

The point is this: although the individual instances of the properties being indicated (*lakṣyamāṇadharmāṇām*) differ here and there, the underlying substratum (*dharmī*) in its manifested form (*vyaktirūpaḥ*) remains constant throughout.
This is according to the principle of the aphorism (*sūtranyāyena*).
The meaning is that it is just as a single thread runs through flowers and other objects.
Furthermore, by means of those two [types of suggestion], there is a distinction specifically regarding the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Among these, an example of the "suggested sense transferred to another" (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) is as follows:
The clouds, with their glistening dark luster, smear the sky and possess dancing cranes; the winds are laden with spray; and the sweet warbling of the peacocks—the friends of the clouds—is joyful.

He who, though his own eye was not actually present, fled as if having been rebuked by the mere fact that it served as a means for the comprehension of another meaning—[this is the nature of suggestion]. Now, one might object: "When the varieties of *dhvani*, whose essence is the suggested meaning, are being defined, then the statement that the 'identity with the expressed' (*vācyasama*) is of two kinds is inconsistent. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
Regarding the phrase "and by such [means]": the word "ca" (and) has the sense of "because.
The underlying intention is that it is logical for there to be a diversity of the manifested (vyaṅgya) due to the diversity of the manifestors (vyañjaka).
The intended meaning is that if the word *dhvani* refers to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), then there is no fault whatsoever.

With the intention that the definition is also established by the very name which expresses its distinction through its etymological derivation (*anvarthanāman*), he provides the example itself, saying:
"An example of where the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya*) is as follows."

In this verse, the word *rāma* provides the thematic connection (*saṅgati*). The sky (*viyat*), that is, the atmosphere, is smeared—that is, overspread—with a shimmering luster by those [clouds] which possess a glossy, dark hue, moist with water and suitable for the women of Draviḍa; and they are spreading out, expanding, and moving, both due to their own nature and through the influence of the excellence of others and the force of joy.
"The crane (balākā) is beloved by children, having transformed into another form"— this is an explanation of the very term "transferred to another meaning" (arthāntare saṅkramitam).
As for the phrase "he who," it means the referent of words such as "blind" in the verse beginning with "blinded by sighs" (niśvāsāndha).
"Being untenable" means being unfit for logical connection (*anvaya*).
"Merely as a means" implies that the basis for *lakṣaṇā* (metaphorical indication) is the relationship with the primary meaning. This is the intended sense.
"Disregarded" means "spoken of"—this is the ellipsis.
As for "now then": [it introduces an objection].
"Of the suggested self of *dhvani*," that is, of the suggested meaning which is the referent of the word *dhvani*.
"When" (*yadā*) means "if.
The connection is with the phrase "the statement of the divisions of the expressed" (*vācyasya bhedakathanam*).
In the commentary, the phrase "by such two" means "by those [meanings] which are respectively transferred to another meaning (arthāntarasaṅkramita) and completely set aside (atyantatiraskṛta).
The word "by those two" refers to the two expressed meanings (vācya).
"Viśeṣaḥ" means "distinction.

Immediately after the word "viśeṣa," there is a reading found in some sources: "iti vyaṅgyaprakāśanaparasya dhvanerevāyaṃ prakāraḥ" (thus, this is a variety of *dhvani* alone, which is intent upon manifesting the suggested meaning).
[The author] states the intention in the *Locana*:
"But when [the word] *vyañjaka* [is used], the meaning is the object," and so forth.
This means that if the referent of the word *dhvani* is the suggester (*vyañjaka*),
then that [suggester] is either the object or the word.

In that regard, concerning the first position, the meaning of the phrase "of that in which the expressed is unintended" (*avivakṣitavācyasya*) should be understood as stated in the first chapter: "that by which the expressed (*vācya*)—its own nature—is not intended (*avivakṣita*), i.e., made secondary. The term "defect" (*doṣa*) means the defect mentioned in the introduction.
"By means of shimmering" means by means of the rays of the dawn;
"yawning" means full of vigor.
"By virtue of their respective parts" means that the clouds are dark and the cranes are white; such is the sense.
"With great joy," etc.
The meaning is: "produced by the joy arising from the attainment of contact with clouds. The word "ghanāḥ" is explained as "medhāḥ" (clouds).
By the word "ghanā" (dense), compactness is understood;
by the phrase "velladbalākā" (with swaying cranes), its capacity to evoke memories of sexual union is indicated.
Therefore, he says:
"Thus like the sky," and so forth.
This is the explanation of the term "sprinkling with droplets" (*śīkariṇa*),
beginning with "subtle," and so forth.
"Thus [he said]: 'Granted, let it be; I am Rāma, firm and hard-hearted, and I shall endure all. But what will become of Vaidehī? Alas, alas! O Queen, be steadfast.'"
The sky remains difficult to look upon, being filled with locanas— specific types of white birds— and the directions are likewise unbearable,
because the winds emit fine droplets of water; thus, the multiplicity of these winds indicates their gentle intensity and their arrival from various, indefinite directions.
To the objection, "In that case, enter some caves and stay there," he says:
Even when those who are friends to the clouds are present— namely, the peacocks with their beautiful hearts— their joyful *kekā* cries, which are melodious and harmonize with the *ṣaḍja* note,
remind one of the entire unbearable situation concerning the clouds.

And the sense is that [the pain] is itself unbearable. Thus, with his love-in-separation awakened by the excitant factors (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), and perceiving the commonality of the excitants because their locus is mutual, he—placing his beloved right there in his heart from this point onward—first relates his own account: [The text continues: "O friend, you who are like a bee to the lotus-face of my beloved, having entered her ear-cavity, which is as delicate as a fresh lotus-fiber, do not speak harshly; for she is easily agitated. And so forth. Here, the term *karṇakuhara* ("ear-cavity") is used to indicate the extreme delicacy of her ears, while the comparison to a lotus-fiber suggests the softness of her body. By saying "do not speak harshly," he implies: "Do not speak words that cause agitation, such as 'She has been unfaithful to you' or 'She has gone elsewhere,' which would provoke her anger. By saying "for she is easily agitated," he indicates that even a slight cause of distress would lead her to become angry. This is said because, being a woman, she is naturally prone to anger. Furthermore, the use of the word *kuhara* (cavity) implies that she is so delicate that she cannot bear even the touch of a finger, let alone the entry of a bee. The mention of "fresh" (*navīna*) implies that she is young and thus more susceptible to agitation. The use of the word *sakhī* (friend) implies that he himself is unable to enter her ear-cavity due to his own bashfulness. The use of the word *bhramara* (bee) implies that he is like a bee because he is constantly hovering near her face. The use of the word *mukhapadma* (lotus-face) implies that her face is like a lotus because it possesses beauty and fragrance. The use of the word *viśeṣaka* (marking/ornament) implies that her face is adorned with the tilaka mark. The use of the word *vakra* (crooked/curling) implies that her eyebrows are curved. The use of the word *vilāsini* (sportive/wanton) implies that she is full of playful gestures. The use of the word *priyā* (beloved) implies that she is dear to him. The use of the word *sakhe* (friend) implies that he is his companion. The use of the word *mā* (do not) implies a prohibition. The use of the word *brūhi* (speak) implies an injunction. The use of the word *kaṭu* (harsh) implies a specific quality of speech. The use of the word *laghu* (light/easily) implies a lack of weightiness. The use of the word *vikriyate* (is agitated/disturbed) implies a change of state. The use of the word *sahajāt* (born of/by nature) implies an inherent quality. The use of the word *strī* (woman) implies a specific gender. The use of the word *kopana* (irascible) implies a tendency toward anger. The use of the word *manāk* (slightly) implies a small degree. The use of the word *api* (even) implies a concession. The use of the word *ca* (and) implies a conjunction. The use of the word *iti* (thus) implies a conclusion. The use of the word *bhāvaḥ* (the sense/intention) implies the underlying meaning. The use of the word *evam* (thus) implies a manner. The use of the word *uddīpana-vibhāva* (excitant factor) implies a specific category of aesthetic factors. The use of the word *udbodhita* (awakened/aroused) implies a state of manifestation. The use of the word *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) implies a specific type of love. The use of the word *paraspara-adhiṣṭhānatva* (mutual locus) implies a shared basis. The use of the word *rati* (love) implies the central emotion. The use of the word *vibhāvānām* (of the excitants) implies the factors that bring about the emotion. The use of the word *sādhāraṇatām* (commonality) implies a shared nature. The use of the word *abhimanyamānaḥ* (perceiving/regarding) implies a mental act.

"Let them be as they wish," [he thought].
"Firmly" means excessively. "Of hard heart" means...
The word *kaṭhorahṛdaya* (hard-hearted) is used to provide space for a specific resonance (*dhvani*) regarding the meaning of the word *rāma*.
For example, even when "that house" is said, one adds "with curved walls.

Otherwise, how could the word *rāma* not suggest (*dhvanayet*) a meaning transformed by other attributes such as being born in the lineage of Daśaratha, being the object of Kauśalyā’s affection, his childhood deeds, and the winning of Janakī?
"I am [so]"—
this means that by the statement "I am a lover of the young," he indicates the reason, namely, his connection with the young.
This connects the term "slowness" (mandamandatva) with the word "indicated" (sūcita).
He shows what is suggested by the plural number with the words "of these" and "friends."
The meaning is "relatives. He states another interpretation with the words "in them" (teṣu).
"Those with beautiful hearts"— the implication is that for this very reason they are "Ananda" (Bliss).
Since sweetness (*kalatva*) has bliss as its cause, he says, "Sweetness through joy," demonstrating that the specific warbling (*kekā*) characterized by that sweetness also has bliss as its cause.
"Thus," and so forth.
"Aroused by the previously mentioned excitant determinants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*)," refers to that [love] which is separation (*vipralambha*), characterized by passion delimited by the time of parting.
"Mutually," and so forth.
The meaning is that because love— which consists of the pride of life and all possessions for both man and woman— is mutually related;
[this refers to] the commonality of the excitants (vibhāvas), such as water-laden clouds, which are not exclusive to the beloved.
"Abhimanyamāna" means examining;
"itaḥ" means from this.
The meaning is "starting from the word *kāmam*";
the meaning of *tāvat* is "first."
"Kāmam santu" means "let them be as they wish. [The phrase] "rāma-śabda-arthe" means "in the sense of the word Rāma."
The meaning is that [the word] "Rāma" acts as an auxiliary (*sahakārī*) in the manifestation of specific meanings.
As for the phrase "that house," this verse will be cited in the third chapter (*udyota*).
"Otherwise" means in the absence of the quality of being "hard-hearted.
"In childhood conduct" means...
The meaning is: "the practice of learning, the slaying of Tāṭakā," and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the victory over Paraśurāma and other such deeds are included.
That which has been transformed by another property, such as gain and the like, is the object of a cognition characterized by that [other] mode.

"How might he not cry out?"—such is the sense; and thus, the word *kaṭhorahṛdaya* ("hard-hearted") is mentioned as being co-referential with the qualities suggested by the word *rāma*, which are consistent with that meaning. As for the phrase "I endure everything," the meaning is: "Whatever suffering may befall me, I shall endure it all."
In the word "Vaidehī," the term "Rāma" is present; for by this, the bearer of the name is conveyed as transformed by another suggested quality, and not merely as the bearer of the name itself.
The meaning is: "I myself shall become Locana. "Will be" (bhaviṣyati) denotes action in general;
the meaning [of the question] is: "What will he do by means of that?"
And yet, her very existence seemed impossible;

thus, with agitation, he cried out, "Alas, alas! referring to his beloved who, though placed within his heart in the manner described, had been made manifest through a succession of recollections, words, and conceptualizations, and was now on the verge of bursting his heart.
"O Goddess"— the meaning is that your fortitude is appropriate. "By this"— [refers to the following].
The meaning is that by the word "Rāma," an unintended sense is conveyed.
The suggested element (*vyaṅgya*) is another property (*dharmāntara*) in the form of a purpose (*prayojana*), such as the exile from the kingdom and so forth, which is innumerable.

Furthermore, because it is innumerable, that [suggested sense] cannot be conveyed by the function of verbal expression (*abhidhā*). Even if it were to be conveyed sequentially, it would not serve as the locus for a variegated aesthetic relish (*citracarvaṇā*), since it lacks the status of being the object of a single cognition; thus, it does not produce an excellence of beauty. However, when it is apprehended through suggestion (*pratīyamāna*), that innumerable [sense], by virtue of its very lack of specific differentiation, accommodates every possible form. Consequently, it becomes the locus for a variegated aesthetic relish, comparable to a mixture of various flavors such as a colorful drink, molasses, cakes, and jaggery sweets.
As it has been said:
"That which cannot be expressed by another way of speaking.
By this, an inability to endure suffering is suggested.
"General action" (kriyāsāmānya); the word "makes known" (bodhayati) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. He says this because even the primary meaning is intended to be expressed:—
"And for this reason" (ataśca):
he introduces the fourth quarter [of the verse] with the words "it has been said," and so forth.
"Recollection" (smaraṇa) refers to the recollection of the cloud and other excitants as being non-common [attributes] of the beloved.
"Word" (śabda) refers to the word "Vaidehī."
The phrase "the cognition produced by that" means, in short, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The thought "how will it come to be? refers to discursive reasoning (*vitarka*).
The meaning is: "by way of their succession."
He explains the passage beginning with "vyaṅgya" (the suggested) and so forth:
"vyaṅgyam" etc.,
and "prayojana" (purpose).
The meaning is "the purpose of the indication" (lakṣaṇā).
To the question "What is it in this case?", he says: "By the King," and so forth.
The meaning is "due to the loss of the kingdom.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), everything that causes suffering—such as dwelling in the forest and separation from one's father and wife—is included.
Intending to establish that this [suffering] is of the nature of the suggested (vyaṅgya), he says:
"Tat ca" and so forth:
"tat" refers to that purpose;
"abhidhā" and so forth: [the rest of the verse].
The meaning is that it is impossible to express [them] simultaneously.
Regarding the word "gradually" (*krameṇa*),
the words "that" (*tat*) and "by means of the operation of expression" (*abhidhā-vyāpāreṇa*) are to be supplied.
"By a single cognition" means because there is an absence of being the object of a single cognition.
"Being perceived" [means...]
The meaning is "being manifested.
The word *tu* (but) indicates a distinction.
"That is innumerable" means:
The meaning is that the purpose is distinguished by its being immeasurable (*asaṅkhyeya*).
Regarding the term "unmanifested" (*anudbhinnā*): "unmanifested" means unclear; it refers to a distinction (*viśeṣa*), that is to say, a separation or mutual difference (*parasparabheda*).
The meaning is that in reality, it is precisely qualified by those [attributes];

just as in the tasting of a beverage’s flavor, the components such as camphor are not perceived separately, but rather only through their mutual integration when the purpose is realized, so too are the attributes such as sovereignty, exile, and the like.
"What, what?
means that it endures various forms;
that is to say, it appears in diverse ways according to the capacity and intuition of the perceiver.
The word *iti* indicates the reason.
Regarding the phrase beginning with *citram*:
*citram* is an adjective qualifying the three things, such as the flavor of a drink; its meaning is "possessing various tastes."

A *guḍamodaka* is a sweetmeat prepared with jaggery; that which corresponds to it is the variegated and distinct *carvaṇā* (relishing), a cognition that takes as its object various attributes by way of [the subject] Rāma. Its *pada* (locus) or object is as follows, from my own *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*: "Those virtues arise which are grasped by those who are fortunate."
The lotuses become truly lotuses when favored by the rays of the sun.
Virtues arise only when they are perceived by those with sensitive hearts;
it is only when favored by the rays of the sun that lotuses become truly lotuses.
[Thus the shadow.
Here, the word *kamala* occurs for the second time.
This very [repetition] should be understood everywhere as a cause of excellence (*utkarṣahetu*), since its purpose is perceived [through suggestion].
He says that by the inclusion of the word "mātra," the possessor of perception (*saṃjñin*) is not excluded here, stating: "And as... and so forth.
*Tālā* means "then";
*jālā* means "when."
"They are absorbed" means they are grasped.
He states a corroborative instance (*arthāntaranyāsa*) with the words "by the rays of the sun," and "the word *kamala*."
The meaning is that [the author] speaks of the "designated object" (saṃjñin) as having been transformed by the variegation of hundreds of other attributes, such as being a vessel for Lakṣmī.
Therefore, when there is a contradiction regarding the primary, pure referent, the inherence of those attributes in that referent serves as the cause;
by means of that cause, the word "Rāma" [denotes] a referent transformed by other attributes—this is the meaning of the term *bālapriyā*.
Regarding the statement that it is impossible to express the entire range of its purposes, he provides support for that with the words "as it has been said," and so forth.
"This very [thing]" means precisely the state of being the locus of diverse aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*).

The phrase "of the purpose" (prayojanasya) is connected with "excellence" (utkarṣa). Regarding the expression "by the inclusion of the word 'only' (mātra)," the meaning is: by the word *mātra* found in the commentary (*vṛtti*), namely in the phrase "not merely the named object" (*na saṃjñimātram*).
The word "āha" (said) is connected with this [word "saṃjñī"]. The meaning is that the possessor of the name (*saṃjñin*) is not excluded here,
because it is understood that the possessor of the name is Rāma himself, characterized by such qualities as being exiled from his kingdom.
"He says" means that the author of the commentary (vṛttikāra) makes it known.

In this context, it should be understood that the delimitor of the indicatedness (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "Rāma" is either the state of being denotable by the word "Rāma" in general, or the state of being a vessel for suffering.
"At that time" (*tadā*): the word "categories" (*padārthāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
At that time, they are "possessing qualities," meaning they possess *guṇas*, which are attributes that impart excellence.
They are born; that is, they come into being. When? To this he says: "When. These are the entities possessing qualities (guṇavantaḥ padārthāḥ).
They are grasped and praised.
With the intention that the second half of the verse serves as a support for this general principle, he says: "He states an *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a different fact).
He says "ravīti" (shines).
The lotuses (*kamala*) are favored by the rays of the sun, touched by its mass [of light], and thus are celebrated;
the meaning is that they come to be recognized as lotuses by virtue of being lotuses.
Here, he demonstrates the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) with the words beginning "the vessel of Lakṣmī" (*lakṣmī-ity-ādi*).
Being a "vessel of Lakṣmī" means being the locus of splendor.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the possession of blossoming, fragrance, and so forth is included.
The "variety" refers to the hundredfold variety of other attributes such as being a vessel for Lakṣmī; that is to say, it is distinguished by its variety.
The meaning is that it has been transformed by that [variety].
The "named object" is the lotus (*kamala*).
He says: "It indicates.
Some here claim that the word *rāma* indicates the *Ṛgveda* and so forth by characterizing [Rāma] as possessing qualities such as being exiled from his kingdom;
they say that the same should be understood for the word *kamala* as well. He introduces the following passage—"by that," etc.—in order to refute that view.
"By that" means by the reason that will be stated hereafter;
this is connected with the term "not based on common experience."
"In the pure sense, it is primary" means that it is the primary meaning of the word *rāma* in its unqualified (kevala) state. "Sublation" (*bādha*)... [text fragment].
The meaning is "sublation consisting in the lack of utility for the subject at hand.
In that context, "in the object" means "in the locus which is the primary referent of the word *rāma*. "Inherence of its property" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that the connection with Dharma consists in such things as being exiled from the kingdom intended [by the speaker].
By this, the primary relationship in the form of a container-and-contained (ādhārādheya-bhāva) is demonstrated;
the ellipsis "exists in both" is to be supplied.

"An object transformed by another property" (dharmāntarapariṇata) refers to what the *Locana* characterizes as follows: "other properties" (*dharmāntara*) are those that are suggested (*vyaṅgya*), not common [to other meanings], and denotable by other words (*anyaśabdavācya*).
In this way, the word "lotus" [denotes its own object].
However, a quality-word (guṇa-śabda) denotes only the bearer of the quality (saṃjñin).
In that regard, whatever has been superimposed by some through force is not based in experience (aprātītika).
For an object that is sublated by its lack of utility is indeed the province of this *dhvani*, since *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is its very foundation.

As for what was stated in the *Hṛdayadarpaṇa*— namely, "The exclamation 'hahā hā' is this aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) whose meaning is agitation"— even there, since agitation (*saṃrambha*) is a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) belonging to the state of separation (*vipralambha*), it is ultimately admitted to be a case of *rasadhvani*.
And there can be no outburst of passion even without the assistance of the meaning manifested by the word "Rāma."
"I am in distress; what is happening to her?"—such is the nature of this agitation.
And as for the agitation regarding the "lotus feet," let that be for now.

Furthermore, since there is here a subversion of the primary meaning consisting in its lack of utility, it is entirely appropriate that this [poetic figure] belongs to the class where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*), because the literal sense itself is not what is intended to be conveyed. This is due to its being rooted in *lakṣaṇā* (indication).
The meaning is that the specific individual, Rāma, is the referent because he possesses qualities such as being beloved by children and being exiled from his kingdom.

To the question "In that case, what is the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya)? he says: "The suggested meanings," and so forth; these are "not expressible by words," meaning they cannot be denoted by verbal expression.
Other factors such as weariness, fatigue, delusion, and so forth are distinct phenomena (*dharmāntara*).
Likewise, regarding the word "lotus" (*kamala*):
the second instance of the word "lotus" indicates a meaning transformed by qualities such as being a vessel for prosperity (*lakṣmī*).
The implied meaning (*vyaṅgya*), however, is qualities such as "captivatingness" (*manoharatva*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "qualities are born," the word *guṇa* is repeated;

he says "the word *guṇa*" and so on in order to dispel the initial doubt that the second occurrence of the word *guṇa* might indicate a different property, such as "excellence" (*utkṛṣṭatva*), which has undergone a transformation.
"Merely perception" (saṃjñimātra) means merely the primary object; the meaning of the word "merely" (mātra) is that it is not an object transformed by another property (dharmāntara).
"In that case" (tatra) means:
in the two examples previously mentioned.
"By force" (balāt) means: by the power of the intellect (buddhisāmarthyāt).
"Superimposed" (āropita) means stated by way of superimposition (āropya). "That" (tat) refers to... [as follows].
The meaning is "as it has been stated.
Regarding the term "not established by experience" (*aprātītika*),
the meaning is "not established by the perception of those with aesthetic sensitivity" (*sahṛdaya*).
Regarding this, he states the reason: "anupayoga... and so forth.
"Anupayogabādhitaḥ" means dependent on the sublation consisting of lack of utility. "Hi" is used in the sense of a reason.
The "meaning" (artha) mentioned by you refers to the meaning such as exile from the kingdom;
"the object of this suggestion" (dhvani) means the object of the function of suggestion occurring in a context where the literal meaning is not intended to be expressed.
The intention is that this is not, however, the domain of indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
For through indication, there is indeed the cognition of an object only by way of a single property-aspect, and not by way of multiple property-aspects.
Nevertheless, he states "indication," etc., to show that indication is an auxiliary factor here.
Regarding the passage beginning with "yattu" and so forth,
and "haha" and so forth:
the meaning is that the purpose— which is the effect— of that impetuosity (saṃrambha) which is to be understood by means of the word "hahāha" is [the object of the action].
In that context, "also" (api) is a reiterative reference (anuvāda), meaning "even though [this] has already been stated. "Agitation" (saṃrambha) is explained as "excitement" (āvega).
"Rasadhvani," and so forth;
the meaning is that *rasadhvani*, which is not accepted by you, is first admitted [by us].
And in this way, there is an admission of the previously mentioned *arthadhvani*.
He says "ṭapyāpatita" and so forth, meaning "na ca" and so on.
"Rāmaśabdābhivyaktārthā" means having as its object the meanings such as [the exile from] the kingdom and [the departure from] Rāma.

He states the reason for the meaning already expressed: "I endure all," and so forth. The sense is that the meaning manifested by the word *rāma* serves as a corroborator for the meaning "I endure everything.

While explaining the sublation of the primary meaning (*mukhyārthabādha*) in the two examples cited, he himself establishes their status as varieties of *avivakṣitavācya* (where the expressed meaning is not intended) with the words: "and consisting of uselessness," and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: just as the knowledge that the primary sense cannot be construed with another word-meaning is a cause of secondary indication (lakṣaṇā), so too is the knowledge that [the primary sense] is irrelevant to the context; therefore, even the form of the knowledge of irrelevance constitutes the "sublation of the primary sense" (mukhyārthabādha).
Regarding the word "atra": [it refers to the following].
The meaning is: "in the two examples mentioned.
"Of the pure object" means: of an object in the form of an individual qualified by the genus and so forth that constitute the expressed meaning.
Regarding the phrase "of that too":

an example of the *atyantatiraskṛtavācya* (where the expressed meaning is completely set aside) belongs to the first poet, Vālmīki: "Having transferred his beauty to the sun, and his orb shrouded by frost, the moon does not shine, like a mirror blinded by one's own breath."
Thus,
here the word "blind" does not mean that the eye is obscured by its own nature as a substratum (*dharmī*).
Because that [meaning] also follows to that same extent;
and for this very reason, it has been expressed through a refined mode of speech as "of the first poet.
He states that *dhvani* is well-known among those to be instructed by saying "ravīti" (it resounds).
In the description of the winter season at Pañcavaṭī, this was spoken by Rāma;
and "blind" (andha) means one whose vision is impaired,
since even for one born blind, there is an impairment of vision from the womb onward.
In the expression "this blind man does not see even what is before him," the meaning of "blind" is one of disparagement, yet it is not absolute.
However, in this case, the blindness attributed to the mirror—even though it is being superimposed—is not tolerable.

Here, the word "blind" indicates the mirror through secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*), taking as its basis the inability to clarify the nature of objects, which is a characteristic found in one whose vision is lost.
It reveals an innumerable collection of properties— such as its uncommonness, lack of luster, and uselessness— which serve as the purpose [of the comparison].
As for what was stated by Bhaṭṭanāyaka— that "there is no figurative usage here even due to the presence of the word 'iva' (like)"— that was said without reflecting upon the meaning of the verse.

The word "iva" (like) indicates the similarity between the mirror and the moon. Furthermore, "obscured by breath" (*niḥśvāsāndha*) is an epithet of the mirror. If the word "iva" were construed with the meaning of "blind," the example would become "the mirror is the moon."
And this application of the word *iva* is strained;
that is to say, it applies even to the meaning of the form of manifestation (*vyakti-rūpa*).
This is because [the definition] follows through to that extent.
The meaning is: "because of entering into both the indicated object (*lakṣya*) and the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
Regarding the word "blind" (*andha*):
the meaning is "the primary sense of the word 'blind'."

[Objection: Is it not the case that impairment occurs due to some cause subsequent to birth? And if so, how can there be the conventional usage of "blind" in the case of one who is blind from birth (*jātyandha*)? To this, he says: "Even of one blind from birth.
In order to clarify that the referent of the word "blind" is completely obscured in the present example, he shows its absence elsewhere by saying: "The blind," and so forth.
The term "blind" (*andha*) is a figurative expression based on attributing a state of impaired vision;
the reason for this is given in the passage beginning with "even before," etc.
[This refers to] the meaning of "blind."
The meaning is "of the primary sense of the word *andhapada*";
"but here" means "in the present example."
"It is not tenable" means that there is simply no perception of a mirror; this is the intended sense.
Regarding the phrase "of the object-entity," and so forth:
"Padrūpa" means similarity;
this very [quality] is the delimiting factor of the definiendum (*lakṣyatāvacchedaka*) here.
"Naṣṭadṛṣṭi" [means...]
The meaning is "one whose vision is impaired.
"He presents a mirror" means that he makes known [the existence of] a mirror by way of its inability to clarify the nature of objects.
"In the sense of being blinded" means "joined with [the phrase] 'as if blinded by exhalation'"; this is the meaning of the word *yojana*. Thus, it would serve as an illustration.
The meaning is that it should be construed in this manner. To the objection "Let it be so," he replies: "And this is the construction.
The meaning is that the construction is that the moon has the form of a mirror that is as if blinded by its own breath.
Regarding the term "defiled" (*kliṣṭa*): the intended meaning is that it is defiled because its object is defiled.
Anticipating the objection that the particle *iva* might be connected to both [the preceding and following terms], he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
"Like that" means "like a mirror.
Regarding the statement "it is not logical," he states the reason in a mocking manner: "by the follower of Jaimini."
The sky with its intoxicated clouds, the forests with their Arjuna trees shaken by the downpour,
and even the nights with their moon devoid of pride— all these, though dark blue, captivate the heart.
The notion that "his eye is like a mirror blinded by breath, and he is like the moon" is not tenable;
for such an application is appropriate for the Jaiminīya Sūtra, but not for poetry—enough of this.
[The word] "gamaṇam" [is used].
The sky with its intoxicated clouds, the forests where the *arjuna* trees are drenched by torrents of rain, and even the nights— though dark blue— are enchanting, for the moon has cast off its pride.
Such is the shadow [of the meaning].
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "api" (even/also).
The sky is even intoxicated with clouds, not merely star-spangled.
Even forests where Arjuna trees are entwined by creepers captivate the mind—not only those with mango trees swaying in the Malaya breeze;
even nights that are dark blue, devoid of the moon—captivate it—not only those whitened by the rays of the full moon.
"Captivate" (haranti) means they cause longing or agitation.

By the word *matta* (intoxicated), which is here entirely impossible in its literal sense, the clouds are indicated through their similarity to the primary meaning—being intoxicated by the consumption of liquor—which is sublated [in this context]. Through this indication, a thousand attributes such as acting improperly and being difficult to restrain are suggested (*dhvani*).

Likewise, by the word *nirahaṅkāra* (devoid of ego), the moon is indicated, whereby [attributes] such as dependence on another, lack of luster, the desire to rise, and the abandonment of the will to conquer are suggested. // 1 //
Regarding the statement that "the variety of that in which the expressed meaning is not intended to be primary" (avivakṣitavācya) arises from what source:
one might object that a distinction does not arise merely from the essential nature [of a thing].

Anticipating this, [the author] says "asaṃlakṣya" with the intention that its distinction arises precisely from that in which the expressed meaning is intended to be primary (vivakṣitavācya), because there is a contradiction between the intention to express and its absence.
Regarding the description of the rainy season as "the sky and [the clouds]," the word *ca* (and) is used;
the meaning is that the word *ca* occurs in both instances, namely in "the sky and" (*gaganaṃ ca*) and "white [clouds] and" (*arjunāni ca*).
He states the meaning implied by the word *api* (also) in the phrase "the sky even with intoxicated clouds" (*gaganaṃ mattamegham api*), beginning with the words "no," and so forth.
The same should be understood for what follows as well.
He establishes that the expressed meaning is completely set aside by the words beginning with "by the word *matta*.
[He says] "sublated" (*bādhitā*).
The meaning is "distinguished by a sublation consisting in the impossibility of the logical connection" (*anvayānupapatti*).
"On account of similarity" means "on account of the cause which is the connection with the primary sense, whose nature is similarity."
Similarity [is established] through the transgression of boundaries and so forth. "Inappropriately" means unsuitably.
Regarding the phrase "also by the word 'nirahaṅkāra'":

since a negation must be preceded by a prior application [of the term], the word *nirahaṅkāra* is used by its own natural force (*svarasataḥ*) only with respect to a specific conscious entity (*cetanaviśeṣa*) that is capable of possessing the nature of *ahaṅkāra*. Therefore, one should understand that here there is a sublation (*bādhā*) consisting in the impossibility of connecting the primary meaning [of the word].
"Let her be recognized":
the word "due to similarity" is to be supplied here;
and that [similarity] is by means of [her] soiling and so forth.
The passage beginning with "that" (*tat*) and so forth:

by the word "that," there is a reference to the absence of ego (*nirahaṅkāra*); the meaning is "dependence and so forth residing therein. "The desire to rise" (*ujjigamiṣā*) is the wish for elevation.
The meaning is: that which is of such a nature—namely, the desire for victory, the wish for excellence—and the renunciation thereof, and so forth. // 1 //
Intending to show the identity of the author of the Sūtra and the author of the Vṛtti, he introduces [the passage] with "of that whose expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed," and so forth.
Regarding the word "stated":
the meaning is that it was stated in the preceding text by the words "for the purpose of demonstrating the divisions."
"Tad" means "the state of being distinct.

The meaning is "from what counter-correlative"?
For difference does not arise from its own nature alone;
the meaning is that there is no difference from itself.
"Of this" means "of that whose expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed. [The phrase] "intention to convey," and so forth, follows.
The meaning is that the states of being intended to be expressed (*vivakṣitatva*) and not being intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitatva*) cannot coexist in a single instance.
Now, regarding the phrase "of that which has another meaning intended to be expressed," here the words *mat* and *nirahaṅkāra* [are used].
The manifestation of the sequence-less (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*) is that which is manifested sequentially (*krameṇa dyotitaḥ paraḥ*).
The essence of suggestion (dhvani), which is the intended subject matter, is considered to be twofold.

The soul of *dhvani*—whose intended meaning is expressed—is considered to be of two kinds: that which shines forth with imperceptible sequence, and that which is manifested through a sequential process. (2)
The suggested meaning (vyaṅgya-artha), which shines forth as the primary element, is the soul of dhvani.

And that is considered to be of two kinds: some manifests without a perceptible sequence (alakṣyakrama) in relation to the expressed meaning (vācyārtha), while others manifest through a sequence (krama).

The term *locana* is a bahuvrīhi compound meaning "that whose sequence (*krama*) cannot be correctly perceived. It refers to that which possesses the activity of illuminating (*uddyotana-vyāpāra*). Because of the proximity of the word *dhvani*, its status as being intended as the primary subject matter and its orientation toward something else is implied here; thus, it was not explicitly stated by [the author] himself.
"Of the resonance" (dhvaneḥ) means "of the suggested meaning" (vyaṅgyasya).
"The self" (ātman) [means...].

In the preceding verse, the distinction of the suggested (vyaṅgya) was stated by way of the expressed (vācya); now, however, [the distinction] is stated by way of the function of manifestation (dyotana-vyāpāra), meaning that the manifested (dyotya) rests solely within its own self. Anticipating the question, "What is the sequence regarding the manifestation of the suggested—of which the essence is resonance (dhvani)—within its own self? he says: "in relation to the expressed meaning" (vācyārthāpekṣayā).
The expressed meaning consists of the determinants (vibhāva) and so forth. // 2 //
Regarding the word "therein" (tatra): it means "from between those two.
That very object which consists of rasa and so forth is the non-sequential (akrama) soul of dhvani; however, it is not merely non-sequential itself.
For its sequential nature also occurs at times;
and it will be stated later that in such cases there is a distinction consisting of the resonance (*anusvāna*) arising from the power of the object.
The word *ātman* signifies intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and expresses a mode.
Therefore, that object which is rasa and so forth is a variety of dhvani called "the non-sequential" (akrama);
that is to say, it is "that in which the sequence is imperceptible.
Now, is the object consisting of rasa and so forth always a type of dhvani?
He says "no"; rather, it is that which appears as the *aṅgin*, that is, as the predominant element.

To the question, "Why was this not stated in the general definition under the phrase 'whose own meaning has been made subordinate' (*aguṇīkṛtasvārtha*)?", he replies with the words beginning "the word *dhvani*," etc.
[The phrase] "as being intended to be expressed" (*vivakṣitābhidheyatvena*).
The meaning is: "by stating that the intended object is the denotation.
Regarding the word "here" (atra), the meaning is: "in the denotation" (abhidheye).
"Projected" (ākṣipta) means "shown. He states the distinction with the words "by the preceding verse," and so forth.
"Right now" means in this verse.
"Abiding solely within itself" means...
The phrase "the distinction has been stated" is to be supplied [from the previous context].
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the explanation of the phrase "the soul of *dhvani*" is given by "for the sake of the primary [meaning]," and so forth.
He introduces the passage beginning with "the expressed meaning" (*vācyārtha*) with the words "of the suggested" (*vyaṅgyasya*), and so forth. // 2 //

In the verse beginning with "rasa," the connection must be stated as follows: "The rasa, bhāva, and so forth, appearing as the primary element (aṅgin), exists as an essence whose sequence is unperceived.
And thus, the meaning established is that such a general category of rasa, bhāva, and so forth is one in which the sequence is imperceptible (asaṃlakṣyakrama).
Yet, that meaning is contradicted.

Since it has been accepted in some cases that even the manifestation of an emotion (*bhāva*) and so forth possesses a perceptible sequence (*saṃlakṣyakrama*), he explains the intended meaning with the words "that which is rasa, etc. and so on.
"Without sequence" (*akrama*) means having an imperceptible sequence (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*); it does not mean that it is literally devoid of sequence (*akrama*).
The meaning is that it is by no means the case that rasa, bhāva, and so forth are entirely devoid of sequence.
To the question "Why?", he says: "krameti" (regarding sequence).
The sense is that they also possess a discernible sequence (*saṃlakṣyakramatva*).
The reading in some manuscripts is "kramavattvam" (possessing succession). [This refers to] that which begins with existence (bhāva) and so forth. It will be explained [later].
The meaning is that [the author] will speak, preceded by the example beginning with "When the divine seer had spoken thus," and so forth.

The phrase "appearing as the primary element" (*aṅgibhāvena bhāsamāna*) is explained by the words "as the primary element" (*aṅgitvena*), etc. He anticipates the objection of redundancy regarding this statement with the words "And that," and so forth.
In that regard:
The sequence beginning with rasa, bhāva, their semblances (ābhāsa), and their pacification (praśānti),
exists as the soul of dhvani, established by appearing through the relationship of whole and part.

The essence of *dhvani*, appearing through the relationship of primary and subordinate elements, is established as consisting of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the emotion (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), their pacification (*tatpraśānti*), and so forth, which are non-sequential in nature.
Although the *Locana* has already been examined,
it has nevertheless been restated here to provide an occasion for elucidating the figures of speech such as *rasavat* and others;
and that *dhvani*, consisting of rasa and so forth, remains firmly established.
For there is no poetry whatsoever that is devoid of that [rasa].

And although all poetry lives solely by means of rasa, nevertheless, due to some particular factor acting as its cause, that rasa— though its very nature is a singular, concentrated aesthetic wonder (camatkāra)— becomes an even more intense wonder.

In this regard, when a certain transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) reaches an intensified state and becomes the cause of an extraordinary aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*), then there is the suggestion of emotion (*bhāvadhvani*).

For example: "She might remain hidden by her power out of the force of anger, yet she does not stay angry for long; she might even fly away to heaven, but her heart remains moist with affection for me."
Even the enemies of the gods are not able to seize her while she stands before me; yet she has become utterly beyond the range of my eyes—what manner of fate is this?

For here, even though the sentiment of separation (vipralambha-rasa) is present, there is a superior aesthetic relish (āsvādātiśaya) produced by the wonder of the transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) known as "doubt" (vitarka).
Transitory emotions possess three characteristics: arising, persistence, and passing away.
As it has been said: "They are called transitory because they move in various ways toward [the dominant emotion]."

In that regard, [the action] occasioned by the state of rising may sometimes occur, as follows: "When the reversal of the lineage reached the path of her hearing while she was on her bed, she contemplated turning over and again resolved to begin [it]. Bālapriyā avoids [this objection] with the words beginning "tathāpi" (nevertheless).
Regarding the phrase "rasavad-ādi":
the sense is that since it was stated [previously] that [the figures] appear as subordinate members (*aṅga*), a question may arise as to what the manner is when they appear as such;
thus, the intention is to explain the word "established" (*vyavasthita*) with the words beginning "And that... (*sa ca*).

"Established" (vyavasthita) means existing everywhere in poetry. With the words beginning with "bhāva," he establishes the suggestion of emotion (bhāva-dhvani) and so forth, preceded by a doubt— beginning with "even though" (yadyapi), etc.
"Of that" means "of that which is born from poetry. The connection is with the words "parts of rasa."
The meaning is that he becomes a constituent part of the aesthetic flavor (rasa).
"He should remain" is a statement by Purūravas in the *Vikramorvaśīya*.
That Urvaśī,
due to the cause of her anger,
was concealed— rendered invisible— by means of her power, specifically through the science of invisibility.
The suffix *liṅ* in "tiṣṭhet" (*should remain*) expresses possibility.
Here, the ellipsis "this is not appropriate because... is to be understood; the same applies in subsequent instances as well.
"For heaven" means for the purpose of going to heaven. "Enemies of the gods" refers to the asuras. "Beyond the range" means being outside the scope of their perception.
"The method" refers to the manner in which he spoke.
The intention is that by the word "various" (*vividha*), its threefold nature is also shown.
"Produced by the state of arising" (*udayāvasthāprayukta*) means produced by the tendency toward arising (*udayaunmukhya*).
Regarding the word *yāta*:
by the slender-limbed woman who had reached the bed and was lying with her beloved,
there was a reversal of the *gotra*— that is, the name— which meant she uttered the name of another woman.
When it has entered the path of hearing— that is, when it has been heard—
its "turning over" (parivartana) has been meditated upon and contemplated; that is,
[it has been contemplated] as something to be undertaken.

The word "parivartanam" (turning away) is to be supplied here, or the word "tat" (that) is to be brought down [from the previous verse]. With her single arm-line slackened and cast aside, the slender-limbed woman repeatedly attempted to turn the gaze [of her lover] back toward her natural state and what she had done; yet, she was not able to pull the weight of her breasts away from the chest of her beloved.

For here, the very state of remaining [in anger] due to the desire to rise up from the lover’s pique—rather than having actually departed—is what constitutes the lifeblood of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*), because it precludes any opportunity for that anger to manifest.
Furthermore, its persistence has been illustrated by the verse beginning with "tiṣṭet kopavaśāt" (she might remain under the sway of anger).
However, in some instances, the charm produced by the subsided state of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) is also employed.
As was previously cited: "On a single bed, by turning away from one another.
This is said to be its *praśama* (subsidence).
Here, it can also be applied that there is a *praśama* of the rasa of *īrṣyā-vipralambha* (love-in-separation through jealousy).
In some cases, even a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) becomes the very object of aesthetic relish (*carvaṇā*) through its integration;
for example: "O beautiful one, I have kissed you repeatedly, by which [act] I have recognized you as being like a cluster of nectar-juices."

In this context, when the anger spoken of in the scripture occurred, he who kissed the face of her whose voice was faltering with the turbidity of rage and who was weeping softly, by him the satisfaction of a succession of restful sips of the essence of nectar was known; thus, the junction of anger and grace is a locus of aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), or rather, it is a source of excellence. Furthermore, again and again... [bālapriyā]... may there be a removal of that [defect]. Once more, however... [punarapi punastu].
"Commenced" means that which was accepted as intended to be done. "Again" refers to its reversal. "The subject at hand" means that which has been made the object of effort.
Regarding the phrase "and done":
the words "that" and "furthermore" are to be supplied to these two.
She was one by whom a single line of her arm—first slackened (made loose) and subsequently cast elsewhere—was thus disposed.
Furthermore, that transformation has been accomplished and performed;
the sequence here is demonstrated as: one knows, desires, exerts effort, and acts.
"But not," [it is said].
The word "but" (tu) indicates a distinction.
The syntactical connection is: "the weight of her breasts was not able to drag away the lover's chest."
This verse was explained by Pratihārendurāja in his commentary on the *Kāvyālaṅkārasaṅgraha*:
"By the mere desire to rise;
that is, by the state of being oriented toward rising."
He explains the meaning of the particle *eva* with the words "but not," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "it has been said," the word "by the predecessors" (*pūrvaiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
He states his own intention with the words "here," and so forth. Regarding "osuru":
it refers to one by whom the face of [a woman] adorned with tears of jealousy has been kissed.
By that, the satisfaction of those who have swallowed the essence of nectar was known.
Thus it appears to be an *chāyā* (shadow/analogy).
In the case of verbs meaning "swallowing" or "eating," the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is used in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in the example:
"Fire is not satiated by wood," and so forth.
In this context, "iti" refers to what was stated in the scripture.
Even though it is expressed by the word "envy" (īrṣyā), its place of rest is [the nectar].

Alternatively, the "swallowings preceded by resting" (viśrāntipūrvakāṇi nigaraṇāni) refer to swallowings after having rested again and again (viśramya viśramya nigaraṇāni) within the essence of nectar.

The phrase ending with "jñāta" (known) is the statement of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*). The remainder is that the "junction of anger and favor" is suggested (*dhvanyamāna*) as residing in the heroine.
In some cases, the very state of being variegated by other conflicting emotions (*vyabhicārin*) constitutes the point of rest (*viśrāntipada*). For example:

"Where is the improper act of the moon-crested one, and where is my lineage? Yet she may be seen once more; alas, my learning was for the sake of quelling my faults! Even in anger, her face is lovely. What will those sinless ones of pure intellect say [of me]? She is difficult to obtain even in a dream. O heart, attain composure! What fortunate youth indeed shall drink from her lower lip? In this verse, the various conflicting emotions—such as shame, longing, pride, fear, and dejection—are so intensely intermingled that they themselves provide the final resting place for the sentiment of love-in-separation (*vipralambha-śṛṅgāra*). This is because the primary emotion (*sthāyibhāva*), which is the essence of the sentiment, is not directly expressed here. Rather, it is suggested through the power of the poetic suggestion (*vyañjanā*) arising from the mutual conflict and the ultimate resolution of these subordinate emotions. Thus, the variegation of the conflicting emotions serves as the very locus of aesthetic repose.

For here, initial application (vitarka), sustained application (vicāra), joy (prīti), happiness (sukha), discernment (mati), mindfulness (smṛti), doubt (śaṅkā), dejection (dainya), steadfastness (dhṛti), and reflection (cintana) exist in pairs as mutually opposing and counteracting factors;
yet, in the end, they all grant primacy to reflection alone, which becomes the locus of supreme aesthetic relish (paramāsvāda).
Other cases should be inferred in this same manner.
These [types of suggestion], such as suggestion through the commingling of excitants (*udbhāvana*) and junctures (*sandhi*), are included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the verse.

Now, one might object: "In this way, since a further aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) is observed even by way of the suggestiveness of excitants (*vibhāva-dhvani*) and the suggestiveness of ensuants (*anubhāva-dhvani*), these too ought to be mentioned.
Do not say so; for excitants and ensuants are, by their very nature, directly denotable by their own words.
Since even that relishing (*carvaṇā*) culminates only in mental modifications (*cittavṛtti*), there is nothing more to be relished than the aesthetic moods (*rasa*) and emotional states (*bhāva*).
But when even the determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*) are themselves suggested (*vyaṅgya*), why is the suggestion of a fact (*vastudhvani*) not also accepted?

And when from a semblance of a determinant (*vibhāvābhāsa*) there arises the emergence of a semblance of love (*ratyābhāsa*), then [it is as in the verse] "Where is the improper act? (*kvākāryam*): *Bālapriyā*.
This is the speech of Yayāti, who desired the path of the gods:
"The attachment to a Brahmin maiden is an improper act.
Through the two locatives, the mutual non-coexistence of the two is perceived.
By this, extreme impropriety is suggested;
here, there is *vitarka* (speculative thought),
beginning with "once again" (*bhūyo 'pi*), and so forth.
Here, "eagerness" refers to the desire for the pacification— that is, the ultimate destruction— of faults such as negligence and the like.
"Śruta" means the hearing of the scriptures. Here, "mati" refers to the thought beginning with "Aho! and so forth. "Kāntamukha" means her face, which is lovely and captivating.
Regarding this, there is a traditional teaching (smṛti):
"Those whose stains have departed" means those from whom stains—namely, evil conduct—have gone away;
"those whose wisdom is established in well-performed deeds."
Alternatively, those whose intellects (*dhī*) have been made—that is, trained—are the learned (*paṇḍita*).
What will they say?
This is the doubt regarding this matter.
Even in a dream, she—who was never before seen or heard of—is difficult to obtain;
here, there is dejection caused by the failure to attain the desired object.
"O mind," and so forth.
In this regard, there is fortitude;
"Who," and so forth.
"Fortunate" means one who is not like me, unfortunate.
"He will hold it; he will drink it.
Here, the underlying thought is expressed.
Thus he says: "For here," and so forth.

The meaning is that [the emotions] such as *vitarka* (initial thought) and *rati* (pleasure), and so forth, are manifested in succession by the two sentences situated in each respective quarter-verse, beginning with "Where is there any improper act? (*kvākāryam*). They are mutually sublated (*parasparaṃ bādhyeti*).
The meaning is that [the mind] is afflicted by initial mental application (*vitarka*) and so forth, through longing (*autsukya*) and so forth.
The dual endings in "bhavantī" and "dadatī" refer to the two [factors].
Regarding the phrase "of reflection" (*cintāyāḥ*):
The sense is that [this] is manifested by the final sentence. "Where is there an improper act?"— this is an utterance of Yayāti, who was longing for Devayānī.
The "improper act" consists of attachment to a Brahmin girl.
Through the two locatives, the impossibility of the coexistence of these two is perceived;
by this, extreme impropriety is suggested.
Here, there is *vitarka* (initial application of thought);
"once again," and so forth,
refers to *autsukya* (eagerness) here.
For the sake of the pacification— that is, the ultimate destruction— of the faults such as negligence and so forth; "learning" refers to the hearing of the treatises.
Here is the commentary:
"Aho" and so forth.
Her face is lovely, that is, captivating.
Regarding this, there is a traditional teaching (*smṛti*):
"Those whose impurities have departed" means those from whom impurity—that is, misconduct—has gone away; "those whose intellects are fixed on what has been well performed."
Alternatively, those whose intellects (*dhī*) have been made—that is, trained—are the wise (*paṇḍita*).
What will they say?
This is the doubt regarding this point.
Even in a dream, she—who is composed of things never before seen or heard—is difficult to attain;
here, there is dejection caused by the failure to obtain the desired object.
"O mind," and so forth.
In this regard, there is fortitude;
"Who," and so forth.
"Fortunate" means one who is not like me, unfortunate.
"He will hold it; he will drink it.
Here, a reflection is expressed.
Thus he says: "For here," and so forth.
"Initial application of thought, sustained application, happiness," and so forth;
the meaning is that [these] are manifested in sequence by the two statements situated in each individual quarter, beginning with "Where is there an improper act? and so on.
"Mutually sublated" means...
The meaning is that [the mind] is afflicted by initial mental application (*vitarka*) and so forth, through longing (*autsukya*) and so forth.
The dual endings in "bhavantī" and "dadatī" are used because there are two [factors].
Regarding the word "cintāyāḥ":
The sense is that [it refers to] "that which is manifested by the final statement.
He raises an objection incidentally with "But surely... and answers it with "Not so."
"Expressible by their own words" means that they can indeed be denoted by their own respective terms.
"Only within mental fluctuations" means only within the relishings (*carvaṇā*) of mental fluctuations such as love (*rati*) and so forth.
"Why is it not tolerated?"—
the sense is that it is indeed desired.
He defines the "appearance" (ābhāsa) indicated by the phrase "in its appearance" with the words beginning "But when," and so forth.
Regarding "the determinants and consequents," this has been explained in detail in the *Rasagaṅgādhara* and other works.
Regarding "from a semblance of the determinants":
When the excitant (*vibhāva*) appears as a semblance (*ābhāsa*), the ensuant (*anubhāva*) also becomes a semblance.
He raises an objection with the words "even though" (*yadyapi*).
[The *Locana* explains: "Because the excitants and ensuants appear as semblances, the relish (*carvaṇā*) is a semblance; thus, this is the domain of the semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*)."
For example, upon hearing the poetry of Rāvaṇa, there is a semblance of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*).
Although the Sage [Bharata] defined it thus: "That which is an imitation of the erotic is the comic (*hāsya*)," nevertheless, the status of the comic rasa in that instance occurs only subsequently.
When his name reaches my ears, it acts like a spell for summoning from afar and deluding; my mind does not remain still for even a moment of time without it.
In this case, however, there is no occasion for the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of humor (*hāsya*).

Now, one might object: "But surely there is no erotic emotion (*rati*) as a permanent mood (*sthāyibhāva*) here, because there is an absence of mutual attachment; by whom was it said that this is *rati*?"
For that is merely a semblance of passion;
because it is a semblance, the realization that "Sītā is indifferent toward me or even hostile" does not touch his heart at all. For if it did touch him, even his desire for her would dissolve.
Nor was it done out of the delusion caused by passion with the certainty that "she is attached to me.

For this very reason, its status as a semblance (*ābhāsa*) is established there in reality, like the semblance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell. And thus, the Sage has described it by the term "imitation of the erotic sentiment" (*śṛṅgārānukṛti*). This is [the meaning of] *bālapriyā*.

And thus, the sense is that it is logical to speak of the comic rasa (*hāsya-rasa*) in that context. "Arising at a subsequent time" means occurring after the aesthetic relish (*carvaṇa*) of the erotic rasa (*śṛṅgāra*).

The meaning is that after the savoring (*carvaṇa*) of that [poetic suggestion], the sentiment of laughter—supported by Rāvaṇa’s longing and so forth—is awakened in the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*), because they perceive that he desires her while she is unattached to him. Regarding the word "dūra" (far):

the second half-verse is as follows: "I do not clearly understand how one who is thus agitated by these limbs, whose passion is shattered and who is tormented by the bodiless god of love, could ever attain the bliss of union with her."
In the phrase "prakuruta," there is also a reading "prasahata. The simile is: "in that mantra which effects drawing from afar and delusion.
By this, the non-deviation [of the power] regarding drawing from afar and so forth is illuminated.

In that name, "Sītā," by these limbs afflicted— that is, rendered agitated and overwhelmed— by the god of love, his delight was shattered and lost; he was one whose taste for other objects of sense had vanished.
Regarding the phrase "of one who has fallen into discontent," the word "to me" (me) is to be supplied as far as that point.
"Not for him" means that the word "at the beginning" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
However, the intended meaning is that there is only the relishing of a semblance of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārābhāsa).
"By whom?"—the grammatical connection is: "By whom was this 'delight' (rati) spoken?
Here, the delight that is being perceived is simply a mental state (cittavṛtti) in the form of longing.
The meaning is that it is not a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*). For that is a semblance of passion (*ratyābhāsa*); "that" refers to the mental state consisting of the longing residing in Rāvaṇa.
"Appearing as joy" means appearing as the stable emotion (sthāyibhūta) of love (*rati*).
"And for this reason" means by the reason that will be stated below.
Toward this Rāvaṇa, who is within my domain,
she is indifferent, possessing equanimity;
she is hostile, possessing hatred.
Regarding "tatsparśe": it refers to the touch that produces such a cognition. Regarding "tasya": it refers to Rāvaṇa.
Regarding "na ca": [it means] not.
*Kṛtam* is a particle expressing negation.
The meaning is "no," in the sense that there is an absence of the certainty that "she is attached to me";
rather, it implies that such certainty does indeed exist.
He states the reason for this with the words beginning "kāma" and so forth.
There is also a reading "niścayena kṛtya"; in that case, the syntactical connection is "na ka kṛtyam" (there is nothing to be done).
The meaning is that there is no purpose in such a certainty.
The point is that this certainty is useless for generating desire.

Therefore, it should be understood that the phrase "due to delusion and so forth arising from lack of desire" in the *pakṣa* (the prima facie view) is connected precisely with the words "it does not touch at all."
For this very reason— that is, for the reason already stated—
there is the appearance of that, namely the appearance of passion (*rati-ābhāsatva*),
in that mental state of Rāvaṇa which consists of longing.
"It is established" means it is established by those who practice; the word "pratipattṛbhiḥ" (by practitioners) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Employing the term 'imitation of the erotic' (*śṛṅgārānukṛti*)" means...
The meaning is that "the imitation of the erotic" (śṛṅgāra) is what is called the "comic" (hāsya). By using [this term], the Sage, employing the word *prayuñjāna*, has also indicated this.
For "imitation," "non-primacy," and "semblance" (ābhāsa) have one and the same meaning.

For this very reason, even when desire is restricted to one [of the two parties], its designation by the term "erotic" (śṛṅgāra) in various instances should be understood as being merely a semblance (ābhāsa) of it.
Through the erotic, even the heroic and other sentiments are characterized only by their semblance-form.

Thus, these varieties beginning with the suggestion of emotion (bhāvadhvani) are the outflow (niṣyanda) of the suggestion of rasa itself; having divided this primary constituent factor in aesthetic relish, they are established separately.

Just as those skilled in the art of perfumery, even when experiencing a fragrance in which many essences have merged into a single flavor, perceive it as "this is the pure scent arising from the application of jasmine and other ingredients," so too is the resonance of rasa (*rasadhvani*). It is that very excellence of aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) produced by the savoring of the latent emotion (*sthāyin*)—which has been manifested through the combination of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*)—for the spectator who primarily perceives the latent emotion therein.

For example: "Having with difficulty passed between her two thighs, and having wandered for a long time upon the region of her hips, she has come to a standstill at her waist, which is uneven with the waves of her three folds."
My gaze, like one parched with thirst, having now ascended to her high breasts, looks repeatedly and longingly at her eyes which trickle with drops of water.

For here, the meaning is that the King of Vatsa [is moved] by beholding the picture-board purified by his own likeness, which is being described as having the form of the heroine; thus "Bālapriyā" is one such meaning.
The words "anukṛti" and so forth are synonyms—this is the sense.
[The phrase] "by means of the erotic sentiment" (śṛṅgāreṇa) [is used].
The phrase "an imitation of the erotic" (śṛṅgārānukṛti) means by means of the word "erotic" (śṛṅgāra) as it occurs in the statement of the Sage [Bharata].
Regarding "of the heroic and so forth":
for these [rasas], there is indeed a semblance when they have elders and the like as their objective supports (ālambana).
He summarizes with the words "In this way," and so forth.
To the question, "How then is there a distinct conventional usage?", he says, "The relish.
The syntactical connection is: "Having thus divided the principal motivating factor into its constituent parts."

"It is established separately" means [established] in a distinct form, such as being a sound of flavor (rasadhvani) or a sound of existence (bhāvadhvani), and so forth. Regarding this, he states an illustration: "just as," and so on.
"Gandhayukti" is the compounding of fragrant substances. "Eka" means a single flavor; even in that [experience], which is the enjoyment of a blended and pervasive fragrance.
It is a specific aromatic substance derived from meat.
The word "iti" (thus) is to be construed with the phrase "is established separately. [The term] "vibhāvya" means...

The realization of the permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) has arisen— that is, it has been produced— from the savoring of that [emotion] through the conjunction of the three, beginning with the transitory emotions (*vibhāva*).
"With difficulty" refers to this statement by the King to the Vidūṣaka in the *Ratnāvalī*.
The word "of her" (asyāḥ) is connected with the five [verses] beginning with "the pair of thighs.

The three folds themselves are the waves; that is, the three folds are like waves. By means of that, she is uneven—having depressions and elevations. She is "as if thirsty," meaning as if due to thirst.
"Jalalavāḥ" means drops of tears; "tatprasyandinī" should be understood as "flowing forth in that manner," as if written.
