The phrase "being relished" (carvyamāṇena) [is explained as follows].
The meaning is: "by way of being the object of aesthetic relish (carvaṇā) for those with sensitive hearts.

Regarding the term *alaṅkāra* (ornament): the meaning is that it is an ornament by virtue of embellishing the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which consists of the power of the king who is the subject of description.

He establishes what was stated with the words "For not," and so forth. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "This sentence-meaning, being thus unadorned, is not indeed like that [other one]."
Regarding the phrase "and in beauty":
the meaning is "and the beauty of the sentence-meaning.

He establishes with an example that [beauty] is produced solely by the rasa of pathos (karuṇa), using the passage beginning with "by the moon, etc. and ending with "what contradiction? to provide the justification.
Regarding the phrase "it is adorned": the ellipsis is to be supplied as "in the poem beginning with 'Her whose face is beautiful like the moon'. He raises an objection with "But surely... (nanu).
He states a counter-objection with "then" (tarhi). He provides the answer with "surely" (nanu).
He provides an equal answer with "even by means of taste" (rasenāpi).
"Sarasīkriyate" means it is made flavorful;
"svasaṃvedyam" means established through the experience of those with aesthetic sensitivity (sahṛdaya);
"tena" refers to that [flavor].
The meaning is "by the reason that will be stated. "That" means "the objection."

Regarding the term *anabhyupagama* (non-acceptance): the meaning is that [the opponent's view] has been refuted on the grounds of not accepting that the *vibhāva* and other factors are the objects of ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*). To the question "In that case, what is the object of ornamentation?", he says: "Of the subject matter at hand," and so forth.

Regarding the "present subject" (*prastutārtha*), which is the intended or relevant matter: in passages such as "What is the use of laughter? and so forth, the majesty of the king is made known by means of describing the conduct of the enemy's women—which serves as the cause for making known the destruction of their beloved. Thus, that [majesty] alone is the present subject; this should be understood similarly in other cases as well.

"Because it is so designated" means because it was demonstrated by the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*). An example of a mixed subordinate sentiment (*rasa*), etc., is as follows: "Seized by the hand, he pushed away; violently struck, he still clung to the hem of her garment; pulled back by his hair, he fell at her feet; yet she did not even look at him."
With agitation, he shows that "the eye" signifies true reality by saying "thus. The meaning is:
such as that in which the majesty of a king or similar authority is proclaimed.
Regarding the term "cast aside" (*kṣipta*): in the context of those who desire, it means disregarded;
in the other context, it means shaken off (*dhuta*).
"He is not desired as an *avadhūta* (an ascetic who has shaken off worldly ties); he is cast aside," and so forth, as found in the *Amaruśataka*.

That Śāmbhava [fire], pertaining to Śambhu, occurring at the time of the burning of Tripura—may that Śāmbhava fire of the arrow, which was embraced by the young women of Tripura whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears like a lover who has committed a fresh offense, burn away your sins.

In this case, since the excellence of the power of the Enemy of Tripura constitutes the meaning of the sentence, the *īrṣyā-vipralambha* (love-in-separation through jealousy), together with the *śleṣa*, functions as a subordinate element (*aṅga*).
Such indeed is the proper domain for figures of speech such as *rasavat*.
For this very reason, because the *īrṣyā-vipralambha* and the *karuṇa* (pathetic) sentiments are established as subordinate elements, their coexistence is not a defect.
He was made fragile by embracing Locanā, while elsewhere he was rendered so by the shaking of all his limbs;
he possessed tears in one place out of jealousy, and in another out of despair.

By this comparison, "like a lover," which is supported by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), the *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation through jealousy) that is evoked becomes a subordinate element (*aṅga*) when accompanied by *śleṣa* and *upamā*, but not when standing alone.

Although the rasa of *karuṇa* (pathos) is indeed present here as a reality, it does not function toward the perception of that [primary] beauty; with this intention, he said simply "accompanied by *śleṣa*," and did not [say otherwise].
The phrase "of that which is accompanied by desire" (*kāmasahitasya*) is also [to be understood].
In order to strengthen this meaning, which has been conceived as something previously unknown (*apūrva*), he says: "of such a kind alone" (*evaṃvidha eva*).
And for this very reason (*ata eva*).
The meaning is: because in this case, the *vipralambha* (separation) is a poetic ornament (*alaṅkāra*) and not the primary sense of the sentence (*vākyārtha*),
for that reason there is no fault.
For if there were predominance of one rasa, a second rasa would not enter into it.

However, *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) has *rati* as its dominant emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) and is therefore a state of dependence; it is indeed opposed to *karuṇa* (the pathetic), which has *śoka* (sorrow) as its dominant emotion and is a state of independence.

Thus, having established the connection through the context of the word "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*), the *Bālapriyā* explains the syntactical relation as: "May the arrow-fire [of Śiva] burn away your sin.
Who is he? He is one whose offense is fresh, having arisen from that [very moment], like a lover who has his hand firmly clasped [by the beloved].

The construction is as follows: "by those Tripura maidens whose lotus-eyes were filled with tears," and so forth. Regarding that, he explains the meaning of the word *kṣipta* (cast) with the words beginning with *kāmī*.
As for the phrase "in the other [case]":
The meaning is "in the case of the arrow and fire.
He himself demonstrates the status of being a subordinate element (*aṅgabhāva*) as stated in the *Vṛtti* with the words beginning "like a lover" (*kāmīva*), etc.
"Drawn forth" (*ākṛṣṭaḥ*) means clearly manifested (*sphuṭa-vyañjita*).
The explanation of the phrase "of that [deception] accompanied by envy" is "śleṣa," etc. Regarding the term "being an auxiliary":

The meaning is that [the sentence] functions as a subordinate member (*aṅgatva*) with respect to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), which consists of the excellence of the power of the Enemy of Tripura.
Regarding the phrase "not of the isolated," it is to be construed with the two preceding words: "its subordinate status" (*tasyāṅgatvam*).
The meaning is that compassion (*karuṇa*) is also a rasa,
and thus it should also be stated that [the term] "accompanied by that" applies to it as well.
"That" refers to [compassion].

The meaning is "compassion" (*karuṇa*). And that [compassion] does not function for the sake of perceiving beauty— that is, for the sake of perceiving the beauty of the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
The meaning is that here, compassion does not function as a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation).
He explains "for this very reason" with the words beginning with "since," etc.
[He says] "the sense of the sentence."
The meaning is that primacy belongs to that which is to be embellished. "Of either one" refers to either of the two, namely, the *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) or the *karuṇa* (pathetic) rasa.
"Preeminence" means equal preeminence. "The second" means that one is distinct from the other of those two.
"One should not combine" means that they should not be combined within a single poetic work; this is the ellipsis. He states the reason for this with the words beginning "rasa" (rasa-ityādi).
This subject will be discussed in the third chapter (*udyota*).
The verse beginning with "In rasa... (*rase*) and so forth is an introductory verse (*parikaraśloka*).

Regarding that, as for the phrase "of all ornaments" (*sarvāsām alaṅkṛtīnām*): how can there be the status of an ornament (*alaṅkāratva*) in a case where *rasa* constitutes the primary meaning of the sentence?
For it is well known that an ornament is the cause of beauty;
however, the self cannot be the cause of its own beauty.
Thus, the summary here is as follows: [the function of an ornament] consists in being arranged by relying upon the primary intent of rasa, bhāva, and so forth.
The establishment of the status as an ornament for all ornaments.
Regarding what was stated—that the *Locana* is of such a nature—he explains the intention of the particle *eva* therein with the words "for where... [and so on].
This refers to all [figures] beginning with simile (*upamā*).

The meaning is as follows: whatever status belongs to figures such as simile in their capacity as ornaments (*alaṅkāra*), that very same status belongs to the aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) and the like.
Therefore, there must necessarily be something else to be embellished.

And although that may be a mere fact (*vastumātra*), nevertheless, because it ultimately results in the form of the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, its purport lies solely in rasa and the like; thus, in every case, the very essence is the suggestion of rasa (*rasadhvani*).
Thus it is said: "the focus on rasa, bhāva, and so forth.
Regarding the word "of that" (tasya):
it refers to the principal [element], which is the very self.

This is what is meant: although by means of a simile the expressed meaning (vācyārtha) is adorned, nevertheless its true ornamentation consists solely in the conferring of the capacity to manifest the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha). Thus, in reality, it is the essence of suggestion (dhvani) alone that is the object of adornment.

For even by means of bracelets, armlets, and the like—which are inherent in the body—it is the conscious self (ātman) itself that is adorned, by virtue of indicating the appropriateness of various particular mental states (cittavṛtti).
For instance: since there might be a misconception of the meaning that "insentient things" refers to the ornaments such as *rasavat* and so forth, he explains: "of the *upamā* [simile] and so forth.
This means "of the *upamā* and so forth, and of the *rasavat* and so forth. Intending to introduce the passage beginning with "in the case of rasa and bhāva," he says: "this is the sense," and so on.
"Of what kind is the report?
means "what is the reason"; and that [reason] is the preparation by another.
The phrase "and that" means "and that which is to be embellished.
The term "mere fact" (vastumātra) refers to this.
As in "What is the use of laughter? and so forth, [the cause is] the power of the king and the like.
"Of that" means "of the object."
Regarding the phrase "of rasa-dhvani": this means "of dhvani consisting of rasa, bhāva, and so forth.

In passages such as "What is the use of laughter?", the sentiment of love (rati-bhāva) directed toward the king who is the subject of description is indeed present within the speaker; manifested by its power, it constitutes the primary element.
"By means of comparison" means by means of comparison and so forth.
"Of that" [refers to the aforementioned].
The meaning is "of the expressed meaning" (vācyārthasya).
"Of the suggested meaning" (vyaṅgyārthe) means "of rasa and so forth."

When various expressed meanings (*vācyārtha*) are described through figures of speech such as simile (*upamā*), they are rendered more excellent and clearly manifest a particular state of mind (*cittavṛttiviśeṣa*) residing in one of the two [the speaker or the listener], just as a poet does; in some cases, they also suggest another meaning (*arthāntara*). Thus, the meaning is that "ornamentation" (*alaṅkāra*) is the act of the expressed meaning—by means of figures like simile—bestowing the capacity to manifest the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*).
This is what is meant by saying it is the "soul of *dhvani*."
The meaning is that the self is of the nature of resonance (*dhvani*).
To illustrate this stated point with a worldly example, he says "bracelet," and so forth;
it is the self alone, not the body.
Regarding how the self is adorned, he says: "tattad" (those various).

Those specific modifications of the mind, such as passion and so forth, which reside in the self—by way of indicating their propriety (*aucitya*), that is, by having the nature of indicating them, these various ornaments indeed indicate for him: "Such a modification of the mind is appropriate for this [self]."

The meaning is that it indicates [the state of affairs] through the following: just as necklaces, bracelets, earrings, and so forth, when located on the bodies of young people, are appropriate for passion (*rāgitva*), whereas staffs, ochre robes, and so forth, when located on the bodies of ascetics, are appropriate for dispassion (*vairāgya*);
[the author] establishes this stated point with the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and so on.
Therefore, wherever rasa and the like constitute the primary sense of the sentence (*vākyārthībhūta*), all such instances are not the domain of alaṅkāra (ornament) in the form of rasa and the like.
That is a variety of *dhvani*, and its poetic ornaments (*alaṃkāra*) are simile (*upamā*) and the like;
however, where the production of beauty is effected by *rasa* and so forth through the primary status of another meaning as the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), [that is *dhvani*].
That [sentiment] is the domain for the status of rasa and so forth as ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
Thus, there is a distinct separation of domains between *dhvani*, the *upamā* and other figures, and the *rasavat* ornament.

However, if it is argued that the domain of the *rasa* and other ornaments consists in their becoming the primary meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) among sentient beings, [the Locana replies]: "Even a corpse does not shine, even if it is adorned with earrings and the like."
Because there is an absence of anything to be adorned;
a body of an ascetic, when joined with bracelets and other ornaments, becomes a source of laughter due to the inappropriateness of the object being adorned.
For there is nothing inherently improper about the body; in reality, the self alone is that which is to be adorned, because of the conceit "I am adorned.
The two genitive cases in the phrase "of the sentiment (rasa) and so forth being ornaments" are in different grammatical relations (vyadhikaraṇa).
That which constitutes the state of being an ornament (alaṅkāratā) for rasa and so forth, that alone is its [the ornament's] domain.
Following this very principle, it should also be applied to the previous sentence:
"the domain of the act of ornamenting, whose agent is rasa and so forth."
"Thus" means by the classification of objects as stated by us.
"Of similes and so forth" [means...]

Where rasa is the object of embellishment (alaṅkārya) and there is no other rasa present as a subordinate element (aṅga), there similes (upamā) and the like remain purely as such; thus, the meaning is that there is no deprivation of their domain by means of "conjunction" (saṃsṛṣṭi). By the phrase "and of the *rasavat* ornament," the ornaments of emotion (*bhāva*) and so forth—namely *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita*—are also included.
"Because there is no one to be adorned"—
the meaning is that the corpse is insentient. By this, it is established that it is only a sentient being who is adorned.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the ascetic’s body" and so forth:
ornaments such as bracelets and the like suggest a state of passion.
Since passion is inappropriate for an ascetic and for the self, the meaning is that bracelets and other such items on the body of an ascetic bring about ridicule.

The meaning is this: when bracelets, earrings, and so forth, which reside in the bodies of various sentient beings, serve as ornaments for those very beings because they are appropriate to their particular mental states such as passion—indicated by the needle—their status as ornaments is established; otherwise, they would merely provoke laughter.
This is the intended sense.
He also states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of experience, beginning with "I," and so forth.
The point is that [the genitive case] is used in a non-co-referential sense (*vyadhikaraṇa*), and not in a co-referential sense (*samānādhikaraṇa*) within those two words.
He explains [the passage] with the words "of rasa and so forth" (*rasādeḥ*). The meaning is as follows:

that which is the state of being an ornament (*alaṅkāratā*) residing in rasa and so forth—that is, the quality of being the agent of ornamentation, or rather, the act of ornamentation performed by rasa and so forth—is precisely its object (*viṣaya*). This is the connection [of the sentence].
The word "sa" (that) is a reference back to one who abides in the practice; it is a restatement of "wherein," meaning "that poetry. "Viṣaya" means the locus or substratum.
Regarding the phrase "in the previous [passage]":

the meaning is that all of that is not the domain of figures of speech such as *rasa* (flavor) and so forth; this refers to the sentence. He states the connection with the words "rasādi" (and so forth).
In this sentence as well, "sa" (he/it) is a reference back to "yatra" (wherein).
He shows the scope of similes and the like, which is distinct from that of the *rasavat* figures and so forth, starting with "yatra" etc.
[He says] "saṃsṛṣṭya" (by being combined).
The meaning is "by means of the combination of *rasavat* and so forth.
This is a detailed explanation of the phrase "the *bhāva* and other ornaments"—namely, *preyas*, *ūrjasvin*, and *samāhita*.
There is also a variant reading: "and *samāhita* and so forth."

When a *bhāva* (emotional state) is not subordinate to another [element], it is the ornament of *bhāva* (*bhāvālaṅkāra*); that very same [ornament] is called "the charming" (*preyas*) or "the beloved" (*preyān*).
When *rasābhāsa* (semblance of rasa) and *bhāvābhāsa* (semblance of bhāva) are not subordinate to another, they constitute the "energetic" (*ūrjasvī*).

Regarding that, an example of the pure *bhāvālaṅkāra* (the ornament of emotion) is as follows: "O Mother, how did your foot—whose sole is as soft and copper-red as the petals of a hundred-petaled lotus, and which resounds with the tinkling sound of moving golden anklets like those of a swan—attain the weight of a great mountain of gold when it was forcibly placed upon the head of the great demon Mahiṣa?"

Thus, in this hymn to the Goddess (*devīstotra*), since the meaning of the sentence consists of [the sentiment] such as deliberation (*vitarka*) and wonder (*vismaya*), these serve as the cause of its beauty. Because that [sentiment] is subordinate, it is the province of the figure of speech "Sentiment" (*bhāva*). An example of the "semblance of sentiment" (*rasābhāsa*) being a figure of speech is found in my own hymn: "Even if you were adorned by the totality of all excellences (*guṇa*) together with the hosts of ornaments, even then you would not shine."
O Speech, if you could somehow please Śiva, who is dear to your heart, then indeed that very act of yours would become truly extraordinary to all the world.

For here, since the mere praise of the Supreme Lord is the most worthy object of speech, the semblance of the erotic (*śṛṅgārābhāsa*), accompanied by *śleṣa* (paronomasia), is the cause of beauty in the sentence-meaning.

Indeed, this is not a complete erotic sentiment, as it occurs when the heroine lacks both qualities and ornaments. The distinction is that [this] is classified as *samāhita* (composed) because the subsidence of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*) is not subordinate to anything else.
"Of the pure" means:
having been embellished by another ornament.
"Thy" [means...].
"O Mother!
Of you... hundred... and so forth.
A *śatapatra* is a lotus.
His foot— belonging to the great asura named Mahiṣa— had a sole that was soft and coppery like a lotus petal; it was resonant with the sound of an anklet resembling a moving *kalahaṃsa* swan.
Having been forcibly placed upon the head—
that great mountain, Sumeru, which is composed of gold.
By the mention of its being made of gold, an excess of weight is indicated.
The connection is: "How did it attain such heaviness? The sense is that the attainment of this weight is certain from the crushing of the buffalo's head.
"In the *Devīstotra*" means when the majesty of the Goddess is being praised, or when there is a state of aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) directed toward her. "Vitarka" [means]...
The word *katham* (how) indicates *vitarka* (initial thought) and so forth.

Although in this case the purity of *vitarka* and the rest is difficult to establish because they are mixed with the aforementioned similes such as "the hundred-petaled lotus," nevertheless, even if only the phrase "the surface of soft copper" were stated, since *vitarka* and the rest could still occur therein, the simile would not be a constituent part of them; thus, their purity—defined as being unmixed with those [similes]—is easily established.
"Samastā" (all):

having superimposed the status of the heroine (nāyikā) [upon Speech], this is a reply in her own voice. "O Vāṇī! Indeed, you are the abundance of all qualities—both the qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and so forth, and those such as beauty (*saundarya*) and so forth."
Even though the groups of poetic ornaments— such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*), simile (*upamā*), and so forth— as well as [physical ornaments] such as bracelets and the like,
together with their multitudes,
may constitute your adornment; yet...
Nevertheless, you do not shine for us.
To the question, "In that case, how does one come to shine? he says: "Auspicious," and so forth.
You are the beloved of the hearts of all, dear as their very self.
Śiva, the Supreme Lord, who is of auspicious form and most beloved;
"yathā" means in whatever manner or by whatever means— whether through the ornament of poetic prose (gumālaṅkāra-sāhitya) or otherwise.
You should delight [them] by demonstrating your virtues, you should gladden them, and thus you should win their affection.
If that is so, then that very act is indeed the winning of their affection.
The meaning is that these constitute an ornament transcending the entire world.
Here, he explains the semblance (*ābhāsatva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) which is implied: "For indeed" (*na hi*), and so forth; for (*hi*) means because.

If the heroine lacks qualities and is devoid of ornaments, the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) does not reach its fullness; therefore, it might be argued that figures such as simile (*upamā*) would then have either a very restricted scope or no scope at all. For when a sentence has as its primary meaning an event involving an insentient object, some connection with the narrative of a sentient being must somehow be established.

Now, even if that [sentiment] is present, it is said that where there is no realization of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) by insentient objects, that is not the province of the *rasavat* ornament.
In that case, a great poetic composition (*kāvyaprabandha*), which is a repository of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), would be declared to be devoid of flavor (*nīrasa*).
For instance, as stated in the *Locana*: "The nature of the highest hero (*uttamayuvaprakṛti*) consists of a brilliant attire."

An example of the presence of the semblance of a positive entity (bhāvābhāsa) is as follows: "May He protect you—He at whose sight the demons, though remaining after their slaughter, tremble with fear even before the blue-lotus eyes of their own beloveds, which are colored with collyrium of a hue identical to His and endowed with great loveliness."
In this context, the fear that is inappropriate for those of a wrathful nature is caused by the power of the Blessed One; thus, there is a semblance of emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*).
In the same way, its role as a subordinate element (*aṅgatva*) in the pacification of that [emotion] may be illustrated.
By the words "my mind," he introduces the refutation of the opposing view which was indicated, beginning with the words "that which... and so forth.

And the intention of the opponent is this: since insentient objects cannot possess the nature of mental states such as *rasa* (flavor) and so forth, the figure of speech *rasavat* is not even to be considered in their description; therefore, the scope of similes (*upamā*) and other figures is strictly distinct from that.
He refutes this with the words "In that case" (*tahi*).
The meaning is: for that reason, on account of that statement.
Anticipating the objection that it has been stated that the subject matter consists of the description of insentient things, he states the reason with the words "because" (*yasmāt*).
The phrase "in some way or other" (*yathākathaṃcit*) means by way of being the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
The word "in that" (*tasyām*) refers to [the poetic composition].
Regarding the application of the narrative of intention (*cetanāvṛttānta*):
"the state of being flavorless" (*nīrasatvam*).
For it is the opinion of others that wherever there is *rasa*, there must necessarily be the figure of speech *rasavad-alaṅkāra*.

Therefore, when it is said that there is no "sentimental" (rasavat) ornament, the state of being "flavorless" (nīrasa) is stated from the perspective of another's opinion, namely that if the rasavat ornament is absent, then surely there is no rasa there.
However, for us, flavorlessness does not follow merely from the absence of the rasavat ornament; rather, it follows from the absence of rasa which constitutes the very soul of suggestion (dhvani).
And such a rasa indeed exists here;
the meaning is that it is not full,
but rather its nature is a semblance (ābhāsa).
The genitive case in the word *yasya* denotes the "remainder" (*śeṣa*) in relation to the agent.
The phrase *tattulyā* means "equal to the color of the Blessed One."
"Self," and so forth;
the phrase "among those being perceived" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Thus, [it is called] the appearance of existence.

In this context, the meaning is that because fear has become subordinate to the delight manifested by the power of the Blessed One, there is the figure of speech *ūrjasvin*, which is the appearance of an emotion (*bhāvābhāsa*).
By the passage beginning with "yadi tu," he states the implied meaning: "of another," and so forth;
and "in its description," etc.
The meaning is "the description of the insentient.
"That" means "that description."
"Divided" means "described as such"; that is to say, described as insentient.
The construction is "that very [thing]. In the commentary, he raises an objection with "Now," and then says "in that."
The meaning is: "in the application of the account of the objects of volition.
"'Asau' (this)" is a reference back to the word "yatra" (where).
Regarding the phrase "than that great":
"that" means then; "great" means more extensive.

He states in the *Locana*, beginning with "For where... and so forth, that the quality of being flavorless (*nīrasatva*) is not asserted according to his own view, but rather in accordance with the views of others;
thus he says, "rasa" (flavor).
The word "pradhāna" (principal) implies "the meaning of the sentence. The phrase "others say" means the opinion of Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, and others.
"Ours"— so it is said—
that she who has waves for her frowning brows and a row of agitated birds for her girdle, dragging along foam like a garment loosened by passion;
she who moves with many stumbling missteps as if struck, surely that intolerant woman has transformed into the form of this river.

For example— slender, with her lower lip washed as if by tears due to the state of the sprouts being moistened by rainwater from the clouds, appearing empty of ornaments because of the departure of her own season, and with the rising of her flowers at rest; she makes her eyes ripple,
those very ripples being her knitting eyebrows, forcibly drawing away and pulling back that which was lingering.
"Vasana" means a silken garment;
the sense is that it is for the purpose of forbidding her from clinging to her beloved.
"Māninī" (the proud woman) means one who, having reflected upon the many lapses and offenses [committed by him], and having unified them all within her heart, is unable to endure them.
And yet, unable to endure the remorse of separation from me, she has turned into a river to allay her fever. As for the word "slender":
though emaciated by separation and consumed by grief, she casts off her ornaments.
One's own time consists primarily of spring and summer;
this is the remainder [of the meaning].
"Such" refers to that.
The meaning is "that which constitutes the very essence of suggestion.
The word "here" means "in the examples that are about to be stated."
"She causes to wave.
This Urvaśī is "intolerant" (asahanā).
There is also a reading: "in the form of a river," meaning "by way of being a river."
In the poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) expressed by "transformed and unstable," the meaning is:
"This is not a river, but rather that [Ganges]— so I imagine."
He establishes what has been stated with the words beginning "taraṅga" (wave) and so forth:
because of the superimposition of "frowning" and the like upon the waves and so on, there is a metaphor (*rūpaka*);
because of the phrase "like a garment," there is a simile (*upamā*).
"By impetuosity" means by the force of anger; "loose" means with a slackened bond.
"'Yathā'" has the sense of "yataḥ" (from which).
The word "tataḥ" (then) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Āviddham" means crooked;
or alternatively, "yathāviddham" may be taken as a single compound word.
The meaning is "without overstepping crookedness.
Regarding the phrase "aiming at a stumble," in the case of the river, it means "having encountered a stumbling block such as a rock.
"Locane" refers to the waves and so forth.
It should be understood that her girdle is a row of birds agitated in this manner.
Regarding the word "aparādhāḥ" (offenses),
the word "of me" (*mama*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
"Māninī" means one who possesses anger;
that is, one who is intolerant.
The meaning is "due to intolerance" and so forth.
Regarding the word *tanvī* ("slender"),
the phrase "this [woman] before this [man]" is to be supplied.
"This is a creeper;
she is 'Caṇḍī,' exceedingly wrathful.
For that very reason, she has remained standing after shaking off and disregarding me as I fell at her feet."
For this very reason, having become remorseful,
she is perceived as being like Urvaśī; these three metaphors regarding her limbs are expressed by the words "slender" (*tanvī*) and so forth.
"Slender" (*tanvī*) is a quality common to both [the woman and the creeper].
This is the creeper (*latā*).
"The state of having sprouts moistened by masses of clouds" (*meghajālairārdrapallavatā*) refers to the condition of that [creeper] in which the sprouts are wet with the clouds.
She is like one whose lower lip has been washed by tears for that reason;
she is as if devoid of ornaments because the emergence of her flowers has ceased due to separation at its proper time.
He provides the justification for the heroine’s abandonment of ornaments with the word "viyoga" (separation).
The meaning is that she is emaciated by separation and consumed by remorse.
Her anxiety is perceived even without the humming of bees, as if she has resorted to silence; and he, having cast me down at his feet, now appears as if overcome with regret.

Or for example: "O gentle one, I know that the leaves on the vine-cottages along the banks of the Yamunā—those companions to the dalliances of the cowherd women and witnesses to the secret trysts of Rādhā—are now turning withered, their dark luster fading, as the soft utility of their shoots for fashioning beds of love has been severed."
She was silent for the sake of devising a stratagem; she was fierce and wrathful, thinking, "Why have I spurned my beloved even though he has fallen at my feet?
She was *caṇḍī*, one prone to anger.
These two verses, though ostensibly descriptive of a river and a creeper, are in their true intent (tātparya) expressions uttered by Purūravas while overcome by madness.
Regarding the word "teṣām" (of them):
O noble one, "of them" refers to those who reside within my very heart.

Of those who are the companions in dalliance and the jesting confidants of the cowherd women—the *gopīs*—for indeed, no one else can serve as a jesting companion to women who are secretly in love. And he states that Rādhā is the preeminent object of their supreme love: "those who are the direct witnesses of Rādhā’s enjoyments."
"Is it well, is it safe for the vine-cottages on the banks of the Yamunā, the daughter of Mount Kalinda?"—this is the question posed with an interrogative intonation (*kāku*).

Having thus questioned her, Lord Kṛṣṇa, who has returned to Dvārakā, his latent impressions awakened by the sight of the cowherd girls, speaks to himself words filled with longing, his emotion of love (*rati*) aroused by the objective and excitatory factors (*ālambana* and *uddīpana-vibhāva*): "Soft and delicate for the purpose of preparing the couch of Smara—the bed of passion..."

The very act of cutting—that is, the tearing asunder—is the utilization, the fruitfulness; and furthermore, that arrangement—that is, the fashioning—upon the bed of love is itself the soft, delicate, and excellent utility of the cutting, the result of the tearing. When that has been severed, what is the point of arranging a bed of love while I remain seated?
This is the underlying intention (*bhāva*).
For this very reason, he says "they know," which contains within it the certainty of mutual passion;
here, the meaning of the entire sentence functions as the object (*karman*).
Now, in the *Bālapriyā* commentary, it is explained that "without the sounds of the bees" (*madhukṛtāṃ śabdair vinā*) means by the absence of their humming;
thus, this thought is as if she has resorted to silence.
Here, the author explains the heroine's silence in two ways, beginning with "by means of a stratagem" (*upāya*), and so forth.
The means of gathering [beings] is the means [itself].
Regarding the word "of them" (*teṣām*):
he explains that "of them" refers to those who have experienced [the teachings], by saying "those who," and so forth.

"He conceals [himself] by means of the appearance of a cowherd. One who possesses latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—aroused and awakened by the experience of a bower of creepers and the like—is the subject. The three words beginning with "having awakened" (*prabuddhya*) are adverbs modifying the action.
There is also a reading: *prabuddharatibhāva*.
The state of passion is directed toward the gopīs;
"for the sake of imagination" means for the sake of manifestation.
"Having made [it] soft" means "because of its softness.
And he states another meaning: "Now, if... etc.
"Recollection of that" means the sense of it being produced by the upper garment and so forth.
"Arrangement" (kḷpti) means... [text fragment].
The meaning is "scattering.
"Excellent" (*utkṛṣṭa*) is an elaboration of the term "delicate" (*sukumāra*).
He establishes the state of being "severed" (*vicchinnatva*) with the words "in me" (*mayi*).
Precisely for this reason— namely, because of the interruption of the previously mentioned utility—
it is said "mutually" (*paraspara*).

This means that even in cases such as "his own [and] of the gopīs," although inanimate things constitute the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), there is indeed an application of the narrative of sentient beings.
Now, where there is the application of the narrative of a sentient being to an insentient object, there [the figures of speech] such as rasa and so forth are the ornaments.
This being the case, similes (*upamā*) and the like would either have no scope at all or an extremely limited scope;

for there is simply no such instance of an insentient object’s narrative where the application of a sentient being’s narrative does not ultimately exist by virtue of its being a determinant emotion (*vibhāva*).

The meaning is: "Their eyes are becoming aged. However, since I am present, because they are constantly provided with what is useful, these eyes shall never suffer the ruin of being worn out by old age.
By the phrase "their dark luster is fading away," it is suggested that even though he has been away for some time, he is filled with intense longing.
Thus, this statement regarding the self, or rather, this deliberative statement addressed specifically to Gopa,
indicates what was mentioned [previously] as being expressed through many examples from a vast and extensive treatise.
Now, beginning with "atha" and so forth...
The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "lest there be a lack of aesthetic flavor (nīrasatva) here.

Now, one might object: "In cases where there is no way whatsoever for the activity of a conscious being to enter, that will be the domain of simile (upamā) and the like. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because," and so forth. The word "antataḥ" means "ultimately."
Even insentient things such as a pillar or horripilation, when described, necessarily imply sentience because they function as *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions);
what more need be said here?

Even something extremely inert, such as the moon or a garden, though described as being self-contained, must necessarily abandon its status as a mere object and become a *vibhāva* (determinant) for a mental state. This means that mutual love, which is the mutual substratum, has as its very core the certainty of that [love].

The meaning is that in the absence of such certainty, what is about to be said would be inconsistent, because it is possible for those cowherd women to have been enjoying other men [while in the bower].
The word "te" (they) refers to those associated with the vine-cottage.
By the words "becoming hardened" (*jaraṭhībhavanti*) and "becoming decayed" (*jīrṇībhavanti*), he indicates what is understood [from the context], namely: "consisting of me" (*mayī*), and so forth.
Regarding the word "unceasing" (*anavarata*):
it is due to the application (*yogāt*) of that unceasing employment (*upayoga*) already mentioned, which was previously described.
"Nema" means "these are sprouts. "Jarā" means... [old age].

He expresses by means of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*)— as in the word "vigalat" ("dripping")— the state of being worn out by old age, which consists of discoloration and so forth; this is indicated by the phrase "of one who has departed for a few [days]," etc.
The word "of the Blessed One" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Regarding "longing": longing is either yearning or the desire to see.
He states the purpose of providing these three examples with the words beginning "by many," etc. The connection is that [the meaning] is indicated by those three examples.

The term "mahataḥ" (of the great) is a restatement of one who abides in their [proper] conduct (*vṛtti*); its explanation is "bhūyasaḥ" (of the more abundant). Regarding the word "atha" in the verse, its meaning is "yadi" (if).

In this context, the construction is "if there is an ornament such as rasa (flavor) and so forth. He reveals the underlying intention by completing the sense with the words "the state of being devoid of rasa" (*nīrasatvam*).
He introduces the passage beginning with "for" (*yasmāt*) with the word "now" (*nanu*).

The syntactical connection (*vṛttānvaya*) is as follows: "That which, ultimately, lacks any application of the account of a sentient entity as a mode of manifestation (*vibhāvatvena*), is not an account of an insentient entity.
Regarding the phrase "application [of it] as a mode of manifestation ultimately," which was stated in the verse, he states its intended meaning with the words beginning "pillar" (*stambha*).
The construction is as follows: even though that which is being described—such as the bristling of hair on the body—is insentient, it necessarily implies a sentient being;
for, by virtue of making known a particular modification of the mind, it indeed becomes an indicator of a sentient being.
The word "tāvat" is used here to express agreement.
"What is said here?"—
the meaning is that since the capacity of an *anubhāva* (consequent emotion) to indicate a *bhāva* (transitory state) is well-established, nothing further needs to be stated here.
He explains the application [of these states] as *vibhāvas* (determinant causes) with the words "extremely dull-witted," and so forth.
The connection is as follows: "Even though [the meaning] such as the moon-grove (*candrodyāna*) comes to rest within itself while being described.
"Coming to rest within itself" means that it has reached its culmination within itself through the cognition of the literal meaning (*vācyārtha*). Thus ends the section on "Consciousness" (*cit*).
Therefore, since they are particular modifications of mental activity (*cittavṛtti*), rasa and the like possess the status of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) as subordinate elements.
On the other hand, that which is the primary element—whether rasa or emotion (*bhāva*)—which is the object to be adorned in every respect, is the very soul of *dhvani*. Furthermore—
Those qualities which support that primary meaning are known as *guṇas*;
however, those dependent on the constituent parts (*aṅga*) should be considered ornaments (*alaṅkāras*), like bracelets and the like. (Dhvanyāloka 2.6)
Those qualities which rely upon that primary object (the *aṅgin*) are known as *guṇas* (excellences);
however, those dependent on the subordinate parts (*aṅgas*) should be considered *alaṅkāras* (ornaments), like bracelets and the like. (6)
Those *guṇas*, such as heroism (*śaurya*) and the like, rely upon that very object which possesses the characteristics of flavor (*rasa*) and so forth as its substratum (*aṅgin*).

On the other hand, those which are based on the factors characterized as the expressed (*vācya*) and the expressive (*vācaka*)—namely, the *aṅgas*—are to be understood as *alaṅkāras*, like bracelets and the like.
[Otherwise] the *Locana* states: "In poetry, it would be truly inexplicable."
Whether in the treatises (śāstra) or in the historical accounts (itihāsa),
having thus refuted the views of others, he concludes by restating his own position with the words "therefore" (tasmāt).
The meaning is that the division of objects as stated by the opponent is not logical.
By the inclusion of the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "or existence" (*bhāvo vā*), [the text refers to] its appearance, its cessation, and so forth.
"In all aspects" (*sarvākāram*) is an adverbial modifier;
by that, the meaning is "in every manner."
"It is that which is to be adorned.
The sense is that for this very reason, it is not itself an ornament. // 5 //
Furthermore, the ornament must be admitted as distinct from that which is adorned,
because it is established as such in the world,
just as a quality is distinct from the possessor of the quality.

Furthermore, the application of the terms "quality" (*guṇa*) and "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*) is appropriate only when there exists that which possesses qualities (*guṇin*) and that which is to be adorned (*alaṅkārya*). And this [distinction] is established only in our own position; with these two intentions, he says "Moreover," and so forth.
Not only is this collection of arguments [valid] regarding rasa being the predominant element (*aṅgin*),...
The phrase "as well as other [cases]" has the sense of a conjunction (*samuccaya*). The verse (*kārikā*) should also be applied according to two intended meanings (*abhiprāya*):
in the first sense, the first half of the verse is to be explained by way of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*).
In this manner, the commentary (*vṛtti*) should also be applied. // 6 //
"Bālapriyā" means the state of being an excitant cause (uddīpanavibhāva). Regarding the word "śāstrā," the term "anākhyeya" (inexpressible) is to be supplied.
The meaning is that there is no object whatsoever that does not awaken some particular modification of the mind.
By the term *pratyāmnāya*— the restatement of what has already been said—
the word *āmnāya* indicates its authority, like that of the Veda.
Regarding the phrase "because of the mention of 'vāk'" (speech):
the word "are grasped" (*gṛhyante*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By stating "that which is to be adorned" (*alaṅkārya*), he indicates what is understood [from the context]—namely, "for this very reason. // 5 //
He introduces the passage beginning with "kiñca" with the words "alaṅkārya," etc.,
and states another intention with the words "guṇa," etc.,
and "sa ca."
The meaning is that there is the conventional usage of "qualities" (guṇa) and "ornaments" (alaṅkāra).
He states the meaning of the phrase "furthermore" (kiñca) with the words beginning "not" (na), etc.
"Collection of reasonings" (yuktijāta) means a multitude of logical arguments.
"By means of two intended meanings"—
this is the sense of what was stated. He demonstrates the application [of the argument] with the words "merely," and so forth.
"By the first intention" means the intention that the ornament must be admitted as distinct from that which is to be adorned;
this refers to the first half of the verse.
The meaning is that it refers to the half-verse beginning with "tamartham" (that object).
Regarding the word "dṛṣṭānte" (in the example):
the meaning is that it is like the example [given] that a quality is distinct from the possessor of the quality.
The intention of the second [verse] is to be understood from both the first and second halves; this is the sense.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the gloss on the phrase "that object" (*tamartham*) is "'characterized by rasa and so forth'.
The qualifier "being the principal" (*aṅginam santam*) means that it has become the primary element (*aṅgībhūtam*).
The example "like bravery and so forth" is to be understood. "'Dependent upon that' means dependent upon the constituent parts (aṅga). // 6 //
And so it is said:
"The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) alone is the supreme, sweet, and most exhilarating of sentiments;
depending upon poetry composed of that [sentiment], sweetness is established. (Dhvanyāloka 2.7)
The erotic sentiment alone is the supreme, sweet, and most exhilarating of sentiments;
it is by relying on poetry permeated by that sentiment that sweetness is established. (7)
[The author of the *Locana*] raises an objection: "Surely sweetness (*mādhurya*) and the other qualities belong to word and meaning;
how then can it be said that the qualities reside in the 'principal' element, such as rasa? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And thus," etc.
The meaning is that this is established by the method of refutation set forth [later] which arises from the intellect (*buddhisthena*).
Regarding the phrase "it is indeed the erotic," he states the reason for its being called "sweet" as follows: "because it is the supreme delight.

For in sexual union, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) exist without interruption across all classes of beings—gods, animals, humans, and so forth; thus, there is no one for whom that [erotic sentiment] does not consist of a resonance within the heart.
For even for an ascetic, there is indeed a sense of wonder regarding that;
for this very reason, it is called "sweet" (*madhura*).

For a sweet taste, such as that of sugar and the like—whether belonging to a person of discernment or one lacking discernment, or whether encountered by one who is healthy or one who is ill—is immediately desirable as soon as it falls upon the tongue.

"Consisting of that" means that in which the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) is presented as its very essence (*ātmatvena*), while [other elements] exist there as the suggested (*vyaṅgyatayā*). "Poetry" (*kāvyam*) refers to this.
The meaning is "word and object.
"It is established" (pratitiṣṭhati) means,
in other words, "it attains a firm foundation" (pratiṣṭhāṃ gacchati).
He introduces the passage beginning with "But if it were so" (nanu) and so forth,
and the passage beginning with "of word and meaning" (śabdārthayoḥ) and so forth.
The intended meaning is that this has been stated in exactly that manner by the ancients.
Thus, he explains this [phrase] "and so forth" in accordance with the context of the subject matter— beginning with "by that" and so on—
and he explains the verse beginning with "sweet" and so on:
"sweet" means characterized by the quality (*guṇa*) known as sweetness (*mādhurya*).
"Reason" (hetu) means "that which makes known" (jñāpaka). He establishes the quality of gladdening others with the words beginning "in pleasure" (ratāv ityādi).
The phrase "when passion is arising" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
Regarding "vāsanā," the meaning is a subtle state that is synonymous with *saṃskāra* (latent impression).
The word *iti* indicates the reason;
"not," and so forth,
refers to that [state of] delight (*ratau*).

"Consisting of heart-agreement" means that it is preeminently characterized by heart-agreement; the connection [of the words] is that there is nothing there which does not possess such heart-agreement. The meaning is that heart-agreement occurs for everyone in sexual union (*ratau*).
Regarding the phrase "its wonder": this means a resonance within the heart during sexual union (*ratau*).
He connects what was stated in the introduction with the words "therefore," and so forth.
He clarifies what was stated by means of an illustration with the words "for sweet," and so forth.
The intention is that in the verse, by the word "sweet" and so on, this very meaning is also intended to be conveyed by way of an illustration.
[This applies to] whether one is discerning or undiscerning.
The meaning is "of everyone indeed. "Only desirable" means the sense is "only refreshing."

Regarding the term *tanmaya*, he explains that the suffix *mayaṭ* is used here according to the rule *tatprakṛtavacane mayaṭ*. He provides the commentary beginning with "That," etc. The justification for the phrase "as the self" (*ātmatvena*) is given by the word "as the manifested" (*vyaṅgyatayā*).
The *Locana* states: what is meant is this—that in reality, sweetness (*mādhurya*) is a quality belonging exclusively to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*).
He states the essential meaning of the *kārikā* regarding the two factors that manifest that sweet flavor (*madhurasa*)—namely, [the words] "this is what has been said," and so forth.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the erotic and so forth" (*śṛṅgārādeḥ*), the pathetic sentiment (*karuṇa*) is included.
As for the word "that" (*tat*):
The meaning is "sweetness. "Metaphorical" means superimposed through a direct relationship.
He states the result [of this] with the words beginning "sweet... and so forth.
The erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) alone is "sweet" (*madhura*) in comparison to other sentiments, because it is the cause of supreme delight.
Since poetry consists of words and meanings intended to manifest that [sentiment], sweetness is its defining quality (*guṇa*).
Furthermore, the quality of being pleasant to hear (*śravyatva*) is common even to the quality of vigor (*ojas*).
In the erotic sentiment known as *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) and in the pathetic (*karuṇa*),
sweetness reaches its highest degree of moisture, because the mind is more intensely engaged therein.
In the erotic sentiment known as the love-in-separation and in the pathetic sentiment,
sweetness reaches its highest degree of softness, because the mind is more intensely absorbed therein.

The term *locana* (the eye) is applied metaphorically to both the word and its meaning as the manifestors; for the definition of sweetness (*mādhurya*) in words and meanings is their capacity to manifest the sweet erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*).
Therefore, it is rightly said, "that meaning," and so forth. He explains the meaning of the verse through the commentary: "the erotic," etc.
Now, is it not the case that the definition of sweetness (*mādhurya*) is: "That which is sweet is desired as being audible and not having words with excessive compounds"?
No, he says: "audibility" (*śravyatva*).
By this, the entire definition is indicated.
Regarding the phrase "ojaso 'pi":
the intended meaning is that in the verse beginning with "yo yaḥ śastram," there is indeed both musicality (*śravyatvam*) and the state of being non-compounded (*asamastatvam*). // 7 //

The *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) is sweeter than the *sambhoga* (love-in-enjoyment), and the *karuṇa* (pathetic) is even sweeter than that; therefore, with the intention that the skill in manifesting these [rasas] constitutes a greater sweetness or the greatest sweetness of both word and meaning, he says "the *śṛṅgāra*" and so forth.
In the phrase "and the *karuṇa*," the word "and" (*ca*) indicates the sequence.
"Excelling" means by way of a progressive gradation, from one stage to the next;
"moistness" refers to this state.

The natural hardness of the heart of a sensitive person (*sahṛdaya*), which consists of being unpenetrated [by aesthetic emotion] and takes the form of an inflamed state such as anger and so forth—this is "śṛṅgāra" (the erotic and other sentiments).
The meaning is "śṛṅgāra and the rest.
This is the definition.
The meaning is "its own nature" (*svarūpa*).
By this, the meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "in its manifestation" (*tatprakāśane*) has been shown.
In the *vṛtti*, the connection is: "because it is the cause of bliss in comparison to other aesthetic sentiments" (*rasāntarāpekṣayā prahlādahetutvāt*).
"Locane"— namely, "nanu" and so forth.
"Not excessively composed of compound words, yet sweet"— the word "poetry" (*kāvyam*) is to be supplied as the subject.
"Thus" (iti) means "as stated by Bhāmaha.
"Definition" (lakṣaṇam) refers to this.
The meaning is that the definition consists of [qualities] such as being worth hearing (*śravyatva*).
This concludes the section containing the objection.
He says, "No."
The meaning is that he says the definition stated [previously] is not [correct] because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpti*).
"All" means everything stated [in the verse] beginning with "that which is to be heard" (*śravya*).

Regarding the term "ojasaḥ": it means "of the poetic work (kāvyasya) possessing vigor (ojasvinaḥ). He demonstrates the over-extension [of the definition] by citing an example, beginning with "yo yaḥ" and so forth.
This verse will be cited as an example in the discussion of poetic meters (vṛtta). //7//
He introduces [the topic] with "In union," and so forth.
The word "iti" indicates the reason. [The phrase] begins with "by means of that," and so forth.
By the word "tat" (that), there is a reference to a flavor that is both sweeter and sweetest.
"States the sequence" means that it is thus characterized by excellence through a gradual progression.
He states this very point: "successively higher.

He explains the phrase "it attains moisture" with the words beginning "of the sensitive reader" (*sahṛdayasya*), and so on; the connection is with the phrase "it abandons [its own] consciousness" (*cetastyajati*).
"Intrinsic hardness" means as it is stated in the *Bhaktirasāyana*: "The substance of the mind is hard by its very nature. Regarding "anger and so forth":
The meaning is that "intensity" (dīptatva) refers to that which is produced by anger and the like; however,

in the cases of the erotic-in-separation (vipralambha-śṛṅgāra) and the pathetic (karuṇa), it is precisely "sweetness" (mādhurya) that reaches its highest degree, because these serve as the primary causes for the supreme captivating of the hearts of sensitive connoisseurs.
The sentiments (rasas) such as the Furious (raudra) and others residing in poetry are characterized by brilliance;
the power (ojas) is established based upon the word and meaning which cause that manifestation. (Dhvanyāloka 2.9)
The sentiments (rasas) such as the Furious (raudra) and others residing in poetry are characterized by brilliance;
and the quality of vigor (ojas) is established based on the word and meaning that serve as the causes for their manifestation. (9)

For the sentiments such as the Furious (raudra) produce supreme brilliance and radiance; thus, by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā), the meaning is that the eye abandons its state of being colored by wonder, laughter, and so forth.
Regarding the word "furthermore" (adhika):
the intention is that it occurs gradually. By this, it is stated that even in the Pathetic (karuṇa) sentiment, the mind becomes entirely fluid.

Now, if sweetness exists in *karuṇa* (the pathetic sentiment) as well, then for what purpose was the restrictive particle *eva* used in the previous verse, stating that it exists "only" (*eva*) in *śṛṅgāra* (the erotic sentiment)?
It is said in reply:
By this, no other aesthetic flavor (rasa) is excluded;

rather, it is indicated by the word "only" that, in the ultimate sense, sweetness and the other qualities belong to the aesthetic flavor itself— which is the very self [of poetry]— whereas they belong to the word and its meaning only figuratively.
He states [the meaning] according to the commentary: "vipralambha... (verse 8).
The word "raudra" begins the list;
the word "ādi" (and so forth) indicates a category.
By this, the heroic (*vīra*) and the marvelous (*adbhuta*) sentiments are also included.
"Radiance" (dīpti) is that which has the nature of blossoming, expanding, and flaming within the heart of the perceiver;
and that is primarily denoted by the word *ojas*.
[The commentary] says: "O wonder! (*vismaya*).
The meaning is that it abandons passion (*rāgitva*), resentment (*rūṣitatva*), and distraction (*vikṣepa*) produced by wonder, laughter, and so forth.
Thus, "moisture" (*ārdratā*) is the mind’s abandonment of hardness and the like, arising from the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) and others.
The meaning is that it is a specific type of function called "fusion" (druti).
This is clear in the *Kāvyapradīpodyota*.
Regarding the phrase "in succession":
The sense is that there is a gradual increase in moisture;
"in every way" means it is exceedingly great.
[The question] "for what purpose? is as follows:
The word *kiṃ* is used in the sense of an inquiry. The meaning is: "that which has what as its referent"?
The intention is that this is because the meaning consisting of the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is contradicted.
He replies: "It is said," and so forth.

The sense is that the particle *eva* (only/just) is intended to exclude other words and their meanings. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the construction is to be understood as "only that which possesses excellence. // 8 //
The term *prakāra* means similarity (*sādṛśya*), and not primacy (*prāthamya*).
The meaning is that there is no fixed rule regarding the fact that the *vīra* (heroic) rasa must immediately follow the *raudra* (furious) rasa.
Regarding the phrase "of the *vīra* and *adbhuta*": if the word "etc. (*ādi*) here includes the *adbhuta* (wonderful) rasa, [then the following applies].
In that case, since the previous text states "astonishment, laughter, and so forth" (*vismayahāsādī*)—
where the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "anger and so forth" (*krodhādi*) is intended to include astonishment— it would be inconsistent to mention "astonishment" (*vismaya*) again.
Therefore, the reading here should be "of the heroic and the loathsome" (*vīrabībhatsayoḥ*).

In the subsequent passage, where it says "in the [rasas] of the comic, the terrifying, the loathsome, and the peaceful," and where it says "likewise even in the loathsome," the word *adbhuta* (the marvelous) should be read in place of the word *bībhatsa* (the loathsome);
if that is done, there is also agreement with the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and other such works.
In that context, the mention of sweetness (*mādhurya*) alone in relation to the peaceful (*śānta*) rasa appears to be intended according to another school of thought.

"Vikāseti": *vikāsa* (expansion) refers to that which has the form of expansion; the blazing (*prajvalana*) that takes that form is its essential nature (*svabhāva*), and its very character (*svarūpa*) is what is called "radiance" (*dīpti*). Such radiance is precisely what is being described.
A sentence devoted to illuminating that [meaning] is one adorned with the composition of long compounds.
The *locana* consists of those [flavors] such as the Furious (*raudra*) which consist of that savor;
by means of that radiance—which is of the nature of a specific savor and exists in the form of an effect—they are characterized as being distinct from other flavors.
Therefore, through the metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect, the Furious and others alone are denoted by the word "vigour" (*ojas*).

Therefore, by means of *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* (indirect indication based on what is indicated), a word intended to manifest that [quality], even if it takes the form of a sentence composed of long compounds, is called *dīpti* (brilliance).
As in the *Bālapriyā*: "the meaning is a certain mental state (*cittavṛtti*).
And [the passage] beginning with "And that... [is as follows].
“*Ojo dīptā*” according to Amara;
“consisting of the relish of that” means they generate mental states characterized by brilliance (*dīpti*).
"Consisting of a specific kind of relish" means having the form of a particular modification of the mind;
"in the form of an effect" means [the same].
The meaning is: "by that which is produced from the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of sentiments such as the Furious (*raudra*).
"They are characterized" (*lakṣyante*) means "they are known" (*jñāyante*).
He completes [the sentence] with "rasa" etc.

The construction is as follows: "By means of metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of the effect to the cause, *raudra* and the other [rasas] are denoted by the word *ojas*, [which is here used] in its distinctness (*pṛthaktayā*), that is, as something separate."
The particle *eva* has the sense of "or" (*vā*).

The meaning is that the word *ojas*, as found in common usage such as "a poem possessing *ojas*" (*ojasvikāvya*), signifies the Furious (*raudra*) and other rasas through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
By this, the passage from the commentary beginning with "the Furious and others" (*raudrādayaḥ*) is explained.
In the commentary, the construction is "by means of *laśaṇayā* (figurative indication) alone.
In the phrase "they are called *dīpti*," the word *dīpti* is an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the term *ojaḥ* (vigor).
[The phrase] "the manifestation of that" refers to this.

The meaning is "the manifestation of the fierce [deities] and so forth. He explains this initial passage of the commentary (*vṛtti*), which takes the form of an exposition on the second half of the verse (*kārikā*), starting with the words "thence" (*tataḥ*) and so on.
Having in mind the syntactic connection (*anuṣaṅga*) of the words "the manifestation of indication (*lakṣaṇā*)" is expressed, he says: "by means of *lakṣitalakṣaṇā*" and so forth.
Some maintain that *lakṣitalakṣaṇā* is an indication (*lakṣaṇā*) by means of a signified object (*lakṣitena arthena*).
Others maintain that "indication by indication" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*) is a mediated relationship of the denoted meaning.
To clarify the explanation of the statement "the word is intent upon manifesting that [meaning]," namely that it is "long" (*dīrgha*) and so forth, he says: "long.
It is said to be "radiance," as for example: "When the pair of thighs of Suyodhana was crushed by the blow of the fierce mace whirled by his trembling arms..."
O Queen, Bhima, with hands smeared with thick, congealed blood and flesh, will dishevel your hair.
The *Locana* states: "‘Cañcat’ and so forth.
Furthermore, when a meaning intended to illuminate that [object] is expressed by clear, intelligible, and expressive words—even without relying on compounds—it is called *dīpti* (radiance).
As in: “*Yo yaḥ*... and so forth.

"Cañcat" means: by that fierce and terrible mace (*gadā*) which was whirled around with both arms moving rapidly and revolving with force, there occurred a blow upon both thighs from all sides; by that, the pair of thighs was thoroughly pulverized and rendered incapable of rising again.

Disregarding Suyodhana, whose two thighs were still joined together, he had hands made red with blood—that blood which was thick and congealed (styāna) due to its state of coagulation rather than drying over time; which remained bound by his hands without losing its form; and which was intensely dense within rather than being merely liquid in nature.
He was one whose palms were thus crimsoned by that gore.

Therefore, he is Bhīma, the one who strikes terror into the cowardly; "of yours" means that he will arrange your hair— your hair upon which all those various insults were inflicted, O Queen, though they were improper— into a floral crest, making it adorned with ornaments.
The poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is that he will join her braid with fragments of blood falling from his hand, as if with a crest (*āpīḍa*) of red flowers.

By the word "Queen" (*devī*), it is established that wrath alone serves as the excitant (*uddīpana-vibhāva*), since the one who has brought ruin upon the noble wife is not an instigator of love; therefore, no suspicion of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) should be entertained here.
Furthermore, Suyodhana’s disregard consists in his failure to exert himself in delivering a second blow with his mace and so forth.
And that [occurred] precisely because his thighs were crushed.
By the mention of "solidified" (*styāna*), the haste in washing away Draupadī’s tears is indicated.

And by the compound, because its inherent nature is to carry a continuous flow, the word *dīpti* (splendor) is indicative of the word *ojas* (vigor). *Bālapriyā*: The word *dīpti* is an indicator for the word *ojas*.
The explanation of the word "prasannaiḥ" (by those who are clear) is "gamakaiḥ" (by those that convey meaning); the meaning is "by those that cause the understanding of the sense instantly.

Regarding the phrase "of Suyodhana," he states that the genitive case is used according to the rule "ṣaṣṭhī cānādare" (the genitive is also used in the sense of disregard), meaning "disregarding Suyodhana."
The explanation of "by *styāna*" is "by way of congealing"; that is to say, by way of becoming solid.
"But not," and so forth.
The meaning is that it does not become bound even by drying out over time.
The explanation of the term "bound" (*avabaddha*) is provided by the words "by the hands," and so forth,
as well as "excessively," and so forth.
"Extreme interiority" here means density.
"Kātara" means one who is timid or fearful.
The grammatical connection is: "even that collection of insults which was improper for the Queen. "Improper for the Queen" (*devyanucitam*) means improper for the Queen who has been consecrated.
[The phrase] "as if with a crest-jewel" (*uttaṃsavataḥ*)...
*Uttaṃsaḥ* means a crest-ornament (*śekhara*). Regarding *kara*: by fragments of blood (*raktaśakalaiḥ*), that is, fragments of gore fallen and trickled from her hand.
"Lohitakusumā" means "red-flowered. The word "sūcitā" (indicated) is to be supplied after "utprekṣā" (poetic fancy).
Regarding "in the family":
it refers to the act of hostility and injury, such as the dragging of the hair performed by Duḥśāsana under the instigation of Suyodhana.
Regarding "hasten": [it refers to the urgency].
The meaning is "quickly [like] Bhīmasena. Regarding the word "sūcitā" (indicated):
the sense is that this was indicated by the very effort to make it into an ear-ornament while it was still in a semi-solid state.

Here he demonstrates that the compound (*samāsa*) is expressive of vigor (*ojas*), stating "by means of a compound" and so forth; specifically, by the compound "cañcat... and so on, and "santatavega... and so on.
The meaning intended to illuminate the compound is expressed by clear words, without requiring the construction of a long compound.

For example: "Whosoever among the armies of the Pāṇḍavas bears arms with pride in his own strength; whosoever among the lineage of the Pañcālas is a child, or advanced in age, or even lying in the womb;

whosoever is a witness to their deeds and moves against me in battle; and whosoever stands in opposition—blinded by anger—I myself shall be the end-maker of each and every one of them, even though I am the end-maker of the worlds."
In such instances, there is a state of *ojas* (vigor) consisting of two elements.
The cognition of the *Locana*, which finds no rest midway but extends all the way to the crushing of the two thighs and the disregard for Suyodhana, exists as a single unit;
thus, it serves as the supreme nourisher of *auddhatya* (exaltation).
Others, however, explain that he is "Red-handed" (Śoṇapāṇi) because of the thick, congealed, and dense blood belonging to Suyodhana that clings to him.
As for the word "yaḥ" (he):
it means one whose weight rests upon his own two arms, and who stands like Arjuna and others in the midst of armies.

Because Dhrishtadyumna, the son of the Panchala king, caused the death of Drona, Ashvatthama was overcome by an even greater surge of rage toward that family; Kanva and others were witnesses to that deed. "I delight in battle"—if one who stands in opposition or hostility is of such a nature, he would indeed be the destroyer of the entire world.

I am the end-maker even for him, let alone for any other human or god; "druta-saṃhita-uccāritatvena" means because it possesses an uninterrupted momentum due to being recited rapidly and in a continuous flow.
"Tāvatyeva" is a qualifier of the cognition, meaning "only when [the recitation] possesses such momentum."
"Crushed," and so forth;
the meaning is that it has as its object the range of meanings from the "whirling mace" up to "disregard for that.
"Cognition" means:
The meaning is "the realization of those with aesthetic sensitivity" (*sahṛdaya*).
"It becomes one" means that it becomes precisely one.
And there is also the reading "it appears as if a single solid mass," which refers to *auddhatya*;
the meaning is that it pertains to the boldness (*dhīroddhata*) residing in the speaker—
that is to say, the anger residing in Bhīma.

However, some say that the genitive case in *suyodhanasya* is used in the sense of a remainder (*śeṣe ṣaṣṭhī*), and that its connection is with the word *śoṇitam* (blood); he states their opinion with the words "others, however" (*anye tu*).
Taking the verb *carati* as being in the present indicative (*laḍanta*), he explains it as "he practices" (*ācarati*).
The meaning is "it performs.
Having understood that [the word] ends in the locative case and is present-participial (*śatṛ*), he says "or else" (*yadvā*).
He explains the sense of the particle *api* in "of that too" (*tasyāpi*) by saying "how much more so," and so forth.

That quality of poetry which consists in its capacity to convey the meaning— wherein the composition does not depend on long compounds, the expressive words are clear, and the subject matter is intended to illuminate that very meaning with respect to all aesthetic flavors (rasas)—
is to be known as the quality *prasāda* (clarity), which functions universally for all. (Dhvanyāloka 2.10)

That quality of poetry which consists in its capacity to convey all aesthetic sentiments (rasas) is to be known as the quality of *prasāda* (clarity), which performs a function common to them all. (10)
Or [the example] "locanam" (the eye).

Here, because the meanings are reflected upon individually and successively, word after word, the wrath (krodha) reaches its highest pitch; thus, the very state of non-compounding (*asamasta*) is the basis for its brilliance.

By demonstrating that sweetness (*mādhurya*) and brilliance (*dīpti*) exist as mutual opposites, residing respectively in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) and other sentiments and the *raudra* (wrathful) and others, [the author] shows the variety of their intermingling in the *hāsya* (comic), *bhayānaka* (terrible), *bībhatsa* (disgusting), and *śānta* (peaceful) sentiments.
This has been shown:

because the comic (*hāsya*) is an auxiliary to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), its sweetness (*mādhurya*) is preeminent; and because it possesses the nature of expansion, its vigor (*ojas*) is also preeminent—thus there is a balance between the two.
Although the fearful (*bhayānaka*) is by nature a state of depressed mental activity, its vigor is preeminent due to the intensity of its excitants (*vibhāva*), while its sweetness is slight.
The same applies to the *bībhatsa* (disgustful) rasa.

However, in the *śānta* (quiescent) rasa, because of the variety of its determinants (*vibhāva*), there is a distinction such that sometimes *ojas* (vigour) is predominant and sometimes *mādhurya* (sweetness). //9//

"Transference" (*samarpakatva*) means "perfect transference," which is the state of engaging [the recipient] through a resonance with the heart and by infusing one's own self into the practitioners; this occurs instantaneously, as illustrated by the examples of fire in dry wood and water free from turbidity. The construction is: "its lack of turbidity and clarity [is called] *bālapriyā*.
He applies this to the example, beginning with "herein," etc.
"By distinct [factors]" means by those understood through various and separate words. "Successively" means—
"Successively" means step by step;
that is to say, pausing again and again.
"By the objects being reflected upon."
The meaning is: by the objects being examined in their respective ways by the speaker.
"Anger" means anger residing in the speaker.
"Dhārām" means "limit" (koṭi);
if the reading is "dīptim," it means "illumination" (prakāśa).
"Dependent" means that it appears so to those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*); this is the ellipsis.
"Non-compoundedness" [is the term].
The meaning is that there is an absence of compounds among the words, or at most only short compounds. "The basis of brilliance" means that which manifests *ojas* (vigor).
He states [this] as a digression, beginning with "In this way" and so forth.
"Sweetness and brilliance" means sweetness and vigor (*ojas*).
"Mutually" means by way of being mutually contradictory.
"Eros and so forth" [is the meaning].
This should be understood according to their respective order.
"Their integration" means the integration of sweetness (*mādhurya*) and vigor (*ojas*).
He provides a justification for what was stated: "Of laughter," and so forth.

The phrase "by way of being an adjunct to the erotic" (*śṛṅgārāṅgatayā*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of its arising from the determinants (*vibhāva*) and other factors of the erotic, as well as its nature of expanding [the aesthetic experience] and its arising from the heroic (*vīra*) and other sentiments. (9)
Regarding the phrase "the quality of being a deliverer," and so forth:
it refers to the quality of poetry being a deliverer with respect to all aesthetic flavors (rasas), or conversely, all aesthetic flavors being a deliverer with respect to poetry.
That is to say, it is the agency consisting in that immediate delivery—characterized by pervasion—which has all aesthetic flavors as its object within the heart of the perceiver.
He is one whose activity, in the form of subsistence, is common to all;
"serenity is to be known as a quality"—this is the meaning of the verse.
He explains this point with the words beginning "the state of being a bestower," and so forth.
"By means of a resonance with the heart" is the reason for the possession (āveśa). "The perceivers" means their hearts.
"Self-nature" (svātma) means its own essential form (svasvarūpa).
The phrase "of all tastes" (sarvarasānām) is to be drawn back [to apply] here as well.
The connection is that there is instantaneous pervasiveness.
Regarding this, he states an example: "dry wood," and so forth;
just as fire [pervades] dry wood.
The meaning is: just as water that is free from turbidity and clear quickly pervades cloth and other objects, so too [is it here]. Regarding the phrase "that lack of turbidity":
it means clarity, which consists in the quality of pervasiveness through the immediate absorption of one's own nature.
Transparency (*prasāda*), however, is the clarity of both word and meaning.
It should be understood as a quality common to all aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and common to all compositions, established primarily with respect to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) alone.
The *Locana* states that it is indeed a quality of all aesthetic flavors.

However, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), that quality of the word and its meaning which conveys such a suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) is also *prasāda* (clarity). He explains this very point with the words "prasādeti. Now, one might object: "Since *guṇa* (quality) resides in the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), how can there be clarity of the word and its meaning? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "sa ca" (and that...).
The word "ca" (and) is used for emphasis:
the quality is common to all tastes,
and that very quality is of such a kind.
This entire composition, pertaining both to words and to meanings, whether composite or non-composite, has its locus therein [in suggestion].
Regarding the phrase "primarily":
the capacity of a meaning to convey [something] is possible only with respect to the suggested sense (vyaṅgya), and not otherwise.
The sense is this: what is so extraordinary about even a word’s capacity to convey its own denotation that it should be considered a *guṇa*?
Thus, according to Bhāmaha’s intention, only the three qualities of sweetness (*mādhurya*), vigor (*ojas*), and clarity (*prasāda*) are logically established.

And these, primarily consisting of the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) of the recipient, are metaphorically attributed to the *rasa*—which is the primary object of that relish—and subsequently to the word and meaning that manifest it; such is the intended meaning. (10)

If it is argued that clarity (*prasāda*) is indeed a quality belonging to the beginner (*bāla*), how can it be said to reside in poetry? To this, he says: "By metaphorical attribution" (*upacārāt*), and so forth.
[This refers to] such a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgye 'rthe*) which consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).
The meaning is "having that as its object.
"Imparting" means imparting immediately.
"That" refers to [the object].
The meaning is that it conveys the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) such as rasa instantaneously. The word "api" is used for conjunction. "Guṇa" means clarity (prasāda).
"How so? means:
how does the transparency of both word and meaning become manifest?
That [transparency] is indeed a quality common to all aesthetic sentiments (rasas).
He states "all," and so forth, to establish that this alone is the quality common to all rasas through a twofold restriction.
Here, the first *eva* (only) excludes its being common to both word and meaning,
while the second excludes [its being restricted] to sweetness (*mādhurya*) and vigor (*ojas*).
"Such a quality" means a quality common to all aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*).
He explains "all compositions," and so forth, with the words beginning with "all," etc.
