In the commentary, the phrase "in the case of an unmanifested meaning" (*avyaṅgyārthe*) and so forth occurs;
the word "that" (*saḥ*) is to be supplied as a grammatical ellipsis (*anuṣaṅga*).
He establishes this point with the words "of the meaning" (*arthasya*) and so forth.
"Of the meaning" (arthasya) means of the expressed meaning (vācyārthasya).
"To such an extent," and so forth—the sense is:
how extraordinary is this quality called the capacity to impart the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyasamarpakatva), which resides in the expressed meaning?
Regarding the term "bhāva" (state): the capacity of word and meaning to convey this or that [object] is not a quality (*guṇa*);

rather, it is the very self-nature of *rasa* itself, which, through its own immersion, instantly pervades the hearts of the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*). Therefore, the quality called *prasāda* (transparency) resides primarily in *rasa* alone.
The intended meaning is that, by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), this applies to both the word and its referent as well.
He concludes with the words "In this way," etc.,
citing Bhāmaha.
The meaning is: "in accordance with the statements of Bhāmaha, such as 'desiring sweetness' (*mādhuryamabhivāñchant*)," and so forth.
"And those," etc.:
those qualities are sweetness (*mādhurya*), vigor (*ojas*), and clarity (*prasāda*).

"Consisting of the savor experienced by the practitioner" means that they essentially consist of those specific mental states (cittavṛtti) characterized by joy, radiance, and clarity which belong to the practitioner; the sense is that they are primarily of that nature.
And their locus is the mind—this is the intended meaning.
"Then," and so forth.
"Those respective relishings" means those produced by the chewing of those respective flavors; thus, they are metaphorically designated as the relishings of those respective flavors.
"Then," and so forth.
The term "are metaphorically designated" (upacaritāḥ) is to be supplied here.
The sense is that words and meanings serve as the causes for the relishing of their respective aesthetic flavors (rasas). // 10 //
The defects such as those offensive to the sacred scriptures (śrutiduṣṭa) and others which have been shown to be non-eternal,
are declared to be avoidable specifically in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), which is the very soul of suggestion (dhvani).

The defects such as those corrupted by the ear (śrutiduṣṭa) and others which have been shown to be impermanent are declared to be abandoned specifically in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), which is of the nature of suggestion (dhvani). // 11 //

The defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* (phonetic flaws) and others that have been indicated are not to be avoided in the mere denoted meaning (*arthamātra*), nor in the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) other than the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), nor even in the erotic itself when it does not constitute the soul of the *dhvani*.

What then? They are cited as things to be rejected only when they occur in the erotic—which is the very soul of *dhvani*—as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) that serves as the primary element (*aṅgin*).
Otherwise, those very defects would not even be considered impermanent.
Thus, this essence of *dhvani*, characterized by the non-perception of sequential order (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), has been demonstrated in its general form.

Locana: Having thus demonstrated that the conventional usage of "qualities" (*guṇa*) and "ornaments" (*alaṅkāra*) is logically consistent only within our own position through such a distinction, he says—beginning with "defects faulty to the ear" (*śrutiduṣṭādayaḥ*)—in order to show that the distinction between permanent and impermanent defects also coheres only within our own position.
And so forth.
Words such as *vānta* (vomited) and others are causes for the recollection of what is indecorous;
they are either corrupt in sound (*śrutiduṣṭa*) or corrupt in meaning (*arthaduṣṭa*), producing an indecent sense through the power of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*).
For example: "Seeking the moon, the cloud, paralyzed with fear, approaches only to strike.

However, defects arising from conceptual construction (*kalpanā-duṣṭa*) occur through the conceptual manipulation of two words, as in the case of the inversion of word order in the phrase "kuru rucim" (make [her] take pleasure).
Examples of difficulty in hearing (*śrutikaṣṭa*) include *adhākṣīt*, *akṣotsīt*, *tṛṇeḍhi*, and so forth.
The term *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) is used as an illustration for the appropriate aesthetic flavors (*rasa*),
since those [flavors] are also excluded in cases such as the heroic (*vīra*), the peaceful (*śānta*), and the marvelous (*adbhuta*).

Regarding the phrase "indicated": their impermanence is not [established] by demonstrating the distinction between their respective objects. As it is said: "Defects of hearing, defects of meaning, and also defects of conceptualization, as well as difficulty of pronunciation—thus they say there are four kinds of defects in speech. This is *Bālapriyā*.

With the words beginning "thus," [the author] demonstrates the defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* (offensive to the ear) mentioned by Bhāmaha, along with examples—namely, "vānta" (vomited matter) and so forth, which are "unrefined" (*asabhya*) and so on.
The connection is: "The *śrutiduṣṭa* [words] are those such as 'vānta' and others that cause the recollection of what is unrefined.
*Śrutiduṣṭaḥ* means possessing the defect characterized by being offensive to the ear.
The same should be understood for what follows as well.
Regarding the term "kāriṇaḥ," the word "sounds" (śabdāḥ) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Chidra" refers to the description of a king;
one who seeks the vulnerabilities of another;
"stabdha" means unshakable.

"For the sake of harming others" means for the sake of their destruction; here, there is the perception of an indecorous meaning in the form of "human waste. [This occurs] by way of figurative construction (*kalpanā*).
The word "become" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
"Alteration of the sequence" means the reversal [of the order], such as changing *ruci* to *kuru*.
*Ciṅku* is a sprout existing within the womb.
"He burnt," and so forth,
is a finite verb form (*tiṅanta*).
Regarding the phrase "śṛṅgāra iti": the meaning is that the word *śṛṅgāra* refers to the fact that erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) exists precisely within the essence of suggestion (*dhvani*).
He clarifies the meaning with the words "But not," and so forth.
"Distinct" means that impermanence is free from defects such as discordant meter (*bhinnavṛtta*) and the like.
"Of these" refers to those [defects] beginning with *śrutiduṣṭa*.

Having demonstrated the classification of the subject matter by showing the division of its objects, [the author states: "but it has not been fully demonstrated" refers to those subdivisions of its constituent parts and those subdivisions inherent within them.
There would be an infinite regress in the conceptualization of their mutual relationship. (DhvK 2.12)
Regarding the various subdivisions of its constituent parts and those subdivisions inherent within them, their infinity arises from the conceptualization of their mutual relationships. (12)

The "status of being the principal" (*aṅgitā*) refers to that which was stated as the single essence of *dhvani*—wherein the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*), such as rasa and so forth, is intended while the expressed meaning is subordinate (*anyapara*).

This consists of: (1) the infinite varieties of the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) which follow the expressed and the expressive; (2) the internal varieties belonging to that principal entity itself; and (3) the characteristics of that principal object, namely *rasa*, *bhāva*, their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and their cessation (*tatpraśama*), together with the presentation of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*).
They are infinite with respect to their own substrates. The *locana* has demonstrated that [the *rasa*] is distinct from defects such as discordant meter (*bhinnavṛtta*) and the like;
nor is it something separate from the qualities (*guṇas*).

Furthermore, since we accept these [qualities] in the *bībhatsa*, *hāsya*, and *raudra* [rasas], while excluding them from the *śṛṅgāra* and others, both their non-constancy and their nature as defects are indeed established.
Existence. // 12 //
"Of the members" means of the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).

"Inherent" (*svagata*) means pertaining to the self; that is, those pertaining to the self such as *sambhoga* (union) and *vipralambha* (separation), or those pertaining to one's own [experience] such as the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth—the point is that when these are arranged like a heap of clods of earth in the relationship of subordinate and principal (*aṅga-aṅgin*), what count can there be?
The "own basis" (*svāśraya*) consists of the suitability of the natures of the woman and the man, and so forth.
"Beholding each other with love" is an elliptical expression that includes conversation and other such acts. This constitutes the "connection" (*sambandha*).

The meaning is that defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* (offensive to the ear), though not [explicitly] mentioned by Bhāmaha and others alongside defects like *bhinnavṛtta* (broken meter), have nonetheless been stated by them;
however, it has not been stated that these are non-eternal (*anitya*),
nor that they are distinct from the poetic qualities (*guṇas*).

The meaning is that even its lack of qualities has not been stated [as a separate point]. "It has indeed been established" means it has been proven by the passage beginning with "in the very nature of consciousness," and so forth.
In the commentary on the verse beginning with "In the erotic [rasa]... and so forth, the word "not" (na ca) is to be understood as an ellipsis (anuṣaṅga).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the phrase "they are declared to be abandoned" (heyā ity udāhṛtāḥ) is also connected to the three subsequent sentences beginning with "those too are not [to be expressed] in the mere object" (te 'pi na vācye 'rthamātre). // 11 //
Regarding the phrase "of the ornaments":

the fact that ornaments serve as adjuncts to rasa and the like has been established in this way in the *Kāvyapradīpodyota*: "Even objects that are beautiful do not produce such aesthetic wonder when expressed by trivial words;
therefore, alliteration and other such figures assist rasa and the like through the medium of the word."

Furthermore, figures such as simile (upamā) and others, by means of enhancing the excellence of the objects such as the excitants (vibhāva) that manifest rasa and so forth, serve as embellishments (upaskāraka) for rasa; and when their excellence is further imparted by poetic figures (alaṅkāra), they produce an intensification of aesthetic relish (āsvāda). For one experiences a certain distinction in what possesses figures compared to what is without them.

Indeed, figures, by heightening the excellence of the excitants and so forth, act as manifold stimulators (uddīpana); in some cases, they are even experienced as consequents (anubhāva), as in the description of a heroine or the like performed by a hero or the like—so they say.

Regarding the term *svagatā* ("belonging to oneself"), he explains that the word *sva-* refers to the self (*ātman*), the supreme self (*paramātman*), and that which belongs to the self (*ātmīya*)—thus: "located in the self," and so forth.
He provides the specific elaboration for "located in the self" with the words "in enjoyment," and so forth;
and for "located in that which belongs to the self" with the words "the determinants (*vibhāva*), etc."
"Of them" means "of the divisions. "By the arrangement of clods" means:
The "prastāra" is a specific methodological procedure for making known the essential nature of a particular metrical form (*vṛtta*).

It is defined in the *Vṛttaratnākara* by the verse beginning with "When the foot consists entirely of heavy syllables," and the meaning is that it is impossible to count its variations according to that system.
Regarding the phrase "in relation to their own substratum" (*svāśrayāpekṣayā*), he explains the term *svāśraya* as "woman" (*strī*).
The meaning is: "due to the suitability of those two natures, which consist of woman and man.
He explains the phrase "the observation of mutual affection" (*parasparapremadarśana*) as "mutually" (*parasparam*).

The *sīmānas* are the specific varieties; when one attempts to conceive of their mutual relationships, it is impossible to enumerate even the sub-varieties of any single *rasa*, let alone those of all of them.
For instance, the primary *rasa*, Śṛṅgāra (the Erotic), has first two main divisions: *saṃbhoga* (union) and *vipralambha* (separation).
Furthermore, *saṃbhoga* itself possesses sub-varieties characterized by the mutual manifestation of love, sexual dalliance, pleasure-gardens, and so forth.
*Locana* refers to sexual pleasure consisting of the sixty-four arts, such as embracing and so forth;
*viharaṇa* refers to going to gardens;
by the inclusion of "and so forth," water-sports, drinking parties, moonrise festivities, and the like are meant.

*Abhilāṣavipralambha* (the separation of longing) is to be understood as occurring when, despite the arising of love characterized by the mutual pride that each is the very life and all-in-all of the other, union is not attained due to some cause. This is illustrated, for example, from the passage beginning with "Why is it said that it gives pleasure? regarding Vatsarāja and Ratnāvalī; however, this does not apply to the earlier [stage] of Ratnāvalī. Now, the *Bālapriyā* explains the passage beginning with "Of separation also," starting with "Abhilāṣavipralambha" and so forth.
"What is meant by 'it causes happiness'?"—
this is a statement by Vatsarāja to the Vidūṣaka in the *Ratnāvalī* play;
it does not refer to [the speech] of Ratnāvalī previously.
The word "hence" (*ityataḥ*) is to be supplied [to the previous sentence].
The meaning is that prior to these words, there was no *abhilāṣavipralambha* (love-in-separation due to longing) on the part of Ratnāvalī.
The implication is that by merely hearing these words, Ratnāvalī became certain of the King's affection for herself.
Showing this very reason, he says: "udeti," etc.

At that time, i.e., in the previous period, there are also various forms of separation (*vipralambha*), such as longing (*abhilāṣa*), jealousy (*īrṣyā*), separation due to absence (*viraha-vipralambha*), and separation due to travel (*pravāsa-vipralambha*).

Furthermore, each of these has its own distinctions based on the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*); and for each of these, there are distinctions based on differences in place, time, substratum, and condition. Thus, with respect to its internal subdivisions alone, a single such [instance] is immeasurable; how much more so when one considers the conceptualization of its various constituent parts!
For when one attempts to conceive of the relationship between each of these subdivisions of the parts and the subdivisions of the whole, they simply result in infinity.
[Locana: In the absence of *rati*, there is merely a state of longing;
*īrṣyā-vipralambha* occurs with a woman who has been humiliated by the breaking of her chastity through infidelity and the like.

The *virahavipralambha* (separation due to absence) is to be considered together with the woman who, though being propitiated by her lover, does not accept his conciliation and subsequently becomes filled with remorse and longs for him in separation;
the *pravāsavipralambha* (separation due to travel abroad), on the other hand, is that which occurs with a woman whose husband is away on a journey— such is the distinction.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) includes [the types of deception] such as those caused by curses and the like. Furthermore, "vipralambha" (deception) is like a "vipralambha" (separation);
for in the case of deception, the desired object is not obtained, and it is the same here.
And "of them" refers to those [deceptions].
In one case, it refers to the enjoyment and so forth; in another, it refers to the determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth.
When it is said that the "substratum" (*āśraya*), such as Mount Malaya, belongs to the determinants like the wind, this is already conveyed by the word "place" (*deśa*).
Therefore, the substratum is the cause.

As it has been said by me alone: "This garland woven by my beloved, which I have constantly placed upon the sanctuary of my heart, even as it withers away, drips the essence of nectar that wards off the pain of the fever of separation."
"Of that" means of the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra).

"The differentiation of the constituent parts," namely the primary sentiments (rasa) and so forth, means the conceptualization of their relationship. In the phrase "in the absence of passion" (ratyabhāve), the locative case is used in the sense of a cause or occasion.

The meaning is: "by reason of the absence of *rati* (pleasure). For *rati*, which has mutual enjoyment as its determined basis, is the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*);
that [which you mentioned] is merely a state of desire (*kāma*).
The meaning is that the passion (*rati*) found in the *Ratnāvalī* is of the nature of longing alone. Regarding "praṇaya":
*praṇaya* means affection or a request.
Regarding the word "khaṇḍitayā":
the connection is with "by the khaṇḍitā" (the neglected wife).
The phrase beginning with "prasādyamānayā" (being conciliated) is an adjective qualifying the khaṇḍitā.
He establishes the usage of the term *vipralambha* for the aforementioned longing (*abhilāṣa*) and so forth by means of the phrase "for the purpose of deception" (*vañcanārtha*).
The intention is that the word *vipralambha* is used here in a figurative sense (*gauṇa*).
He states the similarity between the two [the lover and the actor] with the words "in deception," and so on.
"Thus it is here":
this means "likewise in the case of desire and so forth.

In the commentary, regarding the two phrases "of each of these" (*teṣāṃ ca pratyekam*) and "in the location of these" (*teṣāṃ ca deśe*), he explains the word *teṣām* (of these), which occurs in both places, sequentially with the words beginning "in one place" (*ekatra*).
Regarding the phrase "distinction of place, time, locus, and state," he states "locus" and so forth to show that the interpretation of the word *āśraya* (locus) by some is not tenable.
He says "that" and so forth; the meaning is that if the sense were already established in that way, there would be redundancy (*paunaruktya*).
The reading is "dayitayā" and "śuṣkatarāpi.
The state of being dried up is due to the excessive heat of the heart.

The statement that "the essence of nectar flows and drips" is hyperbole (*atiśayokti*). Here, only a mere indication is given by way of an excitant (*uddīpaka*), so that those of refined intellect may understand.
The intellect, having attained illumination, will exist everywhere.
However, a mere indication is stated here, by which the intellect of those who are discerning and possessed of consciousness shall attain illumination regarding everything. (13)

For by this brief exposition, the intellect of those who are learned and sensitive—having attained illumination through the thorough understanding of the relationship between the primary and subordinate elements (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) even in a single variety of rasa accompanied by figures of speech—will become enlightened in all cases.
In that regard:
[the rasa] of love (śṛṅgāra), which is the dominant element (aṅgin), is characterized by a persistent connection with a single form through effort.
In all these varieties, alliteration is not the illuminating factor.
In all varieties [of poetry], alliteration does not manifest the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra)—the principal element—unless it is made to persist in a single form through deliberate effort. (14)

For among all those varieties of the dominant sentiment (śṛṅgāra) that have been mentioned, alliteration (anuprāsa) occurring in a continuous composition (*prabandha*) by way of being connected to a single type [of sound] is not a suggester (*vyañjaka*).

By the phrase "of the dominant," he indicates that there is freedom of choice (*kāmacāra*) in employing alliteration connected to a single form when the subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the sentiment *śṛṅgāra* is present.

Regarding the statement "by which," the meaning is: by what was stated merely as a direction (a mere indication) concerning the employment of *yamaka* and other figures within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which constitutes the very soul of *dhvani*.
"Of those with feeling" means:
the sense is that of those who desire both great poetic skill and sensitivity.
"Everywhere" [means]:...

The connection is that [the person] is one by whom light—that is, understanding or thorough proficiency—has been attained regarding all [objects], such as aesthetic flavors (rasa) and so forth. // 13 //
"In that regard" (*tatra*) means:
when only a mere indication has been stated.
"With effort" (*yatnāt*) means: [with great exertion].
The intended meaning of the reason "because it is produced with effort" is as follows:

the mention of "single form" (*ekarūpa*) is for the purpose of showing that there is no fault when a varied *anuprāsa* is employed, provided that one [specific] uniformity (*anubandha*) is abandoned. // 14 //
The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "yamaka etc. denotes a variety of types.
Difficult [compositions] include the *muraja-bandha*, the *cakra-bandha*, and so forth.

Through a clever play of words (*śabdabhaṅga*), it is stated that although the garland is a cause of the pain of separation, by virtue of its specific nature as being woven by a beloved, it becomes a source of nectar-like fluid that wards off the pain of separation; thus, it is an instance of [the figure of speech] based on cause (*kāraṇakṛta*).
Distinction. // 12 //
He explains the *kārikā* with the words "by which," and so forth.
By the term "of those possessing consciousness" (*sacetasām*), he states what is intended in the present context with the words "great," and so forth.
The gloss for the word "by which" in the commentary is: "by means of stating merely the direction."
The passage beginning with "of those who are unlearned" and ending with "complete knowledge," etc., is either an elaboration or a justification for this very point. // 13 //
Regarding the phrase "the meaning of the reason" (*hetvartha*):
the sense is that being produced through effort is the reason for its lack of luminosity.
He states the purpose of the inclusion of the term "single form" (*ekarūpa*) in the expression "possessing a continuous single form" with the words beginning with "single" (*eka*). // 14 //

The composition of *yamaka* and other such figures within the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), which constitutes the very soul of suggestion (*dhvani*), is a form of negligence even when one possesses the requisite power; this is especially true in the case of the sentiment of separation (*vipralambha*).
Even when capable, there is negligence, and especially so in the case of deception. // 15 //

Eros (*śṛṅgāra*), which constitutes the very soul of poetic resonance (*dhvani*), being manifested primarily through the signified and the signifier, [requires that] the employment of *yamaka* and other such varieties of alliteration, as well as difficult verbal constructions like *śleṣa*, even if one possesses the capacity for them, constitutes negligence. By the term "negligence," this is shown: although by chance (*kākatālīyena*) some single instance of *yamaka* or the like might occasionally be produced, it should not generally be employed as a subordinate element of rasa (*rasāṅgatvena*), just as other ornaments [should not be overused].
Thus,

by the phrase "especially in the case of *vipralambha* (separation)," an excellence of delicacy (*saukumāryātiśaya*) is established for that [sentiment]. When that is to be expressed, the composition of subordinate figures such as *yamaka* (rhyme) must not be undertaken, as it would be a violation of the rule.
The reasoning for this is stated here:

"That ornament whose composition can be accomplished as something already implied by the aesthetic flavor (rasa), and which is thus produced without requiring a separate effort, is considered an ornament within Dhvani. (DhvK 2.16)
That ornament for which the composition becomes possible through being drawn forth by rasa, and which cannot be accomplished without that [rasa], is considered to belong to dhvani. (16)
Regarding the term "locana" (the eye), [it refers to] *śleṣa* (punning).
In cases such as "raktas tvam" ("you are red"), where there is a pun on the meaning (*arthaśleṣa*), it is not a fault;
however, even a broken word (*śabdabhaṅga*) is faulty only when it is dissonant (*vilaṣṭa*).
But not in the case of the *aśoka* tree and so forth. // 15 //
"Yukti" means a substance that pervades everything; "rasa" means... [text fragment].

In the *Bālapriyā* commentary, the explanation of the phrase "of *yamaka*s and so forth" (*yamakādīnām*) in the context of the combination of *vibhāvas* and other factors through the presence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is given as "of the varieties of *yamaka*s" (*yamakaprakārāṇām*). He states the justification for this with the words "the word ‘and so forth’" (*ādiśabda*).
This is a further elaboration of the very term "varieties of *yamaka*s," namely: "in difficult [compositions]," and so on.
He explains that [verse] with the words "difficult to execute" (*duṣkaram*) and so forth.
Having mentioned "paronomasia through word-splitting" (*śabdabhaṅgaśleṣa*), he states the result: "paronomasia of meaning" (*arthaśleṣa*).
This means paronomasia without word-splitting (*abhaṅgaśleṣa*).
In the opinion of the ancients, *abhaṅgaśleṣa* (unbroken pun) and *arthaśleṣa* (semantic pun) are one and the same; this is clear from the *Kāvyapradīpa* and other such works.
Consider the verse beginning with "raktas tvam" (*You are red*).
Here, there is a semantic pun (*arthaśleṣa*) in words such as *rakta-śilīmukha*.

"But not in the case of 'aśoka' and so forth" means that there is no fault when there is a "bending of words" (*śabdabhaṅga*) in a term such as *aśoka*. The sense is that the word *aśoka* denotes a specific tree by conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), yet through a "bending of words"—that is, by etymological derivation (*yogavyutpatti*) meaning "one for whom there is no sorrow" (*na asti śoko yasya*)—it also expresses one who is free from grief. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says: "'Even when there is [conventional] power [of the word], there is negligence.'"
Thus:

since it will be stated that "the defect caused by lack of proficiency is concealed by the power [of the poet]," even though there exists a power that obscures defects, the occasional production of some single instance of a *yamaka* or similar figure is not to be undertaken, as it serves as an indicator of the poet’s negligence.
The meaning is that it brings about faults. // 15 //
Because the meaning of the words and the reasoning [presented] here has been understood exactly as it was heard, he explains that term—explaining it with the words beginning "all" (*sarva*), etc.
Demonstrating the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the general statement "in rasa" and "in dhvani," he explains the verse with the words beginning "rasa," etc.
The explanation of the phrase "by being implied by rasa" and so forth, in terms of its actual sense, is as follows: "by the presence of rasa," etc.
"By way of being invariably concomitant with that":

by the word "that," the arrangement of the [three] factors such as elimination (*vibhāva*) is referred to; the meaning is "by virtue of being produced by the effort that accomplishes that. "Which" (*yam*): [refers to the aforementioned].

Even when an ornament is marvelous in its perfection, if its composition can only be achieved because it is impelled by rasa, and if that very ornament is attained as an inseparable concomitant while producing the *locana* (the "eye" or aesthetic vision), then that alone is the ornament on the path of rasa, and no other. Therefore, even in rasas such as the heroic (*vīra*) or the marvelous (*adbhuta*), alliteration (*yamaka*) and the like everywhere constitute an act that obstructs the rasa for both the poet and the connoisseur.

The intention is this: however, because the world is deprived of the capacity to ascend to the heights of true aesthetic sensitivity due to being overwhelmed by the flow of trivial, vulgar literature (*gaḍḍurikā*), I have stated that [the rasas] are especially so in the case of *śṛṅgāra* and *vipralambha*.
Accordingly, he will state in general terms later on: "Therefore, these [other rasas] do not possess the status of being subordinate members (*aṅgatva*) within a rasa.
[The phrase] "in their production" (*niṣpattau*)...

The meaning is that, through the favor of inspired eloquence (*pratibhā*), there is no dependence on external accomplishment since [the goal] is perfected by oneself. "Having become a marvel" means that it is a source of wonder, as one thinks, "How has this been composed?"
With her face resting upon her sprout-like hands, her lower lip exhausted by sighing, her throat choked by a surging flood of tears, and the slopes of her breasts heaving with incessant weeping—

while she does not abandon her anger even as she is being propitiated with flattering words, the speaker’s mind remains intent on savoring the transitory states (*anubhāvas*) belonging to the *īrṣyā-vipralambha* (love-in-separation through jealousy).
Consequently, figures such as *śleṣa*, *rūpaka*, and *vyatireka*, though produced effortlessly, cause an obstruction to the savorer’s own process of aesthetic relish (*rasacarvaṇā*).
The meaning is "an ornament dear to the naive" (bālapriya-alaṅkāra).
The connection is: "That very thing is the ornament here on the path of rasa.
This is the explanation of the term "in dhvani": namely, "here on the path of rasa."
"In which the sequence is imperceptible" means in that which is common to all aesthetic flavors (rasa).
"By that" means by the general designation "in Dhvani."
"Vīra" and so forth; the meaning is "in those [poems] consisting of the heroic and other [rasas]. The construction is:
"when there is the production of obstacles to rasa, such as *yamaka* (rhyme) and the like."
The word "everywhere" (sarvatra) is connected with "heroic" (vīra) and so forth.
To the objection that this would contradict what was stated previously, he says: "like a *gaḍḍurikā*.
A *gaḍḍurikā* is a flock of sheep following a ram; it is so called because it runs after a *gaḍḍura*, which is a ram (*meṣa*).
The meaning is that it is a state of following others due to conformity with that [popular opinion].

"By the current of that" means by its uninterrupted flow; "afflicted" means those whose discrimination has been destroyed; and "those people who are devoid of ascending to the heights of the hearts of the connoisseurs"—the meaning is: "with the intention of winning over such people.
"By me" [is the sense].
The meaning is "composed by the author" (mūlakṛt). "Bhāvaḥ" refers to the intention of the author.
He states a supporting argument for the stated point, beginning with "tathā ca" (and thus).
"In its attainment" means "in its arising.
The phrase "by itself alone" is explained by the words "accomplishment," and so forth;
the meaning is: "without depending on any other effort conducive to its accomplishment."
Explaining the essential meaning of the verse beginning with "kapola," he demonstrates the poetic ornaments (alaṅkāras) starting with "kara" and so forth,
and "śvāsa" and so forth.
She is one whose lower lip (*adhara*) is exhausted— that is, withered— by her sighs (*śvāsa*).
The readings "uninterrupted" (avicchinna) and "intermittent" (vicchinnavicchinna) also exist;
[the former] means "it is being clarified."
The speaker is the hero (*nāyaka*); the heroine (*nāyikā*) is angry out of affection—this is the ellipsis.
"Jealousy," and so forth;
the "consequent emotion" (*anubhāva*) consists of sighing and the like, and its "relishing" (*carvaṇā*) is the repeated contemplation thereof.
Regarding the phrase "of the speaker": this statement is intended by both the poet who has composed the work and the hero portrayed by him;
it connects with the term "effortlessly accomplished."
Regarding the passage beginning with "śleṣa" (punning):
in the phrase "the flavor of the lower lip" (*adhararasa*), the word *rasa* has both meanings—taste and poetic sentiment—and thus there is a pun (*śleṣa*) therein.
Alternatively, in this verse, there is a pun on the meaning (*arthaśleṣa*).
For instance, "anger is dear" (*manyuḥ priyaḥ*) is a metaphor (*rūpaka*);
the words "cheek" (*kapola*) and so forth provide the support for that [metaphor];
and the agency of the instigator (*prayojakakartṛtva*) with respect to the action of massaging and so on—which results from the pressure of the palm—is common to both "anger" and "the beloved."
The word *nipīta* contains an internal causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*).
Furthermore, the meaning of *bāṣpa* here is "the sorrow consisting of tears. The phrase "we are not dear [to him]" constitutes a negative comparison (*vyatireka*).
By the first word, alliteration (*anuprāsa*) is understood.
"Of the relisher" means "of the connoisseur."
The connection is "it does not assume [the status of a primary element].
A *lakṣaṇa* (defining characteristic) is a property (*dharma*) that pervades that which is to be defined (*lakṣya*) and is itself pervaded by existence (*sat*).
That [property] would be considered an *alaṅkāra* (ornament) in this *dhvani* where the suggested meaning has no perceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*).
The meaning is that for that [rasa] alone, the status of being a constituent part (*aṅga*) is primary.
For example: "The decorative leaf-design on your cheek has been crushed by the pressure of your palm; this nectar-like essence of your lower lip has been drunk up by your sighs;
repeatedly clinging to your throat, your tears cause your breast-slope to tremble. O you who are indifferent to my requests, it is resentment that has become your lover, not I."

Furthermore, its definition as a subordinate element of rasa (rasāṅga) is that it must be accomplished without a separate effort. Thus, when a poet has resolved to compose a work centered on rasa, if an ornament arises from him having set aside that intention and undertaken a different effort, it is not a subordinate element of rasa.

In the case of a *yamaka* (rhyme/pun), when it is composed intentionally throughout an entire composition, the adoption of a different effort necessarily occurs, consisting in the search for specific words.
If it is argued that this is equally true for other figures of speech as well—it is not so;

for while other figures of speech may appear difficult to establish when analyzed in isolation, they are perceived as "the eye" (locana) by one whose mind is absorbed in rasa. "The eye" means that which is pervasive.
The connection is with the phrase "being performed through a continuous process" (*prabandhena kriyamāṇa*).
For this very reason, since being preceded by conscious intent (*buddhipūrvakatva*) is necessarily present, the term "preceded by conscious intent" has been employed.
An effort other than that [initial effort] which arises from the presence of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is "another effort" (*yatnāntara*).
When examined, they are difficult to accomplish;
the meaning is that even though they were intended to be performed with deliberate forethought, they are impossible to execute.
Likewise, when examined, they are difficult to accomplish in the sense that they are marvelous, such that one wonders how these could have been fashioned.
In the present context, the author states that by the word "tat" (that), only the pervader (*vyāpaka*) is intended, saying: "the meaning is 'the pervader'.
Some maintain that the reading should be "the meaning is 'the indicator' (*jñāpaka*).

The sense is that the fact of not being produced by a separate effort is the pervader of the ornament's being an auxiliary to rasa; thus, the meaning of the commentary (*vṛtti*) is "being an auxiliary to rasa," and so forth.
In order to establish the point already stated, the *Vṛtti* demonstrates the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "yo rasam" and so forth.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "that ornament which is produced.
[The phrase] "that latent impression" (*tāṃ vāsanām*) refers to this.
The meaning is: "the latent impression of the resolve for the bondage of the vital essence" (rasabandha).
"Having transcended" means having gone beyond or abandoned.
"Of one who is established" means of one who has taken recourse [to that].
This connects with the word "of the poet" (*kaveḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "it is not a constituent of rasa":
the meaning is that in that ornament (*alaṅkāra*), there is no status as a constituent of rasa.
He states that "in the composition of *yamakas* and the like, another effort is necessary" with the words beginning "yamaka.

[The word] "by means of a composition" (*prabandhena*) means without interruption. Since there might be a confusion regarding its connection with the term "preceded by intelligence" (*buddhipūrvakam*), he shows the connection in the *Locana*: "being composed."
Regarding the phrase "the adoption of another effort," he explains the term *yatnāntara* with the words beginning with "rasa" (*rasa-ityādi*).
[He explains] "from the conjunction of rasa" as "from that which produces rasa.
He provides a twofold explanation of the phrase "those whose difficulties are being scrutinized" in accordance with the context, beginning with "being scrutinized" (*nirūpyamāṇāni-ityādi*).
Regarding things that cannot be accomplished, they fall upon the inspired poet in a competitive rush, as it were; for example, at the moment Kādambarī beholds [the prince] in the *Kādambarī*,
and likewise when Queen Sītā is overwhelmed by the sight of the illusory head of Rāma on the bridge.
And this is logical,
because the *rasas* must be suggested by specific denotable meanings (*vācyaviśeṣa*) alone;
and the figures of speech such as metaphor (*rūpaka*), which manifest those [rasas], are precisely those specific denotable meanings conveyed by the words that express them.
Therefore, they do not possess the status of being "external" (bahir-aṅga) with respect to the manifestation of rasa;
however, in the case of *yamaka* (rhyme), *duṣkara-mārga* (difficult compositions), and the like, that status remains established.
As for those instances where certain *yamaka*s and other such figures are seen to be possessed of rasa:
In that context, while rasa and the like function as the primary element (aṅgin), yamaka and the like function solely as subordinate elements (aṅga).
Furthermore, even in the case of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa), its status as a subordinate element is not contradictory.
However, when rasa is the primary element to be manifested (vyaṅgya), yamaka and the like cannot be subordinate elements, because they are accomplished through a separate effort.
Summary verses on this very subject: Indeed, certain flavorful compositions of a great poet, complete with poetic ornaments, are brought to completion by a single effort alone.
But in the composition of *yamaka* (paronomasia) and the like, a separate effort is required for this [rasa];
therefore, even for one who is capable, these [figures] do not possess the status of being subordinate members (*aṅga*) to rasa.
The presence of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) as a subordinate element in figures such as *yamaka* and the like is not prohibited;
however, its subordination is not tenable when *śṛṅgāra* constitutes the very soul of the suggested meaning (*dhvani*).
*Locana* means "I am first," which signifies "I shall go first. It means "I shall proceed at the very beginning, I, I.
The state of being "I am first" is *ahampūrvikā*.
The particle *aham* is a substitute for a case ending; it functions in the sense of the word "I.
The term *etad* means rushing forward with the thought "I shall be first."
"Kānicit" means those composed by Kālidāsa and others; the connection is that even for one who possesses [natural] capacity, a separate effort arises.
Regarding the phrase "of these":
it refers to figures such as *yamaka* (paronomasia) and the like.

As for what was stated—that [the sentiment of] love (*śṛṅgāra*) constitutes the very soul of *dhvani*—that is summarized by the half-verse concerning its predominance as "constituting the soul of *dhvani*" (*dhvanyātmabhūta*). // 16 //
The words "of the poet" (*kaveḥ*) are to be supplied after "dear to children" (*bālapriyā*),
and "of the connoisseur" (*sahṛdayasya*) is to be supplied after "wonder-inducing" (*vismayāvahāni*). He explains the term *ahampūrvikayā* with the passage beginning "I," and so forth.
The explanation of the word "pūrva" (prior) is "agṛhīta" (ungrasped).
He states the conclusion with the words "in the ego, etc.
In the commentary, this refers to the phrase "and by the words that denote those [objects]."
The word "to be rejected" (ākṣeptavyāḥ) is connected with this [term].
Regarding the phrase "that which illuminates that" (tatprakāśinaḥ), here the word "that" (tat) refers back to the word (śabda).
‘Of them’ means ‘of [the things] such as form (rūpa) and so forth. ‘That’ refers to—
The meaning is that they possess the status of being external (bahiraṅgatva).
Regarding the phrase "and [their] subordination in the case of a semblance of rasa," the term "of yamaka and so forth" is to be supplied.

The commentator summarizes the points already stated in verses beginning with "rasavatī" and so forth. The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "By a single effort alone, such objects are produced by a great poet.
In the *Locana*, he demonstrates this connection with the words "even for one who is capable" (*śaktasyāpi*). // 16 //
Now, the group of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) that manifests *śṛṅgāra*, which constitutes the very soul of suggestion (*dhvani*), is described:
"The group of ornaments beginning with metaphor (*rūpaka*), when observed and applied to *śṛṅgāra*—which is the soul of suggestion—attains its true significance. (DhvK 2.17)
When the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), which constitutes the very soul of suggestion (dhvani), is perceived and properly established,
the entire class of ornaments such as metaphor (rūpaka) and the like attains its true significance.
"Ornament" (alaṅkāra), O friend, is said to be the cause of beauty for the principal subject (aṅgin) by virtue of its similarity to external ornaments;
and as for the entire class of expressed ornaments (vācyālaṅkāra)— beginning with metaphor (rūpaka) and so forth— which has been mentioned or will be mentioned by some,
they are called such because they are the adornments of poetry.

If all of that is employed after due consideration, it results in the cause of beauty for the entire *dhvani* whose suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), which is its primary constituent (*aṅgin*).
This is the consideration regarding its employment:
[it should be used] with the intention of making it subordinate to something else, never as the primary element itself.
The grasping and the relinquishing [of the meaning] should occur at the proper time, and there should be no desire for excessive elaboration.
Even though the [subsidiary] members have been fully carried out, there should be careful observation with effort;
the intention [of the speaker] is through devotion to that [goal], never by way of being the primary member itself.
Furthermore, there should be taking up and abandoning at the proper time, and no desire for excessive prolongation. (18)
Even though they have been established as auxiliary factors (*aṅga*), one must examine them with effort,
thinking, "This is the eye. Thus, the category of what is to be abandoned (*heyavarga*) has been explained.
The intention is that the category of what is to be adopted must now be stated. Regarding the term "manifestor" (*vyañjaka*),
the words "who" and "how" are to be supplied as ellipses.
"Yathārthatām" means "the state of being a cause of beauty. "Uktaḥ" means "stated."
Regarding the phrase "and will be stated by Bhāmaha and others who composed definitions of poetic figures," he provides the reason: "because poetic figures are infinite.
This means that because they are endless, they will also be [stated] by certain others yet to come. // 17 //
Regarding the word "samīkṣya":
the intention is that it is stated by the word "samīkṣya" in the kārikā.
This proof of its being a constituent part [of the sādhana] applies to the four quarters of a verse (śloka) as well as to half a verse (ślokārdha).
The connection is to be understood with each term, such as "metaphor" (rūpaka) and so forth:
that which one intends to express as a subordinate member of an ornament, rather than as the principal element itself,
is what one employs on the appropriate occasion.
That which one relinquishes at the appropriate time, that which one does not wish to renounce entirely, and that which one regards with effort as a necessary limb [of practice].
When it is thus composed, it becomes the cause for the manifestation of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*); this is the extensive Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*).

Within that Great Sentence, there is the occasion for an illustration (*udāharaṇa*), as well as the nature of the illustration, its application, and its justification; it is to define these that another work [the *Kāvyaprakāśa*] follows the commentary (*vṛtti*)—this is the connection, expressed by the words "And he who...
(*yaśca*).
The meaning is that an ornament is designated according to how it manifests [its effect]; this is the intended sense.

He demonstrates that the term "yathārthatām" (conformity with the actual state) means "anvarthatām" (possessing a literal or etymological correspondence)—this is shown by the words beginning with "cārutve" (in regard to beauty).
Because ornaments are infinite, the phrase "by some" is explained as "by others [it is said] because of the infinity of creative intuition (pratibhā)," and so forth. // 17 //
It was stated in the *Vṛtti* that "this is the examination" (*eṣā samīkṣā*).
To the question, "What is the occasion for this examination here?", he says in the *Locana*: "By the word 'having examined' (*samīkṣya*)," and so forth.
[He explains] by means of this term "having examined."
The meaning is: "by the word *samīkṣya* (having observed) in the phrase *samīkṣya viniveśita*.

Having first stated the essential meaning of the two verses, he demonstrates the connection between the preceding and following sections of the text with the words beginning "yamalaṅkāram" (which ornament...).
[This serves as] the proof for the status of metaphor (*rūpaka*) and other such figures as being subordinate members (*aṅga*) of the category of ornaments. (Dhvanyāloka 2.19)
The establishment of the status of figures such as *rūpaka* as subordinate elements within the class of ornaments (*alaṅkāra*). // 19 //
A poet whose mind is intensely devoted to the binding of aesthetic sentiments (rasa-bandha) intends to describe a particular ornament as a subordinate element of that sentiment.
For example: "You repeatedly touch her tremulous glance with its flickering corners; moving close to her ear, you murmur softly like one whispering a secret;
you drink the nectar of her lips—the very essence of love—as she shakes her hands. We, in our search for the truth, remain mere-handed [empty-handed] bees, while you, indeed, are truly successful."

For here, the poetic figure of *svabhāvokti* (description of natural state), which accords with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), is expressed as: "O bee, [she] whose outer corners of the eyes are tremulous. Locana:
"O bee..."

"Though we are thus inclined toward the flattery of desire, when the true state of reality is investigated through the search for truth, we have become ruined, reduced to being mere vessels of our own exertion.
'You indeed'—by this particle [the king implies] that the fulfillment of his purpose is already accomplished effortlessly right there. This is the speech of Duṣyanta, who is longing for Śakuntalā;
for instance: 'How might I come within the range of her sidelong glances?'"
"How might she hear our secret words that reveal our intentions?
How indeed might we forcibly perform a kiss upon her, even though she is unwilling?"—that which dwells within the path of our imagination is accomplished for you without effort.
For the bee repeatedly touches the gaze that causes suspicion, mistaking it for a blue lotus.
Furthermore, because his eyes extend to the very limits of his ears, the suspicion that they are blue lotuses does not depart; thus, he remains there humming.

And as he drinks from her lower lip—which is the repository of delight, sweet with the fragrance of blooming *aravinda* and *kuvalaya* lotuses, and which is timid due to its innate delicacy—he becomes a bee. This poetic figure (*bhramarasvabhāvokti*) has attained the status of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the primary sentiment (*rasa*) at hand.
Others, however, [interpret] "calāpāṅgām" as having the nature of a bee;
this verse has been explained by us in detail in our commentary on the *Śākuntala*.
By the word "we," he states the implied meaning—namely, "in this way," and so forth.

Those who possess such desires as will be described hereafter; those who are inclined toward and devoted to *cāṭu*, that is, flattering speech. The phrase beginning with "without effort" (*ayatna*) and so forth is an explanation of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
The passage beginning with "How" and ending with "is established" is presented as the speech of Duṣyanta;
the passage beginning with "For the bee," etc., is the speech of the commentator.
"In that very same space for hearing" means in that very same moment of listening.

Regarding the phrase *dandhvanyamānaḥ*: it means "making an exceedingly loud sound. He explains the passage beginning with "the description of the nature of the bee" (*bhramarasvabhāvoktiḥ*) according to its meaning—as follows: "the description of the nature of the bee," and so forth.

Although both *samāsokti* (speech of compression) and *vyatireka* (contrast) are present here, only *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) is mentioned because it presents itself most prominently. The phrase "of the primary rasa" means "of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation)."

The phrase "has indeed attained the status of a subordinate element" (aṅgatām evopagataḥ) means "not as a principal element" (na aṅgitvena). For sometimes an ornament (alaṅkāra), even when intended to be expressed with a primary focus on rasa and so forth, is seen to be intended as a subordinate element.

For example: "He who, by the mere forceful command of the impact of his discus, rendered the festival of love of Rāhu’s wives barren of the unrestrained pleasures of embracing, leaving only the act of kissing."
For here, there is an intention to express the *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) as the primary element, even though the focus is on rasa and so forth.

The *Locana* states: "That which has such speech" refers to the *svabhāvokti* (description of nature) of the bee; they say that here there is a combination of *rūpaka* (metaphor) and *vyatireka* (distinction).
"The mere striking of the [moon's] orb was her irresistible command—an irrevocable decree—by which she reduced the festival of love of Rāhu’s beloveds to nothing but kisses."
Since that festival of love is barren—that is, empty—of those amorous sports in which unrestrained embracing is the primary element;
here someone says: "In this case, it is *paryāyokta* (periphrasis) alone that the poet intends to convey as the principal meaning, and not rasa or the like."
How, then, can it be said that "even though there is an intent toward rasa and so forth"?
It is not so; for what is intended here is the majesty (pratāpa) of Vāsudeva, and that does not shine forth here as the cause of aesthetic charm (cārutva).
However, this is merely a case of *paryāyokta* (indirect expression).

Even though there is no suspicion of any defect in this poem, it nevertheless serves as an illustration of how an ornament (*alaṅkāra*), even when functioning as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), may result in the obscuration of the essential nature of the primary subject (*prakṛta*) that is intended to be emphasized.
And thus, the intention of the author of this work is that in some cases an impropriety arises;
the meaning is that such behavior of the bee serves as an excitant of love (*kāmoddīpaka*).
[The term] "metaphor" (*rūpaka*)... [is used].
Metaphorical contrast (rūpakavyatireka) is a contrast accompanied by a metaphor; here, there is a metaphor because of the superimposition of the status of a hero upon the bee,
and there is also a contrast in the fourth quarter.

In reality, there is no metaphor (*rūpaka*) here, but rather *samāsokti* (speech of compression); with this intention, the word "anya" (other) is used to indicate a lack of satisfaction [with the previous view].
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the explanation of the phrase "by way of being the primary element" (*aṅgitvena*) is given as "by way of predominance" (*prādhānyena*).
‘Sometimes’ (kadācit) means in some poem. In the *Locana*, [the commentary begins with] ‘He made,’ etc.
"Striking with a wheel" means striking from all sides;
it does not mean [striking] by means of juice and so forth.
The phrase "intended as primary" is to be supplied here as well.
"Even though there is an intent toward rasa and so forth" is a restatement of the commentary (vṛtti) text.
He replies with "not so," and so on.
[The term] "intended" [is used].
The word "predominantly" (prādhānyena) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence].
Thus, the intended meaning is that the primary focus here lies in the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa). He states the specific detail: "And that... (sa ca).
"Rather, it is indeed *paryāyokta* (periphrasis)";
the phrase "it shines as the cause of beauty" is to be supplied [to the previous statement]. He raises an objection with the words "Even though," and so forth.
"Never a suspicion of fault" means that nothing whatsoever which would obstruct the aesthetic wonder (camatkāra) should be suspected.
Thus, the sense is that there is no harm even if the suggested meaning (paryāyokta) holds the primary position.
He provides the resolution with the words "even so" (*tathāpi*) and so forth.
"Like the example" (*dṛṣṭāntavat*) means "equal to the example."
"Etad" means "this," referring to the example beginning with "cakra" and so forth.
He explains the state [of being] with the words beginning with "yat."

The connection is: "Even if an ornament (alaṅkāra) is a constituent part (aṅgabhūta), it becomes a subverter of the nature of the primary subject (prakṛta) which is intended to be nourished. The word "in some cases" (kvacit) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The sense is that the verse under discussion serves as an illustration (dṛṣṭānta) in that regard.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And therefore...
[referring to] "in some cases there is impropriety.
An example of this is stated in the *Kāvyānuśāsana* and other works, beginning with the verse: "The beauty of the garland has slipped away," and so forth.
He states the supporting factor: "And so it is.
That which is intended as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) is apprehended at the proper occasion, not out of its place.

An example of apprehension at the proper occasion is as follows: "With unrestrained surges, pale in luster, having begun to yawn, and in an instant spreading her own exhaustion through incessant exhalations..."
Today, beholding this garden creeper—filled with blossoms like another woman possessed by passion—I shall surely cause the face of the Queen to glow with the crimson hue of anger.
And likewise, the author himself will demonstrate this later in the *Locana*:
"To voice a criticism of great souls is a criticism of oneself"; thus, this was not offered as an example of a valid criticism.
[The compound *uddāmakalikā* means] that from which full-blown buds have emerged.
And at that very moment, there arose a thrill and a shivering; a yawn, by which an expansion [of the heart] was initiated—
a yawn being the bodily languor caused by the god of love.
She manifests the exhaustion of her own heart—the heat residing within—by means of the exhalations of her breath, which are like the playful breezes of spring;

she is accompanied by the *madana* tree (or by *madana*, i.e., passion). Here, the simile and the pun (*śleṣa*) stand as a purifier of the path for the impending *vipralambha-śṛṅgāra* (love-in-separation through jealousy), creating a readiness for its savoring; thus, at this opportune moment, when the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) is about to manifest, they act as its precursors.
The sense is that [the meaning] has been grasped.
Furthermore, in this context, there is an illustrative representation (*abhinaya*) for every word regarding the subject at hand.
To the question, "How will she demonstrate it regarding what is not the subject at hand? he says: "Of the great-souled ones," and so on, up to "was given."
"Uddāmeti.
This is from the *Ratnāvalī* play.

It is a statement addressed by the King of Vatsa—having learned that the *navamālikā* creeper he had taken under his care has blossomed through a particular application of the *dohada* rite—to his court jester.
The syntactical connection is as follows: "Today, seeing this garden creeper like another woman, I shall make the face of the Queen [Vāsavadattā] possess a luster crimson with anger.

The meaning is: while he views my flowering creeper as if it were another woman, I shall act so that the face of Vāsavadattā—who has become angry because her own cherished mādhavī creeper has failed to produce flowers—will become as red as the glow of the dawn.
The word *dhruvam* indicates certainty. Considering the latter half of the verse to be clear in meaning, he explains the first half, beginning with *uddāmāḥ*: "excessive" means "intense."
Alternatively, [the word] *bahvyaḥ* [is used];
he explains it in the sense of women as "utkalikāśca" (and longings).
*Ruharuhikāḥ* means yearnings or intense longing.
The phrase "āyāsanam" (distress) is itself explained as "āndolanā" (swaying).
Regarding the statement in the commentary, "herein [there is] both simile and paronomasia," he explains it with the words "herein," etc.
Paronomasia accompanied by simile is "upamāśleṣaḥ."
"Even jealousy"—
the meaning is that it departs upon the arrival of Vāsavadattā.
"Of the future"— [refers to what is about to happen].
"At the end of the second act" means "of that which is about to be described.
"Mārga," etc.,
means "by way of being a manifestor."

Regarding the phrase "that relish" (*taccarvaṇā*), the word "of sensitive readers" (*sahṛdayānām*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The explanation of the term "occasion" (*avasara*) is given by the words "of rasa," and so forth.
"Preceding the aesthetic relish" means being like a precursor to the savoring of rasa. He speaks of "acting" and so forth for the purpose of instructing the actor.
"Aprākaraṇika" means that which has a non-contextual meaning, namely, the form of a woman. In this case, there is a simile (upamā) within the paronomasia (śleṣa).

Moreover, even that which has been adopted is abandoned at the appropriate moment for the sake of conforming to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), in view of another figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*). For example:

"O Aśoka tree, you are red with fresh shoots, and I too am [red] with the praiseworthy virtues of my beloved. Arrows released from the bow of Love come toward you, and likewise they come toward me. The touch of the beloved’s foot brings joy to you, and it does so for me as well; in every respect, we two are equal. The only thing is that I have been made 'full of sorrow' (*saśoka*) by the Creator. In this verse, the figure of speech *Śleṣa* (Pun) is initially employed, but it is subsequently set aside in favor of *Virodha* (Apparent Contradiction), because the latter better serves the prevailing sentiment of pathos (*karuṇa-rasa*). Thus, the poet abandons the former for the sake of the latter.
The *locana* (the glance), however, is performed through the intonation of the sentence's meaning (*vākyārtha-abhinaya*) by means of the minor limbs (*upāṅga*) and so forth;
it is not entirely without abhinaya, as stated by the venerable [Abhinavagupta].
Furthermore, the word *dhruva* (fixed) provides the occasion for the arising of emotion (*bhāva*) and jealousy (*īrṣyā*).
*Rakta* means red;

I too am *rakta*, meaning one whose passion has been awakened. And in that regard, it should be understood that the excitant (*vibhāva*) which awakens [that passion] is his own slight sprout of affection (*sallavarāga*).
In this way, the primary meaning of each quarter-verse should be explained as being characterized by *vibhāva* (the aesthetic cause).
For this very reason, this is a case of *hetuśleṣa* (punning causality);
for among the figures of speech—*sahokti*, *upamā*, and *hetu*—it is most frequently the case that they are supported by *śleṣa* (punning).
With this very intention, [it is said] "by means of the *upāṅgas* and so forth for the beloved of the ignorant";
the word "acting" (*abhinaya*) is to be supplied [to complete the phrase].
"The passion of the awakened" (*prabuddhānurāga*).
The meaning is that I am enamored by the virtues of my beloved; thus, through the *tantra* (systematic arrangement) and so forth, the sense is that passion has been awakened.
To the question "Who is the awakener?", the commentator says: "And there... and so forth. [This refers to] the *vibhāva* (the excitants).
The meaning is "the excitant condition" (uddīpanavibhāva).
The term "tadīya" means "belonging to that," namely,
related to the Aśoka tree.
"Per foot" means in the second and third feet.
"By way of being the dissolution" [means...].
The meaning is "by way of being an excitant determinant" (*uddīpanavibhāva*).
It should be explained as follows:
since the bees—acting as arrows released from your bow, having emerged from the bow of Kāma—are approaching.
Then, even for me, arrows released from the bow of Smara—shafts issuing forth from the bow of Kāma—come rushing toward me.
"O beloved," and so forth: although here the striking with the sole of your beloved's foot serves for your pleasure, it results in the blossoming of flowers.

The literal meaning of the verse is that "likewise, the blow from the sole of my beloved’s foot—referring to a specific position in sexual union—brings me joy. However, the intended sense is that since the hero experiences satisfaction when the *aśoka* tree blossoms due to the blow from his beloved’s foot, it should be explained as a cause-and-effect relationship: "Since this brings you joy, therefore it brings me joy as well.
This is the underlying meaning.

For here, although the *śleṣa* (paronomasia) has been established throughout the composition, it is abandoned for the sake of expressing *vyatireka* (distinction), thereby nourishing a particular aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).

If it is argued that there is no conjunction of two distinct figures of speech here, but rather a third figure characterized by both *śleṣa* and *vyatireka*, like the "Man-Lion" (*narasiṃha*), we say: no.
Because that [paronomasia] is established by means of a different mode [of expression].
For when, in a word whose very domain is paronomasia (*śleṣa*), a cognition of distinction (*vyatireka*) arises through a different mode, that is its domain.
As, for example, in "That god is Hari by name; he is also accompanied by a multitude of excellent horses," and so forth.

Bhāmaha defined *locana* (the glance) by stating, "It is threefold: through its mention as concomitance (*sahokti*), simile (*upamā*), or cause (*hetu*)," and not with the intent of excluding other poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*).
By the term "particularized rasa" (*rasaviśeṣa*), he refers to love-in-separation (*vipralambha*).

By employing the word "sorrowful" (*saśoka*) and thereby bringing in the figure of contrast (*vyatireka*), he provides scope for the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as despondency (*nirveda*) and anxiety (*cintā*), which coexist with sorrow and nourish the sentiment of love-in-separation.
"What then?"—the opponent's intention is this: "This is merely a single *saṅkārālaṅkāra* (mixed ornament); in that case, what has been discarded and what has been adopted?"
"Of that" refers to *saṅkara* (commixture).
For *saṅkara* is the simultaneous manifestation of two figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*) within a single subject matter (*viṣaya*).
In this case, the single subject matter is the word "Hari."
"He is Hari," or "he is with the Haris (horses)," thus "Saharir.
This means a *śleṣa* (paronomasia) accompanied by the figure of speech *hetu* (cause). The term *bālapriyā* [in the commentary] means a *śleṣa* conjoined with the *hetu* ornament.
He provides the justification for what was stated, beginning with "sahokti" (simultaneous mention) and so forth.
The phrase "by this very [means]" means:
specifically by the intention that it primarily serves as a subordinate element (*anugrāhaka*) to *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the author] described [it] by means of this statement. "In conjunction with that" (*tatsahoktau*): "that" refers to the punning speech (*śliṣṭavacaḥ*).
He states what is excluded by the particle *eva* in the phrase "not, however," and so forth.

He explains that the abandonment of a previously adopted figure of speech—due to the desire to employ another figure more appropriate to the prevailing sentiment (*rasa*)—becomes an auxiliary to that very sentiment; thus, in the present context, he clarifies how the figure of *vyatireka* (distinction) nourishes the sentiment of *vipralambha* (love-in-separation) through the word "sorrowful" (*saśoka*), and so on.
"Bring about the exclusion" means "show the exclusion from the speaker's non-sorrow.
"An opportunity has been given" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that "stability" has been demonstrated. In the commentary, the term "śleṣa" means "simile based on paronomasia."
The passage beginning with "not here" and ending with "if" constitutes the section of the objection (*śaṅkāgrantha*).
In that regard, he states the positive state [of the alternative] starting with "what then," namely "in the case of confusion" (*saṅkara*), and so forth.
"In the case of confusion" (*saṅkara*)... [etc.]
The meaning is "the confusion arising from the entry into a single sentence.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), he provides the resolution with the words beginning with "not" (*na*).
He demonstrates the establishment [of the distinction] by means of another method with the words beginning with "where" (*yatra*).
He explains the term *bhāva* [as follows]: "In one place," and so forth. Regarding "ornament" (*alaṅkāra*):
the meaning is the manifestation, that is, the arising, of the intuition (*pratibhā*) which is the cognition of two ornaments.
*Saṅkara* (confusion) is the confusion resulting from the intrusion of two statements into one. For example, in the description of a king: "He is Hari;
yet, although his conduct is incomparable, he does not attain equality with Acyuta. Here, the first half [of the verse] constitutes the confusion.
Here he demonstrates that they share a single object— “sa hari” and so forth.
Regarding the term “object” (viṣaya),
the words “of the two, śleṣa and vyatireka” are to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the phrase "by the name Hari," he says that there are two words here: "saḥ" (he) and "hariḥ" (Hari).
"Saḥ" refers to Acyuta.
"Nāmnā hariḥ" means he is named Hari; that is, his name is Hari.

With the intention that the word *hari*, which denotes a horse, forms a compound with the word *saha*, he explains the second occurrence of the word *sahari* with the words "or else" (*yadi vā*), etc.
"Or else" (*yadi vā*) means "and furthermore" (*atha ca*).
Because indeclinables have multiple meanings; or else, "yadi vā" is a corrupt reading. [The word] "haribhiḥ" means by the horses.
The instrumental case in "nivahena" is used either in the sense of cause (*hetu*) or in the sense of non-difference (*abheda*).
In this final quarter, for indeed, one word is the object of *śleṣa* (punning) and another is the object of *vyatireka* (contrast).
If, in such a case, a separate poetic figure were postulated, it would result in the total displacement of the domain of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction).
If it is argued that, since the essence of *vyatireka* (contrast) is obtained here solely through the medium of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), this is not a domain of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction)—we say no;
for *vyatireka* is seen even by way of other modes. For example: [text omitted]. We say no; for... [text omitted].
Because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also demonstrated by another method, as for example:

"O Goddess, your eye does not tremble even before the wind at the end of an eon, though it [the wind] causes the earth to shatter with its fierce speed. Here, the word *hi* has the sense of the word *tu*.
The meaning is "in the case of [the statement] 'you are red'.
"Another" refers to [the person] who is red and so forth;
and "another" refers to the *aśoka* tree, the *saśoka* tree, and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that "since they rely on a single subject consisting of a single sentence, there may indeed be a commingling (saṅkara) due to having a single object," he says: "yadi" (if).
It should be understood that in such a definition of a sentence, the intended unity refers to the "object" (viṣaya).
If, however, having a single object were asserted with respect to a single sentence, then there would never be any commingling (saṃsṛṣṭi).
Because it is pervaded by a commixture (saṅkara).
Now, one might object: this is a figure of contrast (vyatireka) containing a simile (upamā);
and since the simile arrives precisely through the medium of paronomasia (śleṣa), paronomasia here is the auxiliary of the contrast. Therefore, this is indeed the province of commixture alone.
But where there is no relationship between the benefactor and the beneficiary, even if they reside in a single sentence, there is only *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction);
this is what he states with the words "by means of *śleṣa*" (*śleṣa*).
The meaning is: by way of a simile brought about through the power of *śleṣa*.
He refutes this with "no.
The underlying point is as follows: does the distinction (vyatireka) occur when the simile is expressed by its own word in every instance, or when it is merely implied?
He refutes the first position with the words "by another manner" (*prakārāntareṇa*).
The meaning is that even without the expression of a simile;
the meaning is that it can be extinguished by a *śamyā* (a wooden pin).
However, a lamp-wick can be extinguished by mere wind.
"You are dear to the child" is the ellipsis;
"O Lord" is an epithet qualifying both [the child and Hari].
Although two instances of "he is Hari" are employed here, [they function as a single expression].

Nevertheless, the sense is that because those two constitute a single sequential order (*ekānupūrvī*), they have a single object (*ekaviṣayakatva*). He explains the word "other" (*anya*) occurring in the commentary with the words "red," and so forth; [it refers to] that which is characterized as a sentence (*vākya-lakṣaṇa*), that is, consisting of a sentence (*vākyātmake*).

Demonstrating the fruit of the intention to express unity (*ekatva-vivakṣā*), he explains the meaning of the commentary beginning with "that" (*tad*) and so forth—namely, "in a single sentence" (*ekavākya*) and so on—with the words:

"this is the domain of commingling alone" (*saṅkarasyaiva eṣa viṣayaḥ*). This refers to the commingling (*saṅkara*) that occurs through the relationship of the assisted and the assister (*anugrāhyānugrāhakabhāvena*).
He states that there is no deprivation of the object because of their commingling, beginning with the words "where... and so forth.
"He says this" means he demonstrates this very doubt.
He demonstrates the meaning of the refutation beginning with "no" (na) and so forth through the passage starting with "this" (ayam) and so on.
"Why? is used as an interrogative particle.
"In being understood" (gamyamānatve) means in being suggested (vyaṅgyatve).
By means of the expression of a simile— that is, by the word expressing the simile—
it is not to be imagined as being contained within the *Sūryaśataka*.
The connection is as follows: may that very radiance of the sun,
which possesses hot splendor and serves as the lamp for all continents, appearing in another form, and which is well-known as the wick, bring you happiness.
By the phrase "of another form" (anyarūpa), the dissimilarity from the [ordinary] brilliance is shown; this is further explained by the words "not at night" (no kṛtpe) and so forth.

Of him, whose mountain is being split apart by the merciless and powerful force of the wind—here, the genitive case in "vāyoḥ" denotes the agent. [His brilliance] is intensely emitted; it possesses a radiant splendor that is intensely emitted, and it is not devoid of the collyrium of darkness during the day.

May that very wick of the lamp which illumines all continents—having attained its birth from the moth and having never again undergone destruction by the heat of the sun—now existing in another form, grant you radiance.
For here, the distinction is shown even without an elaborate exposition of similarity:
"The eye is not *locana* (light) itself, but rather *kajjala* (collyrium) by that [name];
it is not 'not devoid' of it, but indeed devoid of it."
But the wick of a lamp, even when joined with darkness, becomes [visible];
for it is not utterly unmanifest, and because of the soot, it remains above the fire, like a moth drawn toward the sun.
Furthermore, the wick of a lamp is destroyed by a moth and does not arise [again].

"By way of similarity" (sāmyena) means: even without that demonstration through the elaboration (prapañca), that is, the continuous discourse (prabandha), using its own words, which constitutes a comparison (upamā).

This is what is meant: the simile (*upamā*), being perceived as such, assists the figure of contrast (*vyatireka*) and does not require its own explicit verbal expression. Therefore, the simile based on a pun (*śleṣopamā*) has not been employed here as an assistant to the contrast.
Now, although this may not be the case elsewhere...

In this case as well, that [beauty] is acquired solely through its inclination toward that [object]; for in the absence of such inclination, it lacks the quality of being an inherent cause of loveliness. Thus, this simile based on paronomasia (śleṣopamā) does not even deserve the status of a separate figure of speech.
As he says: "Not here."

Having grasped in his heart that this [argument] is unestablished because it is sublated by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), he addresses one who denies self-awareness. [The phrase] "ujvalā śrīryayā sā" (she by whom a brilliant splendor has been manifested) refers to the wick.
He shows the dissimilarity with the wick of a lamp by saying "dīpavarti" and so forth.
With the intended meaning that "tamaḥ-kajjalam" signifies both darkness and collyrium, he says "tamasāpi" and so forth.
The grammatical connection is: "We shall smear [her] with collyrium. The evidence for her being joined with both [qualities] is:
"because she is utterly unmanifest."

Regarding the statement that "having attained birth from a moth, it did not again meet its destruction by a moth," the author points out the dissimilarity (vaidharmya) residing in the wick with the words "from a locust" (*śalabhāt*).
According to Amara, "the two *pataṅgas* are the sun and the locust.
Likewise, it should be understood that the wick of the lamp has "dull splendor during the day."
The connection is with the phrase "presentation by its own word.
He states the meaning: "this," and so forth.
[He explains it as] "beneficial."
The sense is that this is because the negative comparison (*vyatireka*) contains within it a simile (*upamā*).
"By its own throat" means by its own word;
"taken up" means expressed by its own word.
"Is it not so," and so forth.
"Elsewhere" means in passages such as "upon the departure of many eons," and so on.
The word "iha" means "in such cases as 'you are red,'" and so forth; that is,
by way of being intent upon that [negation], namely, by way of having exclusion (*vyatireka*) as its primary purport.
The meaning is "by way of being a favorer through exclusion" (vyatirekānugrāhakatvena);
"of that [intuition] itself" is the sense;
"iti" is used in the sense of a reason (hetau).

In this context, regarding the verse beginning with "raktas tvam" (you are red) and so forth: the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the figure] does not indeed possess the status of a separate ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
However, the sense is that it partakes in the relationship of the favored and the favorer along with the distinction;
