"expression" (*abhidhā*) means the act of expressing (*abhidhāna*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "His own," etc.
Regarding the statement in the *Vṛtti*—"the emotion called wonder (*vismaya*) appears"—he asks for what purpose this was said, and replies: "By way of an example," etc.
This is an elaboration of exactly what was stated [earlier] by the word "appears": "wonder," and so forth.
The word "it appears" (*pratibhāti*) is to be supplied [to the previous sentence]. Regarding the phrase "he shows," he states the reason: "due to the connection with favor" (*anugrahayogāt*).
The meaning is that there exists a relationship of the favored and the favorer (*anugrāhyānugrāhakabhāva*) between contradiction (*virodha*) and punning (*śleṣa*).
"Of one" (*eketi*) means that the absence of whatever cause there may be for either abandoning or grasping [one of two things].

He states—by saying "of its own body, more than"—that he intends this [phrase] to be connected also with the word "exclusion" (*vyatireka*) in the expression "only by way of being denotable" (*vācyatayaiva*). Or, for example:
The elephants, whose ichor flows in unbroken streams from temples fashioned like golden lotuses, possess a fragrance produced by the very pollen of his lotus-like arms.
The great elephants, whose flow of rut was unbroken and who crushed the fragrance of the golden lotuses of [his] wounded hearts, were like the circumference of his arms encircling him.

(Thus the shadow. Here, the *śleṣa* (paronomasia), which supports the shadow of the metaphor (*rūpaka*), appears as a primary expressed meaning (*vācya*). And that [metaphor] is an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) that is merely implied (*ākṣipta*) where its nature is not stated by another word; however, where its nature is explicitly stated by another word, it is not so. [In the example: "By the power of reflecting upon the meaning of the word *bhujaṅga*, the word *viṣa*, although denoting water, does not stop there, but rather expresses a second meaning characterized by *hālāhala* [poison]. *Locana*: By the force of considering the meaning of the word *bhujaṅga*, the word *viṣa*, even while denoting water, does not [remain at that], but rather expresses a second meaning characterized by *hālāhala*.
For without that designation, the act of naming itself would remain incomplete.
However, the meaning of "whirling" and so forth, up to "death," is indeed common [to all].
Those very minds of the enemy—which are like golden lotuses—have been shattered because they have been rendered hopeless.
Because they possess essence (*sāra*), by virtue of those [qualities] acting as causes,
the words *mahima* (greatness),

*parimala* (fragrance), and *dāna* (gift)— following the term *gajendra* (lord of elephants)— convey the meanings of majesty, fragrance, and rutting-fluid, even though these words also denote [respectively] greatness, scent, and the act of giving.
Since verbal operations do not cease until completion, even the second meaning, which has been described in the aforementioned manner, is indeed expressed.

Having thus demonstrated what is excluded by the word *ākṣipta* (implied), he says "And that" (*sa ca*) in order to show what is excluded by the particle *eva* (only/indeed). This occurs when a word capable of conveying the sense of fearlessness is employed.
Having stated the reason for the restriction to one particular object, he establishes the *śleṣa* (punning) in the passage beginning with "bhujaga" and so on.

To facilitate comprehension, he demonstrates the essential meaning of the text already spoken and that which is yet to be spoken, beginning with "for the sake of both" (*ubhayārtha*) and ending with "this is the intended purport" (*iti tātparyam*).
When a word is employed that is capable— that is, competent— to convey both meanings,

there occurs a restriction or limitation of the denotative function (*abhidhā*) to one of the two objects; this is the technical usage of *dhvani* as a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) arising from the resonance (*anuraṇana*) of the word's power.
In that case, there is indeed the designation of verbal ornaments (vācyālaṅkāra) such as *vakrokti* and so forth;
for example,
[the verse] "yena dhvastamanobhavena" ("by whom the mind-born [Kāma] was destroyed").
Or where, on the contrary, there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) indicating the presence of a second denotative operation (*abhidhā-vyāpāra*),
as for instance in "tasyā vinā" and so forth; in such cases, [the suffix] "camahia" must necessarily occur at the end.
Thus, it is clear that an object is indeed denotable.
Even in cases where there exists a restricting factor for denotation—such as context (prakaraṇa) and so forth—confining it to a single meaning, denotation does not transfer to a second meaning;
in such a case, that second meaning is said to be "suggested" (ākṣipta).

Even in that case, if there exists such a word by which that restrictive factor—context and so forth—is rendered ineffective in its power, then for that very reason, that denotative power (abhidhā-śakti), though sublated, is as if restored; thus, the intended meaning is that even there, it is not the domain of suggestion (dhvani).
The word *ca* has the sense of *api* and is displaced in its order; the meaning is: "even though it is suggested," or "even though it has begun to be immediately conceived as being suggested."
But this is not a restatement (*ākṣepa*);

rather, by means of another word, it effects a counter-exception (*pratiprasava*) to the previously stated [prohibition], thereby becoming something whose nature has been explicitly expressed. By the use of the word "again" (*punar*), he indicates that this explains the counter-exception.
The meaning is that by that very word "eva," the non-existence implied [by the absence of conjunction] is excluded;
this connects with the term *bālapriyā*, and its cause is conjunction and so forth.
The term *iti* means "in such passages as";
its connection is with the word *yatra*.
"Designation of the second" means the expression of the meaning of the second [case].
In the passage beginning with "without that" and ending with "camahia," [this applies].
The meaning is: "in the four examples beginning with 'even without that'.
Regarding the word "there" (tatra):
it means "in the four [verses] beginning with 'by which' and 'of that'."
