"So 'rthaḥ" (that object) means the second object.
Regarding the phrase "tatrāpi" (even there), and so forth: [the commentary continues].
*Tādgagiti* is a restatement of *yeneti*.
*Yeneti* means "by which word."
"Having its power struck down" means that its capacity for regulation has been obstructed.

"Possessing the power of denotation" refers to the power of denoting a second meaning; although this power was sublated and rendered unfavorable to cognition, it has now been "reinstated," meaning it has been made favorable to cognition once again.
Thus it is said.
And as for the reading "iveti," the word "ca" means the word "ca" found in the phrase "sa ca. "Bhinnakrama" means [the word is] out of its proper sequence.
The meaning is that the subsequent word, having been implied, should be supplied.
The phrase "even though implied" (*ākṣipto 'pi*) is explained by the words "by way of being implied" (*ākṣiptatayā*), and so forth.
By means of the particle *api*, which conveys the sense of possibility, he states the meaning that is understood: "but not," and so forth.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "that is the ornament" means *śleṣa* (paronomasia);
that is to say, it refers to the second meaning.
The explanation of the passage beginning with "by another word" is provided by the words "word," and so forth.
"By another word" means by a specific word.
Now, one might object that it is impossible to designate *śleṣa* (paronomasia) by another word such as *saleśa* (possessing paronomasia); therefore, he says "of the denotation," and so forth.
"Of the denotation" means of the denotation of a second meaning.
"By the word *punar*" means by the word *punar* occurring in the phrase "where again" (*yatra punar*).
It has been explained.
The meaning is "as previously stated.
He states the conclusion with the words "by that" (*tena*).
[He refers to] "by means of indirect speech" (*vakrokti*) and so forth.

The authors of the *Kuvalayānanda* call this very *vakrokti* (indirect speech) *vivṛtokti* (explicit speech). "O Keśava, because my vision was stolen by passion for the cowherds, I saw nothing at all; for that very reason, O Lord, I have stumbled—will you not support me as I fall? You alone are the refuge for all weak women whose minds are distressed by the uneven path. May Hari, thus addressed with a hint of reproach by a cowherd girl, protect us for a long time in the cow-pen.
Locana said: "O Keśava, because my vision was stolen by the dust from the cows, I saw nothing; for that reason, I stumbled on this path.
Since I have fallen, what indeed is the reason that you do not support me with your hand?"
Since you alone are pre-eminently powerful, you are the refuge, the support, and the means for all the weak— including children, the elderly, women,
and others whose minds are distressed and who are unable to proceed over uneven terrain;
even though these words have their denotative power restricted by the context to such a meaning, nevertheless, when the second meaning is explained, the denotative power is not obstructed.
By the phrase "being with a trace" (*saleśam*), [the notion of] existence is revived.
Here, "with a trace" means "with an indication" (*sasūcanam*); for becoming diminished is indeed nothing other than an indication.
"O Keśava! O Lord of the Cowherds!
By a glance stolen by passion"—the connection is either "by a glance stolen by Keśava's own passion" or "by a glance whose passion has been stolen."
"I have stumbled; I have become one whose conduct is shattered; I am fallen"—such was the state of my husband toward me. "The only one" refers to you alone, who possess extraordinary good fortune.

The meaning is that, for all women whose minds are distressed by love, he is the "resort"—that is, the means of protecting their lives—when served as a way to dispel the turbidity of jealousy. Thus, the commentary on the word *parāga* in the *Bālapriyā* explains it as "dust" (*dhūlī*).
The connection is: "I have stumbled on the path."
With the intention that the word *eka* (one) signifies the primary meaning, he says: "exceedingly powerful.
The explanation of *viṣameṣu* (in uneven places) is: "on high and low ground.
The clarification of the intended meaning of *khinnamanasām* (of those with weary minds) is: "to go," and so forth.
The connection is: "these words.
This means words such as *keśava*, *gopa*, *rāga*, and so forth.
The term "by the context" (*prakaraṇena*) is connected with both "restricted" (*niyantrite*) and "constrained" (*niruddhe*).
Regarding the phrase "the power of denotation" (*abhidhāśakti*),
the word "of these" (*eteṣām*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
It has been revived, that is, restored.
He explains the "revival" with the words beginning with "atra" and so forth.
The meaning of "saleśam" is "with an indication.
To the question "How is this obtained?", he says: "alpa... and so forth.
He explains the second meaning with the words "O Keśava," and so forth.
The intention is that "Keśava" and "Gopa" constitute two vocatives.
"O Lord" (*svāmin*) is the gloss for "O Master" (*nātha*).
He states it in another way, beginning with "by Keśava's gaze" and so forth.
"By Keśava's gaze" means by the passion (*uparāga*) directed toward Keśava, that is, by his affection (*anurāga*).
He says "the state of being a husband" (*patitā*) regarding her, explaining it as "the state of being a lord" (*bhartṛbhāvam*).
The prose passage beginning with "atrāntare" is found in the second chapter (*ucchvāsa*) of the *Harṣacarita*.
Regarding the phrase "two months":
the meaning is the two-month period consisting of Caitra and Vaiśākha.
That which has white (*dhavala*) attics (*aṭṭa*) is "white-attic," and that which is laughter (*hāsa*) is "white-attic-laughter" (*dhavalāṭṭahāsa*).

"Full-blown jasmine" (*phullamallikā*) refers to blossomed (*phulla*) jasmine (*mallikā*). He explains the compound *phullamallikā-dhavalāṭṭahāsa* as a *vyadhikaraṇa-bahuvrīhi* (a possessive compound with non-co-referential members), stating: "that [place] wherein there is the white-attic-laughter of full-blown jasmine.
Let all such compounds of this kind be, if they so desire, the domain of *vācyaśleṣa* (verbal punning).

However, wherever another figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*), though implied by the force of the context, is manifested through the power of the words (*śabdaśakti*), that is entirely the domain of *dhvani*.

For example: "In the meantime, bringing to an end the pair of seasons known as the Flowering Season, there unfolded the Great Time (*mahākāla*) called Summer, whose loud laughter was the white blossoms of the full-blown jasmine.
And likewise: "High, with shimmering necklaces, darkened by black aloe-wood paste..."
Whom did the weight of the slender maiden's breasts not make desirous?
Having established the subject matter (*viṣaya*) for the *dhvani*, Locana says: "In which... [and so on].
He concludes by referring to the pair of two months that constitute the season of flowers (*kusumasamaya*).

It is such that its white, heart-pleasing market-stalls (*aṭṭa*) and shops (*āpaṇa*) are present, and where there is the "laughter"—that is, the blooming and whiteness—of full-blown jasmine flowers (*mallikā*).
If one were to explain it as "his white loud laughter is indeed the full-blown jasmine," then this would be equivalent to [the phrase] "born from the cloud-serpent.

Furthermore, he is a "great" time (*kāla*) because of his connection with the difficulty of enduring the length of the day. Here, the power of denotation (*abhidhā-śakti*) is constrained by the context of the description of the season.

For this very reason, Mahākāla and others, rejecting the maxim that "the conventional meaning of a whole is stronger than the conventional meaning of its parts," maintain that these words fulfill their purpose by expressing this very [suggested] meaning;
the subsequent comprehension of the meaning arises solely through the function of suggestion (dhvani), which is rooted in the power of the word itself.

On this point, some hold the following view: "Since a different expressive power (abhidhā) for these words was previously observed in a different meaning, therefore, when such a different meaning occurs, [the comprehension follows]. [The commentary on *hāsa* is: *vikāsa* (expansion/blossoming).]
Thus;
its further explanation is: "it becomes white" (sitimeti), meaning the state of being white (sita-bhāva).
The cool one.
He states the seed for the abandonment of the meaning as it was heard: "In full bloom," etc.;
this would be equivalent to that.
The sense is that, in such a case, there would be no illustration of the intended *dhvani* (suggested meaning).
The phrase beginning with "day" (*dinetyādi*) serves to establish its greatness; the meaning is that it results from the conjunction of the length of the day and the difficulty of enduring it.
"Manifested by the power of the context" (*sāmarthyākṣipta*) means being revealed by the power of the meaning acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakāribhūta*).
"Another ornament" (*alaṅkārāntara*) refers to a specific type of poetic figure (*alaṅkāra-viśeṣa*).

"It shines forth through the power of the word" (*śabdaśaktyā prakāśate*) means that it appears primarily through the power of the word; this explains what was stated in the *Vṛtti* beginning with "here," and so forth.

Those whose denotative powers (*abhidhā-śakti*) are restricted—meaning they are regulated toward their respective meanings—by means of either the description of the seasons (*ṛtu-varṇana-rūpa*) or the introduction (*prastāva*) to that description of the seasons;
for this very reason, [they are understood] from the context alone.
Such is the rule (*nyāya*).
As it has been said: "Etymology is stronger than usage.
This refers to that very point;
the meaning is that it refers to the point previously stated.
Immediately following that is the comprehension of the meaning (*arthāvagati*).

This means that there arises an understanding of such meanings as: "concluding the era of the Kṛta and other ages," "performing a loud laugh white as jasmine," "the terrifying Mahākāla," and "Mahān, a specific deity who is the destroyer of the world.
Here, he shows the differences of opinion with the words "In this regard, some... and so forth.

"Of these" means of Mahākāla and the others. "The eye" refers to the perception of a cognizer who possesses the capacity to understand their denotation; since the cognition arises from these [words] whose denotative power is restricted, it occurs solely through the function of suggestion (*dhvanana*). Thus, the state of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatva*) is rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūlatva*).
And thus it is not contradictory [to our position].

Others, however, say: "That very denotation (abhidhā) is the second [function]; since it relies upon the capacity of the meaning—which consists in its similarity to a terrifying deity of summer—as a cooperative factor, it is therefore called the operation of suggestion (dhvanana)."
However, some maintain that in the case of *śabdaśleṣa* (verbal pun), since there is a difference in the words themselves,
and even in the case of *arthaśleṣa* (semantic pun), since there is a difference in the expressive powers (*śakti*), a second word is brought in according to that view.
And that [second word] is sometimes brought in through the operation of denotation (*abhidhā*), as in the example "The white horse runs" (*śveto dhāvati*) given as a reply to two different questions.
In cases such as questions and answers, there is the status of a verbal figure (*vācyālaṅkāratā*) therein; however,

where [the meaning] is perceived— that is, known— through the very operation of suggestion (*dhvanana-vyāpāra*) in another sense, such as the specific deity who is the destroyer of the world, [that is a case of suggested meaning].
"Seen" (dṛṣṭa) means that by whom the capacity for denoting that [object] has been seen— that is, known. "Restrained" (niyantritā) means...
The meaning is that [the word] is restricted to its contextual sense by means of the context and so forth.
From these words, such as "Mahākāla" and others,
there arises a cognition, namely, the apprehension of another meaning.
The word "iti" indicates the reason. Regarding the phrase "because of being suggested":

since the cognition of that other meaning occurs only for a cognizer who has already grasped the denotative power (*abhidhā-śakti*) of those respective words with respect to their [original] meanings, [the meaning is therefore suggested].

Therefore, the meaning is that [the cognition] is rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūlatva*), and since that cognition arises solely from the operation of *dhvani*— because there is no further operation beyond the function of direct denotation (*abhidhā*)— the object thereof is of the nature of the suggested (*vyaṅgyatva*).
This view is accepted by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* and others.
He states another opinion with the words "others," etc., [beginning with] "the second is that which possesses denotation."
The meaning is that what was previously grasped is precisely the denotation of the second [meaning]. The connection is that it is said to be of the nature of the function of suggestion (*dhvanana*).
To the question "Why?", he says: "Because of the object," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the force of the meaning" (*arthasāmarthyam*):
the meaning is that it is the "force of the meaning" as stated in the text by the expression "implied by the force" (*sāmarthyakṣiptam*).
To the question "What is that?", he says: "Of the summer," and so forth.
"Terrible" (bhīṣaṇā) means that it consists of the visible forms of specific deities through the dissolution of the eon and so forth. "As a cooperative cause" (sahakāritvena) means:
The ellipsis is "for the purpose of making another meaning known.
Regarding the phrase "from that," and so forth:
the functions such as denotation (*abhidhā*) and the rest consist essentially of specific powers conducive to the cognition of meaning.
Their distinction arises from a difference in auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).
The power of a word to convey a meaning through the mere assistance of the apprehension of convention (*saṅketa*) is called "denotation" (*abhidhā*).

However, the power to convey a meaning through the assistance of factors other than the apprehension of convention—such as the inherent capacity of the object—is "suggestion" (*dhvanana*); thus, the point here is that this [power] is said to be of the nature of suggestion.
"One," and so forth.
"Tāvat" (so much/for now) is used in the sense of agreement.
The connection is with the words "if there is a difference in the word."
The meaning is: "because of the existence of difference.
Regarding "due to the difference in capacity" (śaktibhedāt), the meaning is: "due to the difference in capacities conducive to the cognition of those respective objects."
"Due to the difference in meaning"—this is the sense.
"Therein" means:
in both cases of verbal punning (*śabdaśleṣa*) and semantic punning (*arthaśleṣa*).
"It is brought" means by way of connection;
that is the second word.
"Sometimes" means:
when there is [evidence such as] context and so forth for both meanings, at that time.
"From the function of denotation" means: [from the primary expressive operation].
The sense is that two meanings must necessarily be denoted;
the word "is brought" (*ānīyate*) is to be supplied [from the previous context].
He states an example for this: "Just as," and so forth.
"Of the two" means: "Who is running away from here? and "Endowed with what qualities?"—the meaning is that there are these two questions.
Regarding "śveta": *śvā* means "dog," and *itaḥ* means "gone"; thus, *śveta* means "white" or "pale.
It is also used in the beginning of questions and answers as *ve*.
“That which is performed by the wise as an unbroken series of inquiries,
or through sentences in a learned assembly, they know that to be *praśnottara* (question-and-answer).”
Such is the definition.
The word "locana" (eye) has been brought forward;

in that context, it is logical that even by the force of another word, its other meaning—which is being understood—is indeed [the primary] one, because it is based on what is being perceived. Thus it is said.
But as for the other [view]—in the explanation of the second position, by that very capacity of meaning (arthasāmarthya), the denotative function (abhidhā) itself is reinstated;
consequently, the second meaning is indeed denoted and not merely suggested.
However, immediately thereafter, the metaphorical identification (rūpaṇā) of that apprehended second meaning with the contextual first meaning certainly does manifest.
Nor does it arise from any other verbal function; rather, it arises from the operation of suggestion (*dhvanana*),
because in that case, no power of denotation whatsoever can even be suspected,
and for that [suggestion], the second power of the word is the root.
Likewise, because [the function of] *rūpaṇā* (metaphorical identification) would not arise without it, it is therefore correct to say that this is *alaṅkāradhvani* (suggestion of poetic figures).
And it will be stated later: "Lest the fault of expressing an incoherent meaning should follow," and so forth.
In the previous case, however, the lack of connection was already refuted by the very term *saleśa* (possessing a hint).
As in the example from *Bālapriyā*: “‘Who am I?’—the cave speaks; what is the answer to this question? How is it that you do not understand how it was said? Why then, O friend, do you trouble me?”
Thus:
here, the phrase "you treat with contempt" (*kadarthayasi*) is expressed by the syllables *ka* and *tha*, while the response "you show [it]" (*daryasi*) follows.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the verse beginning with "by which [it] is destroyed" (*yena dhvastam*) and so forth is included.
Regarding the term "vācya":
the meaning is "a verbal ornament such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and so forth.
The implication is that both meanings are contextual (*prakṛta*).
"Wherein" means in passages such as "the season of flowers" (kusumasamaya) and so forth.
"Precisely through the function of suggestion" (dhvananavyāpārāt).
The meaning is: "precisely because [the word] possesses suggestiveness through the restriction of its denotation to the contextual sense.
Regarding the phrase "by the power of another word," the meaning is: "by the denotative power (*abhidhā-śakti*) of another word."
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is "even that which is being practiced" (*pratipannam api*).

"Based on what is perceived" (*pratīyamāna*) means that the word (*śabda*) which is understood through *dhvani* (suggestion) is its basis; the meaning is "because it has as its root the function of *dhvani*. In other words, it is because it is rooted in the operation of *dhvani*.
"Only that which is being perceived is the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya).
Regarding the "explanation of the second position," this means the explanation stated in the passage beginning with "But others... and so forth.
"By that" means by the efficacy of the meaning;
"the second designation" [is as follows].
The meaning is that there is an expression of a second object; the connection is "of that second object which has been apprehended.
[The term] "rūpaṇā" means...
The meaning is "the superimposition of non-difference"; that is to say, the non-difference of that which is being superimposed.
This is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for similes and other such figures. As for the phrase "that [simile] first":
"That is the transformation" (sā rūpaṇā),
and so forth;
"it appears" (bhāti) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
The meaning is that it does not appear from anything other than the word;
rather, the intention is that it appears from the word alone.
Regarding the word "therein":
"In the state of being subject to transformation" (rūpaṇāya) is the meaning; "in that" (tasyām) means "in the state of being subject to transformation."
"Because of non-arising" means because the second object, which would serve as its counterpart, is not perceived;
for this very reason, it is because mere transformation and so forth are what is manifested.
"Ornament" (alaṅkāra) means metaphor (rūpaka) and so forth. Thus it is logical.
The meaning is that this statement is logical.
Otherwise, since the second meaning would be suggested (vyaṅgya), there would even be the designation of "suggestion of a fact" (vastudhvani); such is the intention.
This will be explained [later].

The word "in the context" (vṛttau) is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the phrase "in the poetic figure"]. The sense is that by stating "there the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison must be imagined," it is made known that only that specific aspect is what is suggested (vyaṅgya).

The passage beginning with "when [the object] is manifested through the power of the word" (*śabdaśaktyā prakāśamāne*) is also favorable to this position; he states it incidentally as "in the previous [instance]," etc.
"In the previous [instance]" refers to the passage beginning with "by the sight of Keśava. It was "refuted" (*nirākṛtā*).

For in that [verse], it is indeed the second meaning that is intended as primary, while the first meaning is subordinate—just as in the following example: "May the cows—who bestow joy upon all creatures; who, with their waters drawn forth at the appointed time, are scattered in every direction during the forenoon of creation, yet gather together as the day comes to rest; who are like ships for crossing the ocean of worldly fear born of long-standing suffering under the blazing sun; and who are the supreme purifiers—produce in you immeasurable and unsurpassed delight. In this verse, the primary intention is the praise of the cows as divine vessels for salvation, whereas the description of their physical behavior (being scattered in the morning and gathering in the evening) is merely incidental. Thus, the first meaning is not the principal one.

In these examples, since another non-contextual meaning is manifested through the power of the words, one must—by the force of the context—infer a relationship of simile (upamānopameyabhāva) between the non-contextual and contextual meanings so that the sentence does not result in expressing an unrelated sense.

Thus, this paronomasia (śleṣa) is implied by the sense (arthākṣipta) and is not directly expressed by the words; therefore, the domain of suggestion (dhvani) characterized by the resonance of paronomasia is indeed distinct from paronomasia itself.
Others [have argued] that the lack of connection (*asambaddhatā*) has been refuted by the word "even" (*api*) itself;
however, the intended meaning is that the lack of connection does not appear at all in the phrase "by whom [it] was destroyed" (*yena dhvasta*).

Furthermore, the lack of connection is refuted by the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "of him even without," by the word "excessive" (*adhika*) in the phrase "praiseworthy" (*ślādhyā*), and by the metaphor (*rūpaka*) in the phrase "delusion" (*bhramim*), and so forth.
"With waters" means with drinking water and with milk;
"withdrawal" (saṃhāra) means destruction and bringing together in one place.
The rays are "gāvaḥ" (cows) and they are also "surabhayaḥ" (fragrant). "Expressing a disconnected meaning" means that it is simply not being cognized.
The phrase "the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object compared" means that the intention is to conceal that [relationship];
by this, it is also made known that there is no such thing as metaphorical identification (*rūpaṇa*) and so forth in that case.
"It does not appear at all" means that both [the individual soul and Brahman] are under discussion as objects of praise; this is the intended sense.
Up to the word "tātparyam," the view is that of "the others."
Those who follow this opinion, such as the author of the *Kuvalayānanda* and others, [cite] the verse beginning with "annata":
"Where the necklace is shimmering... and so forth.

And where there is a gushing stream, that [youth] is like a dark cloud—black with black aloe-wood incense; "payodhara" refers both to a breast and to a rain-cloud. Of that lovely woman and of the rainy season, which youth, traveler, or [lover] does it not delight?
The phrase "dattānandā" is found in the *Sūryaśataka*.
At the appropriate time, those [rays] which were first drawn in and subsequently emitted constitute the most excellent purification of the radiant-rayed Sun.
He explains the words to be interpreted—namely "payobhiḥ" and so forth—as follows: "locane" (in the eyes).
In the case of the *raśmi* (rays) interpretation, [the offering is] with waters; in the case of the *surabhi* (fragrant) interpretation, it is with milk.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), "denoting a meaning unrelated to the context" means:
denoting a meaning that is not connected with the relevant subject matter.
"Do not fall into [this] error" means: "Let it not become an object of such an erroneous application.
To avoid the objection that this would lead to an undesirable consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he states the underlying intention: "precisely as something not being cognized."
The meaning is that the expression of an incoherent sense is simply not perceived by connoisseurs (*sahṛdaya*).
Furthermore, poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) do indeed occur in *dhvani* where the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) takes the form of a resonance (*anusvāna*) rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśakti*).
For instance, even "contradiction" (*virodha*) is seen to exist in the form of a resonance rooted in the power of words.

As in Bhaṭṭabāṇa’s description of the region called Sthāṇvīśvara: "Where the women walk like elephants and yet possess good character; they are fair-skinned yet devoted to wealth; they have the crimson glow of lotuses and yet have faces as pure as white teeth; and they breathe with the fragrance of wine."
For here, it cannot be said that this is either a directly expressed contradiction (*virodha*) or a *śleṣa* (punning) that follows its shadow;
because the figure of speech "contradiction" has not been manifested by the word directly.
For where the figure of speech "contradiction" is communicated by a direct word, there, in the case of a punning expression, the directly expressed figure of speech is contradiction.

Therefore, according to Locana, in this form of comparison, operations such as exclusion (vyatireka) and concealment (nihnava), being merely functional in nature, constitute the primary locus of repose because the perception of aesthetic relish (rasa) culminates there;
it is not the object of comparison (upameya) and so forth. This should be understood to apply to all instances of suggestion through poetic figures (alaṅkāradhvani).
"By implication" means by the function of suggestion (*dhvanana-vyāpāra*).
"O Mātaṅga! [is the address].
They walk like outcasts (mātaṅga) and yet they approach those very outcasts; this is a contradiction.
They are devoted to worldly riches, yet they are also devoted to that place where Mahādeva has departed.

"Possessing jewels of the color of the *pajha* [lotus]," meaning possessing a redness similar to that of a lotus; "whose faces are pure and stainless with white teeth," meaning whose faces are as pure as those of eminent Brahmins (*dhavala-dvija*)—that is, like excellent twice-born men.
Regarding the phrase "for where... (*yatra hi*):
In that case of paronomasia (śleṣa) which takes the form of poetry,
whatever contradiction or paronomasia occurs therein constitutes the scope of "commingling" (saṅkara);
the meaning is that it becomes its subject matter.
Of what? Of the verbal ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*), or of the state of being a verbal ornament (*vācyālaṅkṛtitva*); such is the meaning.
"By that" refers to the intended meaning (*bhāvārtha*).
By that... [the sentence continues].

The meaning is that this is because [the text] describes the conceptualization of the relationship between the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) as being of the nature of a simile (*upamā*), and because that [simile] serves as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Regarding the phrase "the metaphorical representation of a simile" (*upamārūpaṇā*) and so forth:

it means that in instances of suggestion (*dhvani*) such as the metaphorical representation of a simile (*upamārūpaka*), there occurs precisely the cognitive act of perceiving a simile, a metaphorical representation, and so on.
"Like a Mātaṅga" means like an elephant. And "the Śabaras."
"And Caṇḍālas" is the meaning. "Thus there is a contradiction" means that the act of approaching a Caṇḍāla woman contradicts a character consisting of good conduct.
And that is resolved by the first meaning;
the same should be understood for what follows as well.
"Gaurīḥ" means those who are fair-complexioned and those who are mountain-dwellers (Pārvatīs).
‘Śyāmāḥ’ means those who are dark-complexioned and in the prime of youth. In the commentary, it says: ‘Because [the quality] is not explicitly expressed by the word [itself].
The intention is that in phrases such as ‘possessing good character’ (śīlavatyaḥ), the particle *ca* serves the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaya*).
The phrase "or [there is] a commingling" means that the word "or" (*vā*) in the expressions "of contradiction" (*virodhasya*) or "of paronomasia" (*śleṣasya*) indicates their commingling (*saṅkara*).
The passage beginning with "it" (*sa*) and so forth is an elaboration of the very term "its being the object" (*tasya viṣayatvam*).
He demonstrates the syntactic connection of the phrase "of the expressed ornament" (*vācyālaṅkārasya*) with the word "the scope" (*viṣayatvam*) by means of the question "Of what? and so forth.
He states the literal meaning of "of the expressed ornament" as "of the expressed figure" (*vācyālaṅkṛteḥ*).
He states the intended meaning as "of the state of being an expressed ornament" (*vācyālaṅkṛtitvasya*).
Or, it may be the province of *śleṣa* (paronomasia), as in that same work: "Like a collection of mutually contradictory things;
for instance, 'her radiant form, though possessed of nearby darkness [or: though possessing young girls and darkness]' and so forth."

Or as it is by me alone: "Bow down to Hari-Kṛṣṇa, the sole refuge of all, the imperishable Lord of lords, the master of intellects, the fourfold self, the actionless crusher of enemies, the wielder of the discus."

For here, a contradiction in the form of an *anusvāna* (latent resonance) rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśakti*) is clearly perceived. A distinction (*vyatireka*) of this kind is also observed, as in my own verse: "Those which illuminate the sky, having severed the darkness, and those which shine upon the eyes like nails... In such cases, it is easy to say that the status of a verbal ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*) belongs either to the contradiction (*virodha*) or to the paronomasia (*śleṣa*). This is the sense.
In the phrase "bāleṣu keśeṣv andhakāraḥ," *andhakāraḥ* refers to blackness (*kārṣṇyam*), while *bālaḥ* means both hair and fresh darkness (*tamaḥ*).
Now, even in cases such as "mātaṅga" and so forth, the *ca* (and) used for the two attributes serves precisely to indicate contradiction (*virodha*).

Otherwise, if "ca" were intended to have the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), it would not appear anywhere—either after each word (*pratidharma*) or at the end of all the words. With this intention, he provides another example, beginning with "yathā":
"How can that which is a refuge (*śaraṇa*) be a non-abode (*agṛha*) in its imperishable form? How can one who is not a master of intellect (*dhīśa*) be a master of intellects (*dhiyām īśa*)?"
How can he who is Hari be Kapila?
How can he who possesses fourfold prowess have a self that is inactive?
How can he who is the destroyer of enemies and those joined with enemies bear the discus out of great respect for it?
"Contradiction" (virodha) means the state of being contradictory (virodhana). "Is perceived" (pratiyate) means...
The sense is that it is not explicitly stated by anyone.

Thus, the meaning of the sentence is that the state of being the object (viṣayatva) belongs to the mixture of contradiction and paronomasia (virodha-śleṣa-saṅkara) as defined by its status as a verbal figure (vācyālaṅkāra).
Here, "state of being the object" should be understood as the state of being the locus (āśrayatva).
He states the result [of the argument] with "tatraiva" and so forth.
"Bhāsvanmūrtiḥ" means one whose body is radiant, and also one whose form is that of the sun. He introduces another example beginning with "sarva" by saying "nanu" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "he who made [the conjunction] between two attributes":

the meaning is that in such instances as "those who walk like elephants and are virtuous" or "those who are fair-complexioned and devoted to wealth," the particle *ca* occurs at the end of the words denoting the two attributes.
By the use of the restrictive particle *eva*, the exclusion of its function as an indicator of mere conjunction (*samuccaya*) is established.
He states the reason for what has been said, beginning with "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth.
"Otherwise" means in the absence of its function as an indicator of contradiction; the word "then" (*tadā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
Otherwise, if the particle *ca* were intended in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), it would have to occur either after each individual property (*dharma*) or at the end of all the properties.
The logical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the term] might not exist in some instances.

Regarding the reading *sarvadharmānta*, there is also the reading *sarvaśabdānta*. If the particle *ca* here has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), it is like saying: "Bring the pot, and the cloth, and the book."
The meaning is that such expressions as "bring the jar, the cloth, and the book" or "bring the jar, the cloth, and the book" would be possible [if the objects were not distinct].
The statement beginning with "house, non-house," etc., expresses contradictory meanings.
"Refuge" (śaraṇa) means a protector;
"inexhaustible" (akṣaya) means devoid of destruction—such meanings should be understood as non-contradictory. "Virodhana" means the act of obstructing.
"Clearly" (sphuṭam) means "without doubt. He states that the meaning of "is perceived" (pratīyate) is "is suggested" (dhvanyate), by saying: "it is not stated by anyone."

May those feet of the Lord of Day bring you prosperity—those which nourish the splendor of the lotus yet cast the luster of the actual lotus into shade; those which shine upon the crowns of kings and those which tread upon the heads of the immortals.

In this way, there are other varieties of *dhvani* where the suggested meaning takes the form of a resonance (*anusvāna*) rooted in the power of words; these should be pursued by the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) on their own.
However, for fear of making the book too voluminous, no detailed elaboration of them has been made here.
But another type arises from the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktyudbhava*), wherein the meaning itself is manifested.
That which, by its own nature and with intentional focus, manifests another object without the use of explicit words; // DhvK_2.22 //

But another [type of suggestion] arises from the power of the meaning (arthaśaktyudbhava), wherein a certain meaning is revealed which, by its own force, indicates another reality through its primary purport, even without explicit statement. (22)
Those which shine with their nails in the sky do not necessarily shine in the atmosphere;
both types consist of rays, meaning they take the form of parts such as fingers, heels, and so forth. //21//

Having thus explained *dhvani* arising from the power of the word (*śabdaśaktyudbhava*), he demonstrates that which arises from the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktyudbhava*) with the words "artha... [and so on].
The word "other" (*anya*) means other than that which arises from the power of the word.

The phrase "by its own inherent intentionality" (*svatastātparyeṇa*) is intended to exclude the function of denotation (*abhidhāvyāpāra*); it expresses the function of suggestion (*dhvananavyāpāra*), but does not refer to the power of intentionality (*tātparyaśakti*).
For it has been stated previously that [the word *kha*] is exhausted merely in the cognition of its denoted meaning (*vācyārtha*).
With this very intention, [the commentary] says "kham" in the *Bālapriyā*;
*kham* means the sky (*ākāśa*).
"Those rays" refers to those by which the darkness and evil have been cut down— that is, destroyed— by them. "Those" refers to the feet.
He states the expressed (*vācya*) and suggested (*vyaṅgya*) meanings of the phrase "shining with nails" (*nakhodbhāsinaḥ*) in the passage beginning with "by the nails" (*nakhaiḥ*).
Those rays which nourish the beauty—that is, the luster—of the *saroruhas*, the lotuses; those feet [are so described].
Regarding the word "cast" (*kṣipta*): [it refers to the rays].
Those rays which have eclipsed the beauty of lotuses and destroyed the splendor of lotuses,
and those feet upon the peaks and summits of the mountains (kṣitibhṛtām),
which do not shine when they tread upon— the heads of the immortals (amarāṇām) touching them at the time of prostration.
"Locane"—beginning with "aṅgulī" and so forth;
this refers to the feet.

It should be understood that through qualities such as being most completely severed [of darkness], the feet of the Lord of Day (the Sun), which are comparable to rays, possess a *vyatireka* (poetic distinction) from ordinary rays, due to their illuminating the sky and other such characteristics. // 2.1 //

In the verse beginning with "arthe," the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "But that which arises from the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktyudbhava*) is other [than suggestion]; it occurs where that meaning, even without being explicitly stated, manifests another object by its own inherent intention (*svatastātparyeṇa*)."
To the question "Why is it different?", he says in the *Locana*: "By the word," etc.
He explains the phrase "by its own inherent intention" (*svatastātparyeṇa*) with the words "by its own," and so forth;
the connection is as follows: "this [is] thus."
And the reading is "this word" (*idaṃ padam*);
"that" (*sā*) means the power of intention (*tātparyaśakti*).
"By this," and so forth.
The explanation in the commentary (*vṛtti*) of the phrase "by its own intention" is "by its own capacity"—this is the sense. [The term] "operation of the word" (*śabdavyāpāra*).
The meaning is "designation" (*abhidhā*).
In the commentary, the phrase "graceful" (*alīla*) and so forth is also an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of the downward-facing posture.
Regarding the phrase "it reveals" (*prakāśayati*):
the meaning is that it manifests [the emotion] because it possesses the power of apprehension (*anubhāva*).

One might object: "If there is a cognition of the transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) consisting of shame, then this is the domain of *dhvani* where the suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgya*), and not of *vastudhvani* (the suggestion of a fact). To this, he raises the objection with the words "And not," and so forth.
"‘It is concentrated, it is restrained,’ and so forth.

Now, one might object: is it not inconsistent here to speak of "being directly communicated by the word in the form of being denotable," given that there is a type of *dhvani* called "suggestion arising from the power of the meaning" (*arthaśaktyudbhava*), where the meaning manifests another meaning through its own capacity, entirely without the operation of the word?
Thus, while the divine sage was speaking in this manner, Pārvatī, standing by her father’s side with her face cast downward, began counting the petals of her play-lotus.

For here, the counting of the petals of the play-lotus—which has its own nature subordinated—reveals another meaning in the form of a transitory emotion (*vyabhicāribhāva*) even without the operation of words.
Nor is this the domain solely of *dhvani* with imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama-vyaṅgya*);

because where the realization of rasa and so forth arises from the excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) directly communicated by words, [that is the case].
That is the path for that [type of poetry] alone;
for example, in the *Kumārasambhava*, the description of the Goddess’s arrival while wearing ornaments of spring flowers during the context of the honey-rite,
up to the aiming of the arrows of the Mind-born [God of Love], and the description of the specific gestures of Śambhu as his fortitude was overturned.

The *Locana* explains the phrase "directly communicated by the word" (*sākṣāc-chabdanivedita*) in its commentary as follows: "where the meaning [is conveyed] by its own power" (*yatrārthaḥ svasāmarthyāt*).
The word "by itself" (*svataḥ*) is explained by the word "its own" (*sva-*) [in the compound].
He explains "without speech" as "even without the operation of words.
He provides an example with "just so.
"Another matter" refers to that which consists of shame.
Regarding the word "directly" (*sākṣāt*):

where the perception of transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*) occurs without any intervening delay due to their being of imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*), it is intended that they be conveyed by words directly; thus, there is no contradiction with what was stated previously.
For it was explained at length earlier that because transitory emotions are also "emotions" (*bhāva*), they are not to be perceived through their own specific names, and so forth.

This is what is meant: although objects such as rasa and bhāva are always suggested (dhvanyamāna) and never directly expressed (vācya), nevertheless, not all of them fall within the domain of the "imperceptible sequence" (alakṣyakrama).

For in cases where [rasa] arises instantaneously from fully manifested determinants (vibhāva), consequents (anubhāva), and transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva) that have reached the status of the permanent emotion (sthāyibhāva)...

Since its absence has already been stated previously, [the author] explains the fact that it is directly conveyed by words in the *Locana* with the passage beginning "of the transitory emotions" (*vyabhicāriṇām*), etc.

The syntactical connection is as follows: "In which case, there is a comprehension of the transitory emotions that is devoid of any intervention, occurring through their respective determinants (*vibhāva*) and so forth, such that the sequence is imperceptible."
"Free from intervention" means being without separation.
It recalls what was stated previously— "previously," and so forth—
the connection being that this has been explained at length before.
He states the essential meaning of the concluding commentary passage, "Therefore, this is another variety of sound," beginning with the words "This has been said" and so forth.
The phrase "all of the alakṣyakrama" (of that in which the sequence is unperceived) is the correct division [of the compound].
"From those residing in the sthāyin" means from those related to the sthāyin.
The passage beginning with "In nirvāṇa... is from the third canto of the *Kumārasambhava*.

By the phrase "and so forth" (*ityādi*), [the author] includes such verses as "As if slightly turned aside. However, in this case, the apprehension of rasa occurs through the medium of the transitory emotions (vyabhicāribhāva) suggested by the power of the context; therefore, this is another variety of dhvani. Locana: Let there be the manifestation of rasa therein as having an imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*).

Just as follows: Then, as if fanning his vigor—which was already largely focused on Nirvana—with the excellence of her own form, the daughter of the King of Mountains appeared, escorted by forest deities.
In such passages as these, there is a description of the nature of the complete set of objective and excitant determinants (*ālambana* and *uddīpana-vibhāva*) suitable [for the sentiment].
And because she was dear to him who was full of affection, the Three-eyed Lord proceeded to accept her;
furthermore, the Flower-bowed God fixed upon his bow an unerring arrow named "Enchantment" (*saṃmohana*).
By this, the utility of the *vibhāva* (the determinants) has been stated.
But Hara, his composure slightly shaken like the ocean at the onset of moonrise,
cast his eyes upon Umā’s face, where her lower lip was like the fruit of the *bimba*.

For here, because the Blessed Lady was already inclined toward him from the very beginning, and because he has now become intent upon her, and because of the intensification of the suggested partiality— which, being dear to one who is affectionate— consists of the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*rati*), as well as the transitory emotions (*vyabhicāribhāva*) such as longing, agitation, fickleness, and joy; thus,
the set of objective determinants (*vibhāva*) and consequents (*anubhāva*) has been made common [to all], and it is the very relishing (*carvaṇā*) of these that constitutes the aesthetic experience.
It culminates in the relish (*carvaṇā*) of the transitory emotions (*vyabhicārin*).

Because the transitory emotions are dependent by nature, they rest upon the relish of the dominant emotion (*sthāyin*), which is like a string for a garland; thus, their sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama*).

In this case, however, counting the petals of the lotus and being face-down could also be possible for young girls in other circumstances; therefore, it does not immediately cause the heart to rest upon shame.
Rather, however, [the inclusion of the word "bāla"] is for the purpose of embracing those who recall past events such as her former practice of austerities.
Regarding the words "sampūrṇā" and so forth:
"sampūrṇā" is a qualifying attribute of the description.

O Goddess, the object alone is the objective basis (*ālambana*); the excitants (*uddīpana*) are beauty, the spring season, floral ornaments, and so forth; this is the application of the determinants (*vibhāva*).
The meaning is that there is an application of the state of dissolution (*vibhāvatā*).
"As stated" means that it has been shown by the passage beginning with "to receive" (*pratigrahītum*) and by the passage beginning with "delusion" (*sammohanam*).
The connection here is with the phrase "the group of its manifestations has been revealed.
"Because of being inclined toward that" means because of being attached to Hara.
"Of him" means of Hara.
"Directed toward him" [is the meaning].
The meaning is that she was intent upon the Blessed One.
"By way of being dear to her lover" means by way of undertaking the acceptance of the garland for that purpose.
This connects with the word "sūcitasya" (of what was indicated).

The connection is as follows: there is the "group of determinants" (anubhāva-varga) belonging to that indicated partiality—which consists of the stable state (sthāyibhāva) whose nature is rasa through its intensification—and also to the transitory states (vyabhicāribhāva).
A determinant (anubhāva) takes the form of the turning away of fortitude, the movement of the eyes, and so forth.
The word *iti* indicates the reason.
By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "only the relishing (*carvaṇā*) of the transitory (*vibhāva*) and consequent (*anubhāva*) emotions," other causes are excluded.
[This is] because of dependence (*pāratantryāt*).
The meaning is: "because of its dependence on the stable [permanent emotions].
Regarding the word *sraj* (garland):
the transitory mental states (*vyabhicāribhāvas*) are like a garland.
The term *sthayī* (the abider) corresponds to the *sūtra*;
"here, however" means in such passages as "speaking thus," and so forth.
"Otherwise also" means by a cause other than shame. "The heart" means:
The word "of the practitioner" (pratipattuḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
"Therein" (tatra) means "in shame" (lajjāyām).
"It is precisely manifestation through sequence";
the word "of bashfulness" is to be supplied as the ellipsis;
"previously," etc.
The meaning is: "by means of recollecting" (tadanusmaraṇena) that account of the Goddess's former conduct, such as her ascetic practices;
or alternatively, there is the reading *smāraṇena*, in which case it refers to "reminding" her of it, specifically regarding her shame.
"Produces" means it brings about;
the word "of the practitioner" (*pratipattuḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
Furthermore, that object which, assisted by the operation of the word, is employed as the manifestor of another meaning, is not the domain of this *dhvani*.
For example: "Having perceived that the lover was thinking of the time for their secret tryst, the clever woman closed her play-lotus, its intent conveyed through a glance from her smiling eyes."
In this case, the suggestiveness of the closing of the playful lotus has been stated by its very mention;
since the *Locana* (the commentary) effects the comprehension there, it is indeed a matter of suggestion through sequence (*kramavyaṅgyatā*).

However, even here, the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) appears only from afar when the nature of the transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*) is fully considered; therefore, with respect to that [flavor], it is precisely suggestion without sequence (*alakṣyakramatā*).
However, with regard to modesty (*lajjā*), there is the quality of having a perceptible sequence (*lakṣyakrama*) in that case.

The words "only" (*eva*) and "merely" (*kevala*) indicate this very state. He begins to demonstrate what is excluded by the statement "without verbal expression" (*uktiṃ vinā*) with the words "And where... (*yatra ca*).
The word "ca" (and) has the sense of the word "tu" (but).
The meaning of "asya" (of this) is that even in that case, there may indeed be the "unperceived sequence" (alakṣyakrama). This is the intended sense.
Cite [the example]: "By the convention," etc.;
"suggestiveness," etc.; the remainder is "one understands the time of evening."
"By the very statement" means by the first three quarters [of the verse].

Although here, even in the presence of another word, no word possesses the power of denotation (*abhidhā*) with respect to the sense of "fault," and thus its capacity as a suggester (*vyañjakatva*) is not undermined,
nevertheless, this meaning has been stated by the word itself as being the suggester of another meaning.
"Bālapriyā says: 'The suggestiveness of sequence' (kramavyaṅgyatā) means that bashfulness is indeed of the nature of suggestiveness with a perceptible sequence (saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgya).
Regarding the word 'rasa' (flavor):..."
The meaning is "erotic sentiment" (śṛṅgāra). Here too, in the passage beginning with "speaking thus" (evaṃvādinī) and so forth, [the action occurs] from afar, that is, only after a delay.
This is connected with the phrase "while being reflected upon.

The meaning is that the perception of the transitory emotion (vyabhicāribhāva) in the form of shame occurs only with delay, and once that perception has occurred, the perception of rasa follows immediately.
"In relation to that" means in relation to the rasa.
By the particle *eva* ("only"), there is an exclusion of the possibility of perceptible sequence (*lakṣyakramatva*).
To the question, "If so, how is it that perceptible sequence was mentioned here?", he says: "‘Lajjā’..."; [he explains] that the word *eva* and the word *kevala* [are used].

The meaning is that the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "of that whose suggested meaning has an imperceptible sequence" (*alakṣyakramavyaṅgyasyaiva*), and the word "mere" (*kevala*) in the phrase "that [suggestion] of that mere [dhvani]" (*sa tasya kevalasya*).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the phrase "of this dhvani" (*asya dhvaneḥ*) means "of the dhvani with a perceptible sequence" (*saṃlakṣyakramadhvaneḥ*).
He states the result of saying this: "But the one with an imperceptible sequence" (*alakṣyakramas tu*).
Regarding the word *saṅketa*: he whose mind was fixed on the rendezvous (*saṅketakāla*) at the time of the appointment; that is, one desiring to know about it.
For this very reason, his intention—namely, the desire to know the time of the appointment—was conveyed and indicated by his two laughing eyes.
The connection is with the word "having known.

Regarding the eyes—there is no denotative power (*abhidhā-śakti*) of any word toward the meaning of "evening" (*pradoṣa*). The meaning is that the meaning in the form of "evening" is not conveyed by any word through denotation (*abhidhā*).
The word "iti" indicates the reason.
"Not separated" means that, for this reason, it is logical that this [object] has sound as its very domain; such is the intended meaning.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the word" (śabdena):
the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that the fact that this meaning is a manifestor (*vyañjaka*) of another meaning has been stated by the word itself.
The meaning is that the fact that the closing of the lotus eyes manifests the time of evening has been demonstrated by the words consisting of the first three quarters [of the verse] themselves.
And thus, the connection is that "it is rejected by that.
It means: it consists of that beauty which has arisen—that is, emerged—by way of being concealed (*gopyamānatayā*).
And it has been stated as follows:

"Where a suggested meaning, though already projected by the power of the word and its sense, is further manifested by the poet himself through his own statement—that is another ornament distinct from *dhvani*. (Dhvanyāloka 2.23)

Even when a suggested meaning is already implied by the power of the word and its sense, if it is further revealed by the poet through his own explicit statement, that is another distinct figure of speech belonging to *dhvani*. (23)

Even when a suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) is implied by the power of the word, the power of the sense, or the power of both word and sense, if it is further made manifest by the poet’s own explicit statement, that is a different ornament (alaṅkāra) from this "suggested" (dhvani) type which is compared to an echo;
or, in the case of dhvani where the sequence of suggestion is imperceptible, such an ornament exists as something distinct from it, provided it is possible.
Consequently, that which constitutes the very life of *dhvani*—namely, its beauty arising from being concealed—is cast aside.
As someone has said: "I am profound; no one knows my purpose or what I have indicated;
I shall say something."
On the contrary, by that very [statement], the indication of profundity is actually made manifest.
For this very reason, he says: "by the very expression 'the state of being a manifestor'. (2.2)

With the intention of performing both the conclusion of the two previously mentioned modes and the indication of the third mode with a single effort, the author of the commentary introduces a general transitional phrase: "And thus" (*tathā ca*).
The meaning is that this third mode is also to be understood by means of those two aforementioned modes.
"Word and meaning" (*śabdārthau*) is a *ekaśeṣa* compound [meaning "word" and "meaning"].
The phrase "that is indeed other" means that this is not *dhvani*.
Rather, the meaning is that [it is] an ornament such as *śleṣa* (paronomasia) and so forth.

Alternatively, by the word "suggestion" (*dhvani*), there is the suggestion of imperceptible sequence (*alakṣyakrama*); this is the life-breath of that principal figure which is the object of ornamentation.
He provides an illustration, beginning with "just as," and so forth.

Regarding the term "profound" (*gambhīra*): this statement was made by someone with reference to the worldly condition that a profound person does not speak of their own task with words, but rather sometimes indicates it indirectly.
The logical connection is as follows: "I am not profound;
therefore, since my purpose has been clearly indicated, no one perceives or knows it. Thus, I shall say something."
"By that" means by the aforementioned statement;
it is for the purpose of indicating profundity.
The meaning is that the sense [of profundity] consists in the absence of facial distortions and the like, which indicates depth;
this has been "revealed," that is, made manifest.
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it is stated that "it was communicated precisely by means of the expression of suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatvamuktyaiva*) according to the very intention already expressed.
But he says "for this very reason" (ata eva) because the suggested meaning has not been demonstrated by means of another word. // 2.2 //
Since the literal meaning of the phrase "and thus" (*tathāca*) would lack coherence, he introduces and explains it with the words "that which has been introduced," and so forth.

"The two types of manner introduced" means the two types of suggestion (*dhvani*), namely that rooted in the power of the word (*śabdaśaktimūla*) and that rooted in the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*).
"The third type" means the type of suggestion (*dhvani*) rooted in the power of both word and meaning;
thus, it is a *ekaśeṣa* (a grammatical compound where only one member remains).

The meaning is as follows: "word" (śabda) and "object" (artha) constitute "word-and-object" (śabdārtha); [the dual form] śabdārthau and [the plural form] śabdārthāḥ refer to these. The sense is that by the phrase "capable of those" (teṣāṃ śaktā), all three types of distinction are included. In the verse, the reading is *kṣipto 'pi*; the word division (*cheda*) is *ākṣipta*.
The word "se" (it) is a reference back to the word "yatra" (where);
the meaning is "that poetry.
Alternatively, the word "tatra" (there) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sense.
The meaning is that this is the suggested sense (*vyaṅgyārtha*). The first quarter-verse beginning with "sāmya" has been explained in two ways in the *Vṛtti*;
in accordance with that, he explains the first meaning in the *Locana* as follows: "It is not *dhvani*, etc."

In this regard, an example by the power of the word’s inherent meaning (*śabdaśakti*) is as follows: "O child, do not fall into despair; abandon your upward-thrusting breath of great velocity. Or rather, let whatever be your heavy burden; depart from here, even if it be the wielder of the thunderbolt (*Indra*).

Having caused the gods to accept the rejection [of Lakṣmī] under the pretext of allaying his fear, may that Ocean—by whom Lakṣmī was taken away while he was reeling from churning—burn away your misfortune. [Here, the word *vatse* (child) is used for *Lakṣmī*, and *urujavam śvasanam* (breath of great velocity) refers to *Vāyu*; thus, through the power of the words, the Ocean is shown to have bestowed these upon Indra.]

The meaning is that "the other" refers either to the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya-artha*) or to an ornament (*alaṅkāra*) based solely on the expressed meaning (*vācya*); thus, it is a second, transcendent ornament (*lokottara-alaṅkāra*).
He will explain this very point in two ways in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
[The term] *viṣāda* means one who eats poison (*viṣam atti*).
In the phrase "the fire moving upwards," the meaning should be understood as follows:
"Who is the lord of the waters? Who is Brahmā? Or who is your guru?
[This was said] by Balabhid, that is, Indra; "by the yawning one" means by him who was intoxicated with the pride of sovereignty.
Yawning, which consists of the rubbing of the limbs, destroys strength because it causes exhaustion.
It has been explained that the second meaning here is expressed by the word "pratyākhyāna" (refusal) itself. Regarding the term "kārayitvā" (having caused to do):
For she herself, having risen while keeping only the lotus-eyed one in her heart, effectively rejects all other gods;
yet, because of her natural delicacy, which was agitated by the breaking waves of the ocean tossed by the Mandara mountain, he— while awakening her—
performed what was appropriate for that situation by pointing out faults elsewhere, saying "Go there," and through a particular gesture that demonstrated his regard for all virtues.
For this very reason, he says "confused by the churning" (*manthamūḍhām*).
This is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*).
He explains the second [alternative] with "Or rather," and so forth.

In the former case, "of the *dhvani*" (*dhvaneḥ*) is in the ablative case and refers to *saṃlakṣyakrama-dhvani* (suggested meaning with perceptible sequence); in this case, however, it is in the genitive case and refers to *asaṃlakṣyakrama-dhvani* (suggested meaning with imperceptible sequence). He states this with the words "by the word *dhvani*" and so forth;
the phrase "it has been said" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the word "anyat" (other) in the phrase "tādṛg anyaḥ," he explains the word "anya" in accordance with the commentary (*vṛtti*) by saying "the expressed [meaning]" and so forth.
The explanation of "tādṛg" (such) is as follows: "lokottara" (supramundane). Regarding "vatse" (O child):
O child, do not fall into despondency or sorrow.
"Abandon the upward-moving, high-velocity breath, the long exhalation"—there is also a reading "restrain it.
Since the literal meaning of "heavy," "great," and so forth is already clear, he explains another sense [of the passage] starting with "poison" (*viṣa*).
Regarding "despair" (*viṣāda*):
The meaning is "Śiva. The explanation of the term "proceeding upwards" is "the fire"; and the word "and" (ca) should be understood as having the sense of "also."
The meaning is that the conjunction "and" (ca) should be understood as including both "breathing" and "proceeding upwards.
The word *guru* means father.
He states the literal meaning of the phrase "by the yawning Indra" (*balabhidā jṛmbhitena*) in passing, beginning with the words "yawning" (*jṛmbhitaṃ ca*).

He demonstrates the manifestation of the second meaning through his own statement with the words "the rejection" (*pratyākhyānam*). [The phrase] "by speech alone" (*vacasaiva*) is to be construed with the word "reported" (*niveditam*).
"The second meaning" means the meaning consisting in the form of abandoning Śiva and the others. "Let him cause [it] to be done."

In this context, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) consists in performing an action capable of [eliciting] that [feeling], and not in the form of instigating one who has not yet begun; for the latter would be inconsistent with the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). Thus he says, beginning with "For she... and so forth.
The connection is with the phrase "confused by her delicacy."
The word "tām" (her) is to be supplied as the object.
The syntactical connection is that by awakening her, he performed an act conducive to that end.
By him—by that ocean.
"In another place" means among the gods such as Śiva and others.
"By exposing the fault" means...
"By means of words such as 'despair' (viṣāda), etc. means by the manifestation of faults such as the consumption of poison.
"In this [context]" means in Śrī Nārāyaṇa, who is distinguished by supramundane qualities.

An example by the power of the sense (artha-śakti): "Here lies my mother, aged and at the head of those whose years are ripe; and here is the slave-girl Kumbha, her body weakened by the exhaustion of all the household chores. In this place, I alone am a sinner, for my lord of life has been away for several days. Thus did a young woman speak to a traveler, using the pretext of a statement made at the opportune moment.

An example of [suggestion] by both powers (*ubhayaśakti*) is as follows: "By his glance, which was captivated by the passion for Keśava and the cowherds... and so forth. According to the manner stated in the *Locana*, the connection is as follows: by means of the pretext of dispelling fear, the ocean—having caused Lakṣmī, who was bewildered during the churning, to reject the gods—gave her to him; may he burn away your misfortune (*durita*).
"O Mother!"—
here, the suggestiveness of each individual word is easily discernible by those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), and thus it has not been stated explicitly by the author himself.
In this context, the word *vyāja* (pretext) refers to his own statement.
Having thus examined two modes with examples under the guise of a summary, he states the third mode with "ubhaya" (both):

first, verbal power [is manifested] by virtue of word-pun (*śabdaśleṣa*), such as in the word *go* (cow/earth) and *parāga* (dust/darkness); [and second], by the power of meaning, as in the term *sakala*.
This is the *Bālapriyā*.
The meaning is: [it is] by that which shows one's own high regard for all the qualities related to the Blessed One.
"For this very reason" means: because the performance of what is capable is the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*).
Regarding the phrase "confused by the churning":
the sense is that this serves as an indicator of that [fact].
He explains the second half of the verse with the words beginning with "iti" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "having caused [him] to be marked with the *lakṣmī*": the designation of the object (*karmasaṃjñā*) is applied by the rule "hṛkroranyatarasyām.
A certain unchaste woman, her passion aroused upon seeing a handsome traveler, addressed him as "Mother! (*amba*).
The word "lies down" (śete) is to be supplied also in the subsequent clauses. Of those whose age is fully matured, i.e., the elderly;
she whose body is slackened and unwell due to the fatigue resulting from household duties performed by herself in their entirety.

Regarding the word "avasare": it refers to an occasion (*avasarasya*), such as the mother or others being asleep at that particular place; the pretext (*vyāja*) is a statement (*ukti*) made under that guise. That which has such a preceding [pretext] is described thus.
Here, it is possible for the two of us to enjoy ourselves according to our desire, and no one would know of it.

The suggestion—that she, afflicted by desire at the sight of you, says "delight me with pleasure" and thereby instructs him—is manifested to sensitive readers who possess knowledge of the speaker’s particular qualities and so forth.
However, the poet has revealed this suggested meaning through the word "pretext" (*vyāja*), as it was uttered under the guise of an opportune pretext.
This is easily understood.
By the two terms "Mother" and "Father," because they possess natural affection for their children, [the speaker implies] that those two are indeed favorable toward him in every respect.
By those two qualifiers, [he indicates] her state of being overcome by sleep and her inability to rise without the assistance of another;
and by the word "entirely" (*niśśeṣa*), etc., he indicates the servant girl's state of deep slumber.
By the reasons stated, their unreliability is established;

by the word "slave-girl" (dāsī), her subservience to her own kin is indicated; and by the word "sinful" (pāpā), her lack of experience in the enjoyment of fresh sexual union due to recent affliction is shown.
The intended meaning is that it should be inferred as follows: by the word "alone" (*ekā*), the absence of enjoyment with any other man is indicated;
by this very fact, there is a longing for sexual union;

by the phrase beginning with "for a few moments" (*katipayā-*) and so forth, it is shown that the husband's return before long is not to be doubted; and by the term "lord of my life" (*prāṇanātha*), the absence of passion directed toward any other husband is illuminated. This is the sense.
The word "iti" indicates the reason. "Not stated by his own throat" means that it was not demonstrated through his own direct explanation.

The meaning (artha) that serves as an illuminator (dīpaka) of another matter is also to be known as twofold: that which is possible by its own nature, and that whose body is produced solely through bold assertion (prauḍhokti). (Dhvanyāloka 2.24)

The meaning (artha) that illuminates another matter is also to be known as twofold: that which is possible by its own nature, and that whose body is accomplished through bold assertion (prauḍhokti). // 24 //

Regarding the *dhvani* in which the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) takes the form of a resonance arising from the power of the sense (*arthaśaktyudbhava*), there are two types of the suggestive meaning (*vyañjaka-artha*) that have been mentioned: first, that whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of either the poet or a speaker fashioned by the poet; and second, that which is inherently possible (*svataḥ-sambhavī*). As for the "power of the sense," it arises by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*).
As long as it is not known that Rādhāramaṇa is the locus of the weightiness of the concealed passion of all young women, no other meaning is perceived;
thus, the phrase "with a hint" (saleśam) here refers to his own statement. // 2.3 //

Thus, the general definition of that which arises from the power of meaning (*arthasakti*) has been established, and its distinct domain has been stated as being differentiated from figures of speech such as *śleṣa*.
Now, he proceeds to determine its specific varieties, beginning with the words "by bold assertion" (*prauḍhokti*), and so forth.
That meaning which was described as an illuminator (*dīpaka*) or suggester (*vyañjaka*) of another meaning is also of two kinds.

The meaning of the word "also" (api) is that not only is the first type [of suggestion] twofold, being like an anusvāra, but even its second variety is twofold by way of the two kinds of suggested meanings (vyañjaka-artha).
He states a further internal subdivision even of the "bold assertion" (prauḍhokti) with the words "of the poet" (kaveḥ).
Thus, there are these three varieties:

one who has attained excellence (*prakarṣa*) through the object to be accomplished—that is, one who has mastered it—is called "mature" (*prauḍha*). Furthermore, speech that is appropriate for conveying the object to be conveyed is also called "mature."
The *Bālapriyā* explains what was already stated—that the power of the meaning (*arthaśakti*) depends upon the context—by means of the passage beginning with "as far as" (*yāvat*), etc. (2.3).
Regarding the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "the meaning also," he explains its sense with the words "not only," and so forth.
He introduces the passage beginning with "of the poet" with the words "from the mature expression" (*prauḍhokteḥ*).
These are the three varieties.

The meaning is that there are three varieties: established solely through the poet's bold assertion (*kaviprauḍhoktimātrasiddha*), established solely through the bold assertion of a speaker created by the poet (*kavinibaddhavaktṛprauḍhoktimātrasiddha*), and possible in itself (*svataḥsambhavī*).
He states the mature proficiency in word-formation: "prakarṣeṇa" and so forth.
The explanation of the term "ūḍha" is "sampādya" and so forth. As for "tat":
"Therefore" means this:
because it is only possible for one who is already skilled to attain the state of the object to be accomplished; such is the sense.
"Proficient" (prauḍha) means this.
The meaning is that it is called "prauḍha.
When *prauḍha* is established, the vowel lengthening (*vṛddhi*) occurs by the rule "prādūhoḍhe" and so forth.
[The form] is "samarpayitavyā."

An example of one whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet: "Prepare the spring month; it does not yet bestow upon the faces of the lakhs of young women the arrows of the God of Love, which have the fresh *sahakāra* flower as their point and the tender new leaf as their feather."

An example of that whose body is produced solely through the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of a speaker composed by a poet is as cited above, beginning with "In the mountain-peak" (*śikhariṇi*). The *Locana* says: "The month of spring prepares [the arrows] but does not yet discharge them; it prepares for the God of Love his arrows, which have fresh mango blossoms as their tips and are adorned with young sprouts and leaves, and which take the faces of young women as their targets."

In this context, since the state of spring— characterized by the bursting forth of the *sahakāra* tree— is described through an expression skillful at presenting the object to be delivered, namely, "the conscious Spring, the friend of the Bodiless One, merely prepares [the bow] but does not yet discharge it," it therefore manifests the beginning of the torment of Love, which will gradually become more and more intense.
Otherwise, the mere fact that "mango trees put forth sprouts in spring" would not function as a suggester (*vyañjaka*). And this statement, "O Śikhariṇī," is the bold utterance of the poet himself.
In this case, [the statement] "the parrot bites the red bimba fruit" possesses no suggestiveness whatsoever.
However, when it is a bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) by a speaker—a youth established by the poet—who is full of longing, then it possesses suggestiveness.
This means that it is fit to be offered to the hearts of sensitive readers (*sahṛdaya*).
In the commentary (vṛtti), the reading "and the second [type] is inherently possible" (*svataḥsaṃbhavī ca dvitīya*) is found in some manuscripts.

Regarding the word *sajjayati*: it refers to the month of *surabhi*, that is, a month connected with spring; those whose faces—meaning their tips—are such that young women alone are their targets (*lakṣyāṇi*).

Regarding the reading *lakṣasahān*: it means those which endure them, that is to say, those [flowers] which are to be employed specifically for them. Regarding *navān*: they take up (*lānti*) or receive those which are new shoots (*pallava*) and leaves (*patra*). Thus, [the compound means] "those who take up the new shoots and leaves."
"Abhi" means [flowers] such as fresh mango blossoms;
these very things are the arrows of Anaṅga.
The logical connection is that he prepares [them], but does not yet employ them.
He states "the spring is conscious" in order to establish the logical connection with the act of preparation and so forth; the intended meaning is that the spring is superimposed as being conscious.
The term *saha* means "together with"; the meaning is that it possesses the emergence (*udbheda*) or manifestation (*prakāśa*) of the mango tree (*sahakāra*).
The word *sahakāra* is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for other flowers as well. Thus it has been stated.
The meaning is "designated"; the connection is that it is "spoken" by means of speech.
Hence, the phrase "that which is being suggested" (*dhvanyamāna*) and so forth:
by the statement "he merely prepares the arrows of such a bodiless one (*anaṅga*)," the commencement of the crushing of the Mind-born God (*manmatha*) is indicated;

and by the statement "he does not yet discharge them," the future discharge is suggested, thereby manifesting the intensification of the state of the crushing of the Mind-born God. This is the meaning.
"Otherwise" means in a manner exceeding the previously stated mode.
He states that mode, beginning with "In spring," and so forth.
The word "iti" means that this is what is to be established by the statement.
"Not," and so forth.
The meaning is that [the word] would not manifest the stated sense.
Regarding the passage beginning with "here," etc.:
instead of the reading *śukte*, there is also the reading *ayaṃ śukapotakaḥ*.
"Thus," and so forth.
The meaning is that there is no suggestiveness whatsoever in that which is conveyed by the words "thus.
"In this manner": [as follows].
The meaning is that it takes the form of *śikhariṇī* and so forth. For example:
*Sāaraviiṇṇajovvaṇahatthālambaṃ samuṇṇamantehim...* (With hands raised by those who have been granted youth by the ocean...)
It is as if a direct blow to the heart has been dealt to you by your breasts.
That which is inherently possible is that whose existence is conceivable even in the external world, and whose form is not produced solely by the power of verbal description;
as in the example cited beginning with "when he spoke thus," and likewise:
Adorned with earrings made of peacock feathers, the merchant’s wife wanders about proudly in the midst of her co-wives,
who have laid aside their ornaments out of grief for their husbands’ deaths.
Your two breasts have offered their gaze, with the hand of youth respectfully extended as a support for rising up from the ocean; it was like an act of rising in greeting by Manmatha himself.
In this context, the two breasts are primary; even more honored than they is Desire, which is offered hospitality by rising up to meet them.

And youth stands as their attendant. By such a variety of expression, he has artfully made his own intention known: "Who would not fall into a state of passion increased by the sight of your breasts?"
The phrase "for your breasts are elevated by your youth" possesses suggestiveness;
the sense is that it is not merely [the literal meaning],
but rather the variety of expression (*uktivaicitrya*) is in every way useful.
The proud wife of the hunter, her ears adorned with peacock feathers, wanders amidst her co-wives who are decorated with ornaments fashioned from pearls.
For one who is attached to her alone, his duty is merely to kill a peacock;
however, it is stated in the words that he killed even elephants when attached to others, which indicates his supreme good fortune (*saubhāgya*).
This is what is meant by "suggestiveness" (*vyañjakatva*) in the *Bālapriyā*.
The suggested meanings (*vyaṅgyārtha*) have been demonstrated in the first chapter (*udyota*).
[Regarding the words] "respectfully" (*sādara*) and "having done" (*kṛtvā*):
The construction is as follows: "In that [state] filled with that [beauty],
where youth has respectfully offered its hand-hold— that is, where it has grasped her by the hand— there,
by your two rising breasts, an emergence has been granted even to the God of Love."

Here, with the intention that the *samāsokti* (condensed expression) based on the superimposition of the mental states of the attendants and others onto youth and so forth is a subordinate element (*aṅga*) of the *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), he explains it starting with "the breasts," etc.,
and "for thus," etc. The meaning is that when such a statement exists, that which is expressed by it does not possess the quality of being a suggester (*vyañjaka*).
The phrase "not only" (*na kevalam*) serves as a partial citation (*pratīkadhāraṇa*).

With the intention that the meaning intended by the term "possible in itself" (*svataḥsambhavī*) is "even though it is possible in the world," it is explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by the words "ya" and so forth.
In that context, he shows the implied meaning through the passage beginning with "not only" by stating "the variety of expression" (*uktivaicitryam*) and so on.
"Useful"—
the word "poetry" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The sense is that in the absence of variety in expression, there can be no state of being a work of poetry.
"Śikhī" (The Crested One):
this verse will be cited and explained by the author of the commentary in the third chapter.
"Jāyā" (The Wife).
The meaning is "one recently married.
*Prasādhana* means ornamentation.
Regarding the phrase "of co-wives":
The meaning is "of those previously married.
Regarding the term *śikhī*:
