Where another figure of speech is perceived through the power of the meaning (*artha-śakti*), with its suggested element comparable to a resonance (*anusvāna*), that is another variety of *dhvani*. (DhvK 2.25)

The threefold alternative is: "or indeed the eye itself.
This should be applied to the examples as appropriate. He provides an example: "attained," etc.

When a certain king possessed of infinite strength resided on the shore of the ocean, a tremor arose in the sea due to causes such as the rising of the full moon and the plunging of his army; since this [tremor] is imagined through doubt, it should be described as the figure of speech *saṅkara* (commixture), arising from the commixture of *sasandeha* (doubtful) and *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Through this, the nature of Vāsudeva will become clear in these examples. *Bālapriyā*. These examples will become manifest.
Regarding the phrase "one who has attained glory" (*prāptaśrī*): this king is one by whom glory (*śrī*), that is, prosperity and splendor, has been attained;
therefore, he once again experienced that [feeling] toward me.
Why, or for what reason, would one produce—that is, perform—the exhaustion of churning, the suffering caused by churning?

Here, first there is doubt expressed by "again" and so forth; subsequently, there is an inquiry regarding another result, expressed by "why," based on the thought of attaining the fortune that constitutes the fruit of churning.
The same should be understood for what follows.
"Of him whose mind is untiring," meaning free from sloth; this is a phrase containing a reason.
I do not even consider, nor do I doubt at all, that this king ever experiences sleep.
Regarding the word "setu" (bridge):
the phrase "consisting of this" is to be supplied.
This [bridge] is that which has been followed by the lords of all the islands.
Therefore, why does he build a bridge over me again?
When you have arrived—that is, when you have come into my presence—what doubts, such as "might he churn [the ocean]" which are to be understood from the previously mentioned words, does he harbor?
The connection is that the trembling of the ocean—the agitation of its waters and, moreover, its physical quaking—appears as if it were bearing those very doubts, as if from the act of holding them.
Here, he explains the expressed and the suggested figures of speech, beginning with "In a certain... and so forth.
"That" means trembling.
Here, it should be understood that there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between the flickering of water and trembling.
By the phrase "by this doubt," the meaning is:
by the doubt expressed in the sentence "he might churn [the ocean]," namely, the doubt as to whether he would indeed churn it.
Regarding the phrase "it is poetically imagined" (*utprekṣyate*):
by means of the effect, namely trembling, which serves as the cause for the aforementioned form of doubt, the [trembling] is poetically imagined as being in the cloud.
Alternatively, the meaning is that the trembling in the form of the water's agitation is poetically imagined as being a shudder caused by the aforementioned doubt.
"Because of confusion" means because of the confusion arising from the entry [of two figures] into a single sentence.

In such a case, since the aesthetic charm of the poetry is established by relying on a metaphor (rūpaka) consisting of a resonance (anuraṇana), the designation "suggested metaphor" (rūpakadhvani) is appropriate.
The designation "suggestion of a simile" (upamādhvani) is appropriate, as in:
"The heroes do not find delight in the embrace of their beloved's breasts, red with saffron, even then."
Just as when thick vermilion is applied to the surface of a broken water-pot, [the reflection appears distorted].
The eye of that king is suggested [as being like a lotus];
and although a contrast (vyatireka) shines forth here,
nevertheless, it is [contrasted] with the nature of the former Vāsudeva.
Not from the present day;

for if it were the present day, even the Blessed One would be existing as one who has attained glory and, being free from indolence, as a conqueror of all the continents. Nor is there an implication of a metaphor (*rūpaka*) by the force of the impossibility of doubt or poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
For by this, the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) serves as an embellishment for the expressed meaning (vācya), because there arises the possibility of such meanings as:
"Whosoever has not yet attained fortune, yet is overcome by sincere desire for victory, he shall crush me," and so forth.
Furthermore, this implied sense is drawn out by the words *na ca punarapi*, *pūrvām*, and *bhūyaḥ*.
Furthermore, even when there is a difference in agents, the identity of the ocean remains possible through its mere oneness;

as for example, the earth was first conquered by Kārtavīrya and then again by the son of Jamadagni. Moreover, since prior sleep is established even in states such as that of a prince, it is proven that this is indeed a case of *rūpaka-dhvani* (metaphorical suggestion).
Because the apprehension of the metaphor occurs through the power of the beauty of the meaning alone, even without the operation of words; therefore,
by that *saṅkara* (commixture),
there is the nature of being Vāsudeva.

The meaning is that there is non-difference between the Blessed One and Vāsudeva. As for the phrase "a distinction appears," the meaning is that a distinction of the king from Vāsudeva appears by virtue of his having attained prosperity and so forth.
And thus, the sense is: how can there be an appearance of non-difference? That [non-difference] is the distinction [from] the nature of Vāsudeva as previously described.
The meaning is: from the very nature of that Vāsudeva who was previously intent on churning [the ocean], intent on awakening from sleep, and intent on building the bridge;
"not from one belonging to today"—this is the sense.
The word "shines" (bhāti) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].
He states the reason for this with the words "because of being contemporary," and so forth.
"Because of being present" means because of being qualified [by that specific time].
Thus, since no difference from such a Vāsudeva belonging to the time of this very speech is perceived, the intended meaning is that their non-difference is here suggested (dhvanyate).

Now, one might raise the objection: "In this case, without the perception of [the ocean] as Vāsudeva during the night, the aforementioned reflections on the part of the ocean would not be possible; therefore, that suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) must be subordinate because it serves merely to justify [the literal sense]. To dispel this doubt, he says "And not," and so forth.
The word "by which" (yena) [is used].
The meaning is: "by means of an objection based on impossibility.
"A verbal ornament" (vācyālaṅkāra) means: a combination (saṅkara) of doubt (sasandeha) and poetic fancy (utprekṣā).
Regarding the statement "there is no objection," he provides the reason with the words beginning "whosoever":
"Just like Vāsudeva, whatever person has not yet attained fortune,
may each such person churn me."
The meaning is that there arises a doubt such as: "Whosoever is overcome by a sincere desire to conquer, let him each build a bridge for me," and so forth.
Anticipating the objection that his own statement might reveal the intended implication (*vyaṅgya*), he refutes it with the words beginning "And that... (*tac ca*).
"This is the meaning" means that the king's nature is that of Vāsudeva.
The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason.
The logical connection is that it is established that this is indeed *rūpaka-dhvani* (metaphorical suggestion).
Here he states the reason— namely,
"the function of the word" (*śabda-vyāpāra*), which is denotation (*abhidhā*).

In some manuscripts, a reading such as "Just as in *Jyotsnāpūra*" and so forth is seen immediately after the verse beginning with "prāptaśrīḥ. As stated in the *Locana*: "On this sandy bank of the Sarayū, white as the spreading flood of moonlight, a game of dice was played for a long time by two Siddha youths.
One said: 'One [of us] first killed Keśin'; the other said: 'No, Kaṃsa. The first replied: 'Tell me the truth; which of you two was killed there first?'"
Some recite this as an example here,
but that is incorrect; for by the power of the word "bhavataḥ" (of you), the meaning "you are Vāsudeva" is made clear in this context.
He by whom the quarters of the sky have been rendered heart-stealing, filled with, and distributed through both *lāvaṇya*— which is the charm of form— and *kānti*, which is radiance;
now, immediately following the turbidity of anger, he is oriented toward graciousness.
An address to her whose eyes are habituated to smiling slightly, tremulous, and beautiful with the expansion [of joy] from the swinging of her favor;
furthermore, it does not come now,
but at another moment, once it has occurred, she fell into agitation.

A sensitive person, due to agitation and mental instability, would perceive your face—reddened by anger and passion, yet smiling—as nothing other than the orb of the full moon reddened by the twilight.
And this is not surprising, for it is clearly evident that the name of this "ocean" (jalarāśi) is true to its meaning, as it brings about the birth of dullness (jaḍatva).
[The commentator] states "yathā ca" and so forth, explaining that words such as *jala* primarily denote the abstract state (*bhāvārtha*), while *tvapapāṭha* is a misreading.
He states the reason for [the claim] that "that is false" with the words beginning "by you," etc., ending with "because it has been made clear.

The meaning is: because the non-difference of that [king] from Vāsudeva has been made manifest by stating that the king—who is the referent of the word *bhavat* (*your majesty*) and the subject of description—is the agent of the killing.
Thus, the sense here is that the suggested meaning (vyaṅgya) has become subordinate (guṇībhūta).
To avoid redundancy, he explains the intended meaning by the word *lāvaṇya* as "saṃsthāna" [structure];
the meaning is the beauty of form (*ākṛti*).
The phrase "hṛdyāni" and so forth is an elaboration of the term "saṃvibhaktāni.
The expression "diṅmukhāni" means the starting points of the directions.

The sense is that those directions which have a connection with the face by way of its own gaze are the "directional faces" (*diṅmukha*). He explains that the word "now" (*adhunā*) is connected with the word "smiling" (*smerā*), stating "anger," etc.,
and "grace," etc.

The meaning is that [the two] are beautiful by virtue of their movement and expansion through grace (*prasāda*). He states another implied meaning (*vyaṅgyārthāntara*) that accords with the poetic quality (*guṇa*), beginning with "And yet" (*atha ca*).
The intention is that the word *adhunā* ("now") is also connected with the phrase *na eti* ("does not come").
Now, by the phrase "it does not go," he shows another meaning that is understood: "when it has occurred," and so forth.
"Occurred" means having passed away;
"at another moment" means at a specific subsequent moment.
"At the time of the moon's rising" means until that point;
"it reached agitation"—
the word "ocean" is to be supplied as the subject.
The sense is that the agitation of the ocean has been observed.
He demonstrates the *rūpakadhvani* (suggested metaphor) with the words beginning "kopa" (anger), etc.;
the word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
The meaning is that such a face is non-different from such a digit of the moon;
that is to say, because of seeing it [the moon]. Regarding the phrase "it must be so" (bhāvyam) and so forth:
The meaning is that a person of sensitive heart (*sahṛdaya*) must experience agitation in the form of mental instability consisting of the transformations of love (*madanavikāra*);
whereas for the ocean, agitation is characterized by the surging of its waters.
Here, there is an identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) between these two types of agitation.

If the term *kṣobha* (agitation) were intended to mean merely the flickering of the mind, then only the excellence of the face's beauty would be suggested (*dhvani*), and not its non-difference from the moon.
Therefore, it is also intended that *kṣobha* here signifies the agitation in the form of the surging of the waters, which is an effect produced by the rising of the moon.
And this is not so... [etc.].
"The ocean" implies "is agitated.
"That" means "because there is no occurrence of agitation."
It was stated previously that "the accumulation of dullness" refers to the eye;

here, however, the agitation—which consists of the transformation of passion—arises in the sensitive reader (*sahṛdaya*) through the beholding of your face. Since the denotative function (*abhidhā*) comes to rest after conveying only this much, the metaphor (*rūpaka*) is merely suggested (*dhvanyamāna*).
Furthermore, the expressed ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*) here is *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
And that [suggestion] is not the manifestor.
Here, the beauty of poetry is established on the basis of that form which consists of a resonance (anuraṇana) and is manifested by the power of the meaning;
therefore, the connection is that the designation [of the poem] is made precisely by means of that [resonance].
Because they possess an equal number of syllables (*ujana*), the definitions of simile (*upamā*) and the path of sound (*adhvan*) have not been explicitly applied by the author himself.
"The heroes do not take such delight in the embrace of their beloveds' breasts, red with saffron,
as they do in the frontal globes of their enemies' elephants, which are thickly smeared with vermilion."

Although his gaze was wavering due to his intentness on consoling his beloved whom he had just adorned, as well as his mind being hurried by the immediate onset of battle, there was nevertheless an exceeding haste for the fight; this is the figure of speech *vyatireka* (distinction) as a verbal ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*). In that context, however, there is this suggested simile (*dhvanyamānopamā*) expressed through the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) of the locus and the occupant: "O dear one, [the elephants] are eager to crush the frontal globes of the enemy kings—which cause terror to all people—even while those enemies are themselves intent on crushing [us] amidst their foes. This is the meaning. It is an expression based on the identification of the support (*āśraya*) and the supported (*āśrayin*).
The word "I think" (manye) is connected with this; its meaning is "I ascertain.
For when such a face is manifest, there is no occurrence of agitation.
The meaning is that I determine the great dullness spoken of by the people to be that of the ocean.
Here too, it should be understood that there is an identification (*aikyādhyavasāya*) between the referent of the word "dullness" (*jāḍya*), namely ignorance, and water.
[The phrase] "those whose primary sense is the state of being" (*bhāvārthapradhānāḥ*)...
The meaning is that they primarily denote objects such as dullness and so forth.

By refuting the status of the aforementioned suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) as being merely a subordinate factor for the establishment of the expressed sense (*vācya-siddhyaṅgatva*), he establishes *dhvani* with the words "And here," etc.,
[and] "By the beholding of your face," etc.
There is also a reading with a locative ending (*saptamyantatayā*). "To this extent" means:
"I conclude that the ocean is a mass of insentient matter because it lacks the attainment of such agitation"—this is the meaning of the phrase.
"Rūpaka" (metaphor) means the non-difference between the heroine's face and the full moon. "Śleṣa" (paronomasia) means...
The meaning is that this is a pun residing in the word *jaḍa*.
The point is that it is not a suggester (*vyañjaka*), because such a [literal] metaphor is of no use in the aforementioned type of suggested metaphor (*rūpakadhvani*).
He explains the phrase "metaphor in the form of resonance" (*anuraṇanarūparūpaka*) and so forth with the words "the metaphor which is of the nature of resonance," etc.

Now, one might ask: why has the suggestion of simile (*upamā-dhvani*) in the two examples from the *Vṛtti*, such as "of the heroes" (*vīrāṇām*), not been explicitly stated by its own word? To this, he says: "tulya...
and so forth. By his own word—that is, by his own expression—[he means] "of the heroes."

The construction of the sentence is as follows: the gaze of heroes, which delights upon the frontal globes of enemy elephants smeared with thick vermilion, does not find such pleasure on the bosom of their beloveds, which are reddened by saffron (*ghusṛṇa*).
*Ghusṛṇa* means saffron (*kuṅkuma*).
He explains [this] with the words "prasādhitā" and so forth: *prasādhitā* means adorned;
*samāśvāsana* means gladdening through sexual union.
"Samanantarībhūta" means being proximate;
"ḍolāyamānā" means unsteady or oscillating.
Thus, this is a verbal figure (*vācyālaṅkāra*).

Since it demonstrates the excellence of the heroes' vision in sporting upon the frontal globes of enemy elephants over and above their sporting in the laps of beloved women, an intensity of haste in battle is understood in comparison to the haste in sexual union; because this [intensity] is manifested through the expressed meaning, it possesses the status of a verbal figure.
Alternatively, the phrase "iti vyatirekaḥ" means that the *vyatireka* (contrast) is that which manifests this meaning;
and that [contrast] is what was previously mentioned.
Here, he explains the suggestion (*dhvani*) of simile (*upamā*) with the words beginning "tatra tu," and so forth.
Regarding that statement, "yeyam" and so forth—the word "upamā" (simile) is connected with the phrase "on the frontal globes of elephants. The meaning is:
this simile, which is suggested [by the context], has the frontal globes of elephants as its correlate (*anuyogin*) and the bud-like breasts of the beloved as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).
He explains her preeminence with the words beginning "sakala" and so forth.
These qualifiers of the Kumbha-sthala are intended to describe the actual state of affairs.
Or, for example, as in my own *Viṣamabāṇalīlā*, regarding the subduing of the Asuras by Kāmadeva:
The flower-arrowed god [Kāma] has fixed the hearts of beloved women— whose essence is singularly devoted— to that lower lip of Bimba, which is an ornament of jewels to its sister, Lakṣmī.
The hearts of those beloveds, which were single-mindedly intent on seizing the jewel that was their sister’s fortune, have been directed by the flower-arrowed god toward the bimba-fruit lips.

Thus is the *chāyā*. An example of *ākṣepadhvani* (suggestive power through preclusion) is as follows: "He would be capable of enumerating all the virtues residing in Hayagrīva, were he able to measure the limits of the great ocean with jars of water."

Because they take pleasure [in him] by his power, there is great respect for him, as if he were Rati herself; thus, she alone produces the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) of the excellence of heroism, which establishes the primacy of the simile.
Regarding the phrase "in the subduing of the Asuras":
for his conquest of the three worlds is described therein.

Regarding those Asuras dwelling in Pātāla—who have repeatedly performed such deeds as the crushing of Indra’s city—what indeed have they not done? Their heart is such that it is unshakable in its resolve even amidst those various most difficult tasks;
and this [heart] belongs to those who are like brothers to Śrī, and for that very reason possess an indescribable excellence. This is the meaning.

In the matter of seizing all those jewels from every side, that supreme heart of theirs— which was of a single flavor— was directed by the Flower-Arrowed God (Kāmadeva) toward the bimba-like lips of beloved women, using the most delicate of implements; for that God of Love accomplished his purpose merely through their being gazed upon, kissed, and seen, instilling in them the conceit of having fulfilled their desires.

That is to say, their hearts were burning intensely with the fire of the desire for conquest. Here, the poetic figure (alaṅkāra) expressed is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole). Regarding "among the enemies" (*śātraveṣu*), it means among those who have become foes.
Or [it occurs] toward those unrelated to the enemy.
The word "api" (even/also) indicates a contradiction regarding the arising of pleasure and great esteem.
The phrase "on the frontal globes of elephants" is connected with both "pleasure" and "great esteem."
By their power— that is, by the power of the simile—
she was taking up, that is, bearing, delight and joy.
Regarding the phrase "as if in recognition":

the meaning is that for those heroes who cherish the frontal globes of elephants because they bear a resemblance to the bud-like breasts of their beloveds, there is, as it were, great esteem (bahumāna) for them.
"Taking pleasure" means being devoted, or else it means "as if [she were] devoted. The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason (*hetau*).
"That very same" refers to the aforementioned simile itself.

Regarding the term *vīratā*: it means that which effects—that is, brings about—the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*), which is the state of producing wonder, arising from the extraordinary valor (*vīryātiśaya*) of the warriors as it is being perceived.
It "effects" means it accomplishes or produces it.
The word "iti" indicates the reason;
the meaning is "by virtue of being an embellishment for the heroic sentiment (vīrarasa).
Regarding the phrase "tatrāsya":
The meaning is "in the play of the uneven arrows" of Kāma.
The phrase "of them" (*teṣām*) is explained by "by whom" (*yaiḥ*), and so forth.
The explanation of "that" (*tat*) is "which [was given] from them," and so forth.
"Unshakable" (*akampanīya*) means "immovable" (*acālanīya*). This is a statement of its meaning: "inexpressible" (*anirvācya*), and so forth.
And regarding "sukumārā" and so forth, he states the essential meaning (*bhāvārtha*) of the phrase "placed upon her bimba-like lower lip" with the words beginning "that," and so on.
By the passage beginning "their heart which... and so forth, there is a statement of the essential meaning of the first half-verse; the word "that" (*tat*) is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
The connection is that Kāmadeva performed that act— possessing the conceit of having fulfilled his purpose through the mere sight and kissing of her—
this constitutes the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole).

Here, by means of this *atiśayokti*, there is the manifestation of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), which serves to reveal her extraordinary particularity by demonstrating the inexpressibility of Hayagrīva’s qualities.

The suggestion (dhvani) of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth) can occur both as a suggestion based on the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) and as a suggestion based on the power of meaning (*arthāśaktimūla*).
Of these, an example of the former is as follows:
"When the fruit has been given by fate, what can be done? We can only say this much:"
The sprouts of the *kaṅkelli* tree are not equal to other sprouts.
And the simile is both expressed and implied;
for their high regard that "the bimba-lip is equal to the essence of all jewels" is indeed real.
For this very reason, it is not a case of the suggestion of metaphor (rūpakadhvani).
Since the metaphorical object (rūpaka) is being superimposed, it is unreal;
therefore, the similarity of those asuras manifests through the very nature of things (vastuvṛttyā).
And that very similarity is primarily the cause of aesthetic charm (camatkāra).

"By means of hyperbole" (atiśayokti) means by way of a verbal figure of speech. The very nature of *ākṣepa* (paralipsis) consists in the demonstration of the impossibility of description, because it takes the form of a negation of what is intended.
He states its predominance by means of its qualification: "asādhāraṇa" (uncommon).

By the word "sambhavati" (is possible), he indicates that, as a consequence, the investigation here concerns that which is rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*). "That speech which, by reason of its cause, has a scope transcending the world... [Bālapriyā]
Where non-difference is bound within difference, and difference elsewhere.
Likewise, Udbhaṭa and others have stated its definition with the words: "Hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is the expression [of a state] based on a matter that is so highly probable," and so forth.

In the case of [the example], "That heart which was of a single flavor during the seizing of the jewel has been placed upon the bearer of the reflection," there is a difference in reality between the two, consisting of specific modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*).
The meaning is that since the identity of the two hearts is established here, this is a *bheda-atiśayokti* (hyperbole of difference) consisting of non-difference;
or alternatively, it is a *sambandha-atiśayokti* (hyperbole of relation), because a relation is described despite the absence of a relation of residence.
[This is] the "implied" [meaning].
The meaning is "being suggested.
He explains what was stated with the words beginning "sakala" and so forth:
the quality of being worthy of complete acceptance and so on constitutes their similarity to the essence of jewels.
"For this very reason" means for the reason that will be stated below.

"By way of being the object of superimposition" (āropyamāṇatvena) means by way of the imagined non-difference [of the self] from the standard of comparison (upamāna), which is the essence of jewels (ratnasāra).
And there is also the reading "rūpakasyopacāratvena" (by way of the metaphorical application of a poetic figure).
Regarding "sādṛśya" (resemblance):
the meaning is that the lower lip resembles the essence of a jewel (*ratnasāra*).

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it was stated "by way of non-exaggeration" (*anatiśayoktyā*); he explains that by means of the words "in the form of a verbal ornament" (*vācyālaṅkārarūpayā*) and so forth.
The intended meaning is: because of the composition of a matter that is being imagined [as possible] through the verse beginning with "He who, with jars of water... (*yo 'mbukumbhaiḥ*).
He states the reason why this is precisely the demonstration of its indescribability with the word "iṣṭa" (desired).
The sense is that what is intended here is the demonstration of its describability.

He shows the result of the statement beginning with "asādhāraṇe" (in the uncommon) by means of the connection: "he expresses its predominance through the two qualifiers beginning with 'tasya' (of that)."

Here, by means of the hyperbole (atiśayokti) beginning with "with jars of water," the figure of preclusion (ākṣepa)—which consists in establishing that the qualities of Hayagrīva are beyond description—is suggested;
the intended meaning is that, through this, there is an extraordinary distinction in those qualities.
To the question, "What is the connection between the statement in the commentary beginning with 'the power of words' and the present context? he replies: "It is possible," and so forth.
In this regard,
since this *dhvani* is a manifestation of words (*padaprakāśa*), there is no contradiction even when the sentence has a different intended meaning.
An example of the second type is as follows:
Persuading me, whose anger is suppressed within my heart and whose face is tearful, it is truly impossible for you, O wise one, to provoke anger even in me, though I have offended you.

"O man of great learning, even though you have harbored anger in your heart and my face is not yet free from resentment, please grant me your favor; for even though I have offended you, it is truly not possible for you to remain angry."
[Thus the shadow: "The eye [of fate] depends on a fruit that is subject to destiny; what can be done? Yet we say this much:
the sprouts of the red Aśoka tree are not equal to the sprouts of any other."
The *aśoka* tree has no fruit, like a mango tree;
what can be done? Its sprouts alone are exceedingly charming—by this much the statement is complete.
Here, by the power of the word "fruit" (*phala*), the justification for this matter is understood even before [the conclusion].

For even in the case of one who has set out toward the means for attaining supramundane victory, the fruit characterized by prosperity may—due to fate—not come to pass at all; such is the general nature [of the matter]. Now, one might object: "Since *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise) is primarily suggested by this entire sentence, how can *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration) be its suggested meaning?
For it is impossible for two figures to be primary in one place simultaneously. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "by the word *prakāśa* (manifestation)."
For it will be explained that the entire proliferation of sound (*dhvaniprapañca*) consists of the manifestation of words (*padaprakāśa*) and the manifestation of sentences (*vākyaprakāśa*).
In this context, the phrase "in the investigation of the basis of the power of meaning" (*arthaśaktimūlavicāre*) means [the discussion] regarding the *bālapriyā*.
The explanation for the passage ending with "what can be done? (*kiṃ kriyatām*) begins with "of the Aśoka tree," etc. (*aśokasyetyādi*).
The explanation of the second half [of the verse] begins with "pallavā" and so forth.
Regarding the word "iyatā":
it means by the mere extent of what has been stated.
He explains the *dhvani* (suggested meaning) with the words "here," and so forth.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: here, this general nature of the thing, which serves as its support, is understood even before [the literal meaning] through the power of the word "fruit" (*phala*).

For when it is said, "What can be done when the fruit depends on fate?", the word "fruit," by virtue of the context, expresses the meaning of "crop" through the primary function of denotation (*abhidhā*).
From this, the contextual meaning—that there is no fruit for the *aśoka* tree—is obtained;
furthermore, the word "fruit" (*phala*) through *śaktimūla-dhvani* (suggestion based on denotation) conveys the sense of a result consisting of prosperity (*sampat*).

Consequently, the general meaning—that all prosperities depend upon fate and might perhaps never occur—is obtained as a support for the previously mentioned contextual meaning. This is the intended sense.
The meaning of "it is understood even beforehand" is that at the very moment of hearing the words "for the fruit depends on fate," [the point] is understood.

He introduces the passage beginning with "the illumination of the word" (padaprakāśa) with the words "Now then" (nanu), etc. [This refers to the figure of speech known as] Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Indirect Description).

The meaning is that the subject matter at hand (prastutārtha) consists of the praise of the virtues of a certain king or similar person who, despite having applied himself to skillful means (upāya), has not yet obtained the fruit characterized by success.
It is said to be "predominantly suggested" (vyaṅgya) because,
in the context of Aprastutapraśaṃsā (Praise of the Irrelevant), the subject matter at hand is what is suggested.
It was stated in the first chapter (udyota) that in some cases the *pradhāna* (the predominant element) [is suggested];
this refers to the fact that the *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration by a general truth) is suggested.
The term "predominantly" (*prādhānyena*) is to be supplied [to complete the sense].
To the question "Why?", he says: "Of the two," and so forth.
He states the meaning of the term *bhāva*: "For all," and so forth.
But in the case of a sentence, there is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).
The remainder [of the phrase] is "the suggested meaning is predominant.

Now, one might ask: if this is so, how is the conventional usage established here? For in this case, another general statement, which serves as a support for the specific expressed meaning—namely, that it is impossible to provoke the anger of a learned man even when he has committed an offense—is revealed through the power of *tātparya* (intentional implication).
In the word *phala*, there is primarily the suggestion of *arthāntaranyāsa* (corroboration);
however, in the sentence as a whole, there is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).

Even there, it is the predominance of the relationship between the power and the supported—which is conveyed by the word *phala*—that appears; thus, the sense is that this is indeed a case of *arthāntaranyāsa-dhvani*.
Since you have placed your resentment within your heart and not manifested it outwardly,
even as you seek to appease me whose face shows no sign of anger— O man of great learning,
it is truly impossible for you to be angry, even though you have committed an offense.
In this context, the address "O you of great learning" culminates in a specific meaning;
however, what follows immediately thereafter is that which produces aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*)—namely, the general form of support perceived through the contemplation of that meaning.
For she, being a woman whose lover had been unfaithful and who was then conciliated with cleverness, spoke thus while manifesting resentment toward him.
"Whoever is a learned rogue, even when he has committed such an offense, covers up the opportunity for his own transgression; therefore, do not harbor false self-conceit.
[The word] "connected" (anvitam) means that the universal is related to the particular; this is the intended sense.
Bālapriyā says: "In that case as well," and so forth.

Regarding the word *phala* (fruit): the meaning is that when the term *phala* is employed, there is primacy for the state (*bhāva*) of those two meanings—the efficient cause (*samarthaka*) and the effect (*samarthya*)—which are conveyed by it.
"It shines" means it manifests to those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*).
Regarding the phrase "in another sense" (*arthāntara*) and so forth, the intended meaning is that,
according to the maxim "designations occur primarily [based on the predominant factor]," the designation "suggestion of corroboration" (*arthāntaranyāsadhvani*) applies here alone.

To a certain woman who harbors anger within but has not manifested the signs of her resentment, and who is being propitiated by her beloved after she has committed an offense, this is the reply: "O heart," and so forth.
He explains: "placed in the heart," and so forth.
The word "prasādayan" (propitiating) is in the vocative case.

Or alternatively—the word "you" (tvam) is to be supplied [as the subject]. Indeed, it is not possible for me—this is the ellipsis—to cause anger. The word "by me" (mayā) is to be supplied [as the agent].

The meaning is: "O you who possess great knowledge (*bahujña*); because you are propitiating me, I am unable to harbor anger toward you even though you have committed an offense. Regarding the word "of one who possesses great knowledge" (*bahujñasya*).
"Regarding the omniscient one": the meaning is "in relation to.
"'Impossible'":
the meaning is "not possible for anyone at all."
The sense is that [he did so] because he concealed his own offense through his own ignorance.
Regarding the word "iti":
it means "of such a form."
The phrase "another [meaning] is connected" is a qualifier of the statement "the capacity is the same.
"It is manifested through the intended meaning" (tātparyeṇa) means that it resounds (dhvanati).
He explains the very meaning stated in the commentary with the words "here," etc.:
"it culminates in a particular [instance]" means, "I am not at fault; I do not think of another woman."

The meaning is that [the word] "bahujña" (omniscient), by means of its primary sense (*prakṛtārtha*), implies the phrase "be gracious to me who am devoted solely to you," and so forth, through its familiarity with the singular number (*ekavacanābhijña*).
He demonstrates the *dhvani* (suggested meaning) with the words "immediately thereafter," etc.,
stating that the form of the *sālambana* (having an object) is the supporting factor (*samarthaka*).
That [subject] will be explained by the words "yaḥ" (who) and so forth—she is the heroine under discussion; that is the meaning. She is called "khaṇḍitā" (the one whose lover has been unfaithful).
"The definition of that [state] is: 'when [the lover] has been perceived as altered by attachment to another woman, and made turbid by the jealousy of the [beloved] who has been humiliated.
She was appeased by her own lack of guile—that is, she was propitiated by the hero through his own lack of guile; this is the ellipsis."
To the question "How so?", he says: "Those who," and so forth.
You should not harbor false pride regarding your own extensive knowledge;
for even those who are truly learned, when they commit an offense, use various pretexts to conceal the opportunity for their transgression—this is the meaning.
By the word "endowed" (*anvitam*), he shows that the intended relation is one of the nature of the universal and the particular—this is indicated by the words "the particular," and so forth.
He explains the term "distinct" (*vyati*) with the words "its own," and so forth.
Furthermore, the expression of distinction (*vyatireka*) can also take both forms.
Among these, an example of the first has already been shown previously.
An example of the second is as follows:
"Like a crooked, hollow-trunked tree might grow in a forest glade,"
In this human world, let me not be one who is destitute and poor.
"May I be born in a forest region as a mere crooked tree with fallen leaves,
rather than as a poor man in the world of humans whose sole delight is in renunciation."

"Thus [is] the shadow. For here, the lack of welcome for the birth of a poor man whose sole essence is renunciation, and the welcoming of the birth of a *pādapaja* (tree-born) that has broken leaves and is bent, are directly expressed by the words. Furthermore, through the cognition of the relationship between the object of comparison and the standard of comparison (*upamānopameyatva*) based on such a tree, the text reveals—by means of its underlying intention (*tātparya*)—the greater degree of pitiable wretchedness of such a man.
An example of the suggested figure of poetic fancy (*utprekṣādhvani*) is as follows: "Suffused with the breath of the serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees..."
In the springtime, this Malaya breeze causes travelers to faint.
"Locana states that there is also 'suggestion through contrast' (vyatirekadhvani).
By the word 'also' (api), he indicates that it possesses two varieties, just like the figure of speech 'corroboration by another matter' (arthāntaranyāsa).
[The phrase] 'previously'..."

"May I be born in a forest region, in a secluded and dense part of the woods where, due to the abundance of many clearly visible trees, no one can even see me. "The sky they illuminate," and "You are reddened by fresh shoots. May I be born there.

The meaning is as follows: one who is hunchbacked is useless for tasks such as dancing; likewise, one whose leaves have fallen does not even provide shade—what, then, could he possess in the way of flowers and fruit?
The intention is that even such a thing might sometimes be useful for a charcoal-burner or as a dwelling for owls and the like.
As for the word "human," the intention is that it refers to a person who easily obtains what he seeks.
Regarding the word "loka" (world):
the sense is that it is a great calamity when that which is sought after by those in need is not at all possible to provide for them.
Here, [the phrase] "those who illuminate the sky exceedingly brightly" refers to the *bālapriyā*.
Immediately following this, the reading "raktas tvaṃ navapallavair" is seen in some places, but that is an error;
nor is the reading "na tu raktas tvam" and so forth correct.
The shadow is indeed "kubja" (humpbacked).
He states "vanetyādi," explaining that the particle "eva" (indeed) is connected with the phrase "vanoddeśe" (in the forest region);
"vanasya" and so forth is the gloss on the term "vanoddeśe."
He states the meaning to be understood with the words "where," and so forth;
it should be understood in this way for what follows as well.
"The arrangement of forms" means:
The meaning is "the fashioning of images and so forth.
Regarding the term *galitapatra*,
there is also the reading *truṭitatra*.
"Of the charcoal-burner" means one who subsists on charcoal. "May I be born as a hunchbacked tree with fallen leaves in a clearing," he thought.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is: "May I be poor in the world of men, with renunciation as my sole essence.
Regarding the phrase "expressed by the word" (*śabdavācya*), its connection is with the word "manifests" (*prakāśayati*).
For here, in the springtime, the Malaya breeze causes the fainting of travelers precisely by inflicting the torment of the god of love (*manmatha*).

Since that [heat] is imagined as being "faintened by the breath of serpents clinging to the sandalwood," it is a figure of *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). Although not explicitly stated, it is perceived through the power of the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha-sāmarthya*) in the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*).

Nor can it be said that in such a context there is a lack of connection without the employment of words such as *iva*; for because it is indicative (*gamaka*), it occurs elsewhere as well. Thus, there is no poetic figure whatsoever that is merely denotable (*vācya*).
By the term "comparison" (upamāna), he effects the purification of the path through contrast (vyatireka).
"Excellence" (ādhikya) means contrast.
Regarding the term *utprekṣitam* (imagined):
for one who is fainted by the wind of poison becomes swollen and intensified, thereby causing delusion;
and furthermore, one who is fainted in the midst of travelers causes others as well to lose their fortitude and fall into a faint. Thus, there is a double-layered poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*).
Surely, in this case, the qualifier fits precisely as a logical reason (*hetu*).
What follows from that? For there is no such thing as a logical reason in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).
Nevertheless, to claim that a logical reason is merely imagined (*utprekṣyate*) is quite trivial.
The *Bālapriyā* states: "It effects the purification of the path.

The meaning is that the cognition of the relationship between the object of comparison (*upameya*) and the components of the comparison (*upamāṅga*), which consists of some similarity to a property (*dharma*), is indeed a constituent part of the cognition of the distinction (*vyatireka*).
In the commentary (*vṛtti*), it says: "'In the sandalwood...'"
The meaning is "the sandalwood tree situated on the Malaya mountain.
"In spring" (*madhau*) means during the season of Vasanta.
"To the traveler," and so forth.
The meaning is: "the state of causing delusion to people separated from their lovers.
Regarding the word "manmathe" (in love):
the meaning is "by means of the cause that bestows objects through the kindling of desire."
The term "tattvi" means the state of causing fainting in travelers. The passage beginning with "in sandalwood" [is as follows].
The meaning is that it is a poetic fancy (utprekṣita) based on the reason of being fainted by the breath of the serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees.
He explains this with the words "by the poisonous wind," and so forth;
"by the poisonous wind" means by the air mixed with poison.
The sense is that, in the present context, the contact with poison is understood through the connection of the breath-wind with the serpent.
The root list (dhātupāṭha) states: "mūrch is used in the senses of fainting, delusion, and heightening.
Therein, taking the sense of heightening as primary, he explains it as "bṛṃhita" (augmented), which is further clarified by the word "upacita" (accumulated).
"It causes delusion" means that by its own attachment, it produces a state of delusion in another.
He explains with the intention of clarifying the meaning of the word "gopa" (protector): "And one," and so forth.
Here, by virtue of being a single entity, the wind—which acts like a traveler—should be understood.
The meaning is that the loss of fortitude occurs through its agency.
"Into a swoon" (mūrchām) means "into a state of delusion" (moham).

"Poetic fancy in both ways" (ubhayathotprekṣā) means that the two states— being intensified by the poison-like wind and the attainment of the stage of delusion— are poetically fancied as the causes for the Malaya breeze inducing a swoon in travelers.

In the commentary (*vṛtti*), he demonstrates through a doubt and its resolution that the passage "imagined as being in a state of fainting" has the purpose of presenting a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) based on the stated reason—beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*), etc.
The term "qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*) refers to the qualification beginning with "sandalwood," etc.
The phrase "precisely as a reason" (*hetutayaiva*) [is explained as follows].
The meaning is: "precisely by virtue of containing the reason within itself.
He provides the resolution with the words beginning with "tataḥ":
"tataḥ kim" means "even though it contains the reason within itself, what [follows]?"
Why is this? To this he says: "For not," and so forth.
The meaning is that, although that qualification brings about a fainting spell, it does not possess causal efficacy in reality.
Nevertheless, however... [the text continues].
"But what" is the meaning [of *kiṃ tu*]. "The causality is poetically imagined" (*utprekṣyate*) means that the causality of the two things already mentioned is poetically imagined.
The reading is also *hetutāpi*.
In that interpretation, by means of the word *api*, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the two metaphors (*utprekṣā*) regarding the Malaya breeze.

The qualifying phrase "intensified and connected by the breaths of the serpents clinging to the sandalwood trees" is intended merely as a description of its essential nature; therefore, it should be understood that the literal meaning is fully established.

In the commentary, the phrase "even though not explicitly stated" means "even though not conveyed by words such as *iva* and so forth"; for it is observed that even when those words are not employed, their meaning is understood.
Just as—
this full moon, having attained similarity today to your face which is clouded by anger, does not seem to fit [within it], as if it were merely upon your body.
"Indeed, even though your face is clouded by jealousy, this full moon—
having attained a likeness to it today, O fair one— is simply not contained within it."
Thus [ends] the shadow-commentary (*chāyā*).

Regarding the phrase "that," even when words such as *iva* and so forth are not employed, we observe that there is a perception—that is, a comprehension—of that meaning, which consists of a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*).
He illustrates this very point with the example beginning "just as."

Even if it were to bear a resemblance to a face that is slightly reddish-hued yet turbid with envy, what could it ever do? For your face is something that lies beyond even the path of one's desires—this is the intended meaning of the word "even" (api).
It does not merely fit within its own body; rather, it fills the ten directions, since it cannot be contained within its own limbs.
"In this much time" means for the duration of a single day.
Here, the filling of the quarters by the full moon is poetically imagined (*utprekṣyate*) as being accomplished through its own inherent nature (*svarasasiddha*).

Now, one might think that by using the word "nanu," which expresses the form of a conjecture or poetic fancy (*vitarkotprekṣā*), the lack of logical connection has been refuted; thus, [the suggestion] is of the nature of a resonance (*anuraṇanarūpā*), where the sequence of the suggested meaning is discernible (*saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgyā*). This is the *Bālapriyā*.
"It is perceived" means it is known.
He raises an objection with the words "And not," etc., meaning "in such a case," which refers to instances such as [the verse] beginning with "attached to sandalwood.
"[It would be] incoherent" means...
The meaning is that *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy) is not connected to the sentence;
that is to say, it is not conveyed by the sentence. He provides the resolution: "Because it is indicative (*gamakatvāt*)."
The meaning is that qualifiers such as "sandalwood" (candana) convey their sense through the cooperation of the perceiver’s intuition and other factors.
He states the proof for this with the words "even elsewhere," etc.
He explains the passage beginning with "in the absence of its [use]," etc., with the words "of that," etc.
"Out of jealousy" (*īrṣyā*) means: this is the speech uttered to appease the heroine who is angry;
it is the explanation of the phrase "of one turbid with jealousy," beginning with "slightly," and so forth.
He states what is implied by the word "api" (even/also) with the words "yadi tu" (but if), etc.
In both instances, the word "candra" (the moon) is to be supplied as the object of "udvahet" (should carry) and "kuryāt" (should perform).
By the word "adya" (today), he indicates what is understood: namely, "at all times."
"What should one do then?
means that due to an excess of contentment, one does not know what one might do;
such is the state of being.
The meaning is that it becomes like the moon.
"Only in the body" refers to the shadow (*chāyā*).
He says "no," and so forth, explaining that the particle *eva* (only) is to be construed with the word "measures" (*māti*).
Here he states the implied reason: "since it fills the ten directions.
He explains the word *adya* (now) with the words beginning "to such an extent" (*iyatā*).
He demonstrates the *dhvani* (suggested meaning) with the words beginning "herein" (*atra*).
Regarding the phrase "filling the directions":
by the expression "it shines with its limbs," the meaning obtained is that it fills the directions with its own radiance.
This is established by its own nature (*svarasasiddha*) and is not adventitious (*asvābhāvika*).
"It is thus imagined" means that it is imagined on the grounds of attaining similarity to the face, as in the phrase "as if having attained similarity to your face.
He introduces another example with the words "Now, etc. (nanvityādi).
"By the word *nanu*": the meaning is "by the word *nanu* occurring in the verse.
The intention is that the word *nanu* is to be construed by attaining a state of similarity [with the preceding term].
He explains the verse beginning with "In fear" (*trāse*) and so forth with the words "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*) and so forth.
The connection is with the phrases "around the dwellings" (*niketān paritaḥ*) and "not pursued" (*nānubaddhaḥ*).

Or as it is said: "Though he fled in all directions from his dwelling, agitated by fear, and was not pursued by any archers, the deer nevertheless did not stop anywhere; for the beauty of his eyes had been struck by the arrows of the women’s glances, which reached as far as their ears."
In the conventional usage of words and their meanings, common consensus (*prasiddhi*) alone is the authority.

An example of *śleṣadhvani* (double entendre suggestion) is as follows: "In which [city], the young men, together with their wives, frequented the balconies whose rafters were bent down; balconies that, having obtained banners, were 'delightful' (*ramyā*), and which, by increasing passion (*rāga*), were 'secluded' (*viviktā*)."

In this context, after the comprehension of the sentence-meaning that "the women, along with the young bride, resorted to the roof-terrace," he states another example beginning with "or as" (*yathā vā*) to illustrate how the eyes of the bride are like [those of others].
The deer, leaping and attacking dwellings on all sides, was not pursued by any of those bow in hand; nevertheless, it did not stop anywhere due to its natural fear and restlessness.

Here, a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) is suggested: its beauty of eyes—the very essence of its being—was struck by the women with arrows of glances drawn back to their ears, and for that reason, it did not stay.
Anticipating the objection that even this might be incoherent, he says: "śabdārtha...
[and so on]. They have obtained flags and banners because they are beautiful.

"Flags" refers to those who have attained renown. Of what nature is this renown? It is of the nature of being "beautiful. Because they are "secluded"—that is, due to the absence of crowds of people—they increase passion, meaning the desire for sexual enjoyment.
Others, however, interpret "passion" as the splendor of their variegated beauty.
Likewise, they increase passion and affection,
because they are secluded, with well-defined limbs,
and charming; those in which the rafters— the edges of the roof— bend down.
The creepers, which possess the characteristic of three folds, are bowing;
"together" (saham) is the meaning of "simultaneously" (samam).
Now, one might object that from the word *sama* the sense of "equal" is also understood.
Regarding the phrase "followed by Bālapriyā," he says "trāsa... and so forth, explaining that the actual reason for her not standing still is indicated by the expression "agitated by fear.
With "eye-arrows"—meaning arrows which are the eyes themselves—drawn back to the ears, that is, reaching as far as the ears and drawn to the edge of the ears.
"Therefore he did not remain":
the meaning is that for the very reason already stated, he did not stay.
Thus, the sense here is that there is a suggestion (dhvani) of the poetic figure *hetūtprekṣā* (poetic fancy based on a cause).

In this case as well, one should understand that the completion of the sentence's meaning consists in the description of the essential nature [of the figure], such as "listen to the praise of the woman's gaze" and so forth.
The phrase "this too" means "even the example already mentioned."
"Incoherent" (asambaddha) means that which does not convey a meaning in the form of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā). In the commentary, the word "in sound" (śabde) [is used].
The meaning is that such linguistic usage (vyavahāra) constitutes the meaning of this word [‘iva’]. ‘Established convention’ (prasiddhi) means simply the cognition of those who understand [the text].

Thus, the point is that since the meaning in the form of a poetic fancy (utprekṣā) is perceived by connoisseurs even in the absence of words such as ‘iva’ in the aforementioned instances, it is not reasonable to charge [the poet] with the fault of incoherence (asambaddhatva).
He explains: "The banners," and so forth.
Here, the first meaning connects with the *valabhīs*, while the second connects with the young women (*vadhūs*).
He states another explanation: "others" (*anya*).
"Laṭabhās" means beautiful women.
[He addresses the objection] beginning with "nanu" and so forth.
"Because of the word *sama* (equal)"—
this is true;
for that [meaning] also arises by virtue of *śleṣa* (punning conjunction).

Furthermore, this *śleṣa* (paronomasia) is not suggested by the function of denotation (*abhidhā*), but rather arises solely through the power of the beauty of the meaning; thus, in every respect, the *śleṣa* is indeed something manifested (*dhvanyamāna*).
For this very reason, although the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) stated "the watchtowers are like brides," he did not say that there was a suggestion of a simile (*upamā-dhvani*).
For in this case, *śleṣa* (paronomasia) alone is the fundamental basis.
For if the word *samāḥ* were clearly [used in its conventional sense], then because the *upamā* (simile) would be explicit, the *śleṣa* would be merely implied by it.

However, the indeclinable *samam*, which primarily functions in the sense of "together" (*saha*), attains the status of verbal paronomasia (*śabda-śleṣa*) precisely through the power of suggestion (*vyañjanā*) by virtue of being an adverbial modifier of the action.
And without that [suggestion], there is no lack of fullness in the expression itself.
For this very reason, only when the expression is complete is that second meaning apprehended by sensitive readers (sahṛdayas) without any separate effort.
As was stated previously: "merely by knowing the science of words and their meanings," and so forth.

And this [principle] is to be followed in all examples. In the case of "Fat Caitra does not eat during the day," the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*) itself remains incomplete; therefore, that very function draws in another meaning or another word in order to fulfill its own purpose. Thus, it is equivalent to inference (*anumāna*) or presumption based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*).
This is the meaning of the word "equal" (*samam*) in the text.
The word "api" (also) has the sense of "equal" (tulyārtha).
By the word "api," there is a conjunction with the previously mentioned sense of "together" (saha).
That [conjunction] also implies that even though the meaning is one of equal form, it occurs by virtue of the power of *śleṣa* (paronomasia).
The meaning is: "by the power of another object belonging to the lineage of the husband.
"And *śleṣa*" means:
"and another object."
"Because of the function of denotation"— that is, due to the operation of *abhidhā*—
it is "not implied," meaning it is not cognized.
The sense is that because the words possess case-endings identical to those of the word "valabhī" (ridge-pole), the power of denotation is restricted to the meaning connected with the ridge-pole.
"From this very reason" means "from the very reason that is about to be stated.
"'Equal' means... [end of fragment]
The word "evenly" (*sama*) has the word "in place" (*sthāne*) as its ellipsis.
To the question, "When it is said 'evenly,' why is there no clarity [of the sound]? he says: "Evenly," and so forth;
that is, "directly" (*añjasā*), meaning "instantly" (*jhaṭiti*).
The term *sahārthavṛtti* means that which conveys a meaning in the form of coexistence (*sāhitya*).
The sense is that the subject matter under discussion is the act of young men together with their wives resorting to the turret (*valabhī*).
[This occurs] by way of being an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇatvena*).

The meaning is that [the word "equal"] functions as a qualifier for either the action of "serving" or the unexpressed action [of "being"]. "It attains the status of a verbal pun" means that it conveys a different sense, namely, "it is equal."
He establishes the suggestion based on double entendre (*śleṣadhvani*) with the words "And not," and so forth.
[The phrase] "without a separate effort" means without another distinct exertion.
He states this incidentally with the words "Fat," and so forth.

"Unfinished" (*aparyavasita*) means that because the expectation—"How can there be corpulence in one who does not eat during the day?"—is present, a cognition in which that expectation has been satisfied is not produced; this is the intended meaning.
"Regarding its own object" (*svārtha*)... [etc.]
The meaning is: "having as its object a thing characterized by fatness and so forth.
"Another thing" refers to eating at night.
"Another word" refers to the expression "he eats at night."
It draws [the object] toward itself and causes it to be connected;
this refers to inference (*anumāna*) and so forth. Here, the correspondence should be understood according to their respective order.
He explains the term *yathāsaṃkhya* (correspondence) in the commentary, beginning with "For this reason" (*ata hi*), etc.:
"In accordance with the order of enunciation" (*yathoddeśam*) means without overstepping the sequence of the initial mention;
"in the subsequent enumeration" (*anūddeśe*) means when there is a later specification.

"That which constitutes beauty" refers to that suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) which produces beauty, which is of the nature of resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa*), and whose sequence [of perception] is discernible (*saṃlakṣyakrama*).

"In *madanā*"—the words such as *aṅkurita* (sprouted) and so forth, which serve as qualifiers for *madana* (love), have as their referent the slight manifestation and so on that has arisen; "located therein" means dependent upon that [referent].
The word "tat" (that) means the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) consisting of a sequence that produces beauty;
that, moreover, is simply a correspondence of number according to the order as heard in the text.
"Of the *madana* and the *sahakāra*" means "of those two, which consist of cause and effect. "Equal," etc.
The meaning is: "from the definition of that kind of conjunction (samuccaya) which consists in a simultaneous connection" (*tulyakālasambandha*).
Regarding the phrase "to be expressed" (*vācya*), the meaning is "to be understood" (*bodhya*) by means of the two *ca*-particles.
"Atiricyamānam" means "excellent";
"ālakṣyate" means "is perceived" or "is known."
The apprehension of the pun (*śleṣa*) as being primary occurs even without explicit words, through the power of the sense (*artha-sāmarthya*).
An example of the suggestion of "respective order" (*yathāsaṃkhya-dhvani*) is as follows: "The mango tree has sprouted, put forth leaves, formed buds, and blossomed;
so too has passion (*madana*) sprouted, put forth leaves, formed buds, and blossomed within my heart."

For here, in the subsequent enumeration (anūddeśa) corresponding to the initial statement (uddeśa), that beauty consisting of resonance (*anuraṇana*), which resides in words such as "sprouted" (*aṅkurita*) functioning as qualifiers of Madana, is perceived as surpassing the expressed meaning characterized by *tulyayogitā* (parallelism) and *samuccaya* (conjunction) between Madana and the mango tree (*sahakāra*).

In this same way, other figures of speech [are to be understood] according to their respective application. There is no occasion for the theory of Suggestion (*dhvani*) for the Logicians (*tārkika*) and the Mīmāṃsakas; so, enough with this prolixity.
Thus he says: "even though not denoted by words" (*aśabdāpi*).
"Thus others as well":
it is observed that all poetic figures (*arthālaṅkāra*) can function as suggestion (*dhvani*).
For example, the suggestion of the figure *dīpaka* (illumination): "May neither fire, nor wind, nor an elephant intoxicated with rut, nor an axe [harm] you..."
Or like a thunderbolt hurled from Indra’s hand, may there be well-being for you, O tree, together with your creeper.

In this passage, the beauty is produced by the realization that [the speaker] is an object of extreme affection, derived precisely from the lamp being concealed by the phrase "it has been extinguished. There is also the suggestion (*dhvani*) of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise):
"Roaming about, you will die among the thorny ketaka groves."
O bee, wandering about, you shall not obtain that which is like a jasmine flower.

A certain heroine, sporting in a garden with her beloved, speaks thus to a bee; this is the meaning of the term *bhṛṅga*. In the *Bālapriyā*, the reading "in the case of the word *aṅkurite*" (*aṅkurite* being in the locative case) is also seen in the first half-verse.
This is illustrated in the *Locana* by the phrase "and as follows" (*yathā ca*).
And likewise, the reading is "iti ca.
Here, the phrase "ity atra" is also connected with the words "dīpakadhvaniḥ.
He explains the *dīpakadhvani* [suggestive illumination] with the passage beginning "bādhiṣṭha," etc.

"bādhiṣṭha" means "from the lamp," etc.; that is to say, from the form of the verb *bādh* ending in the *luṅ* suffix which conveys the sense of the optative (*māṅ*), [it follows] the property connected with many things such as fire, and so forth.
"Entirely," etc.
The meaning is: by perceiving that the tree accompanied by the creeper is the object of the speaker's unsurpassed affection.
"The production of beauty" connects with the phrase "therefore, there is the suggestion of the *dīpaka*."

In this context, as in the verse beginning with "yaśca nimbaṃ paraśunā" (and he who [cuts] the neem tree with an axe), one should understand that the completion of the expressed meaning occurs through the ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) of the verbs *dhākṣīt* ("may it burn") in the case of "mā bhavantamanalaḥ" ("may fire not [burn] you"), *bhāṅkṣīt* ("may it break") in the case of "pavano vā" ("or the wind"), and *bhaitsīt* ("may it split") in the case of "paraśurvā" ("or the axe").
"It is also the suggestion of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise)" means that it is also the suggestion of *aprastutapraśaṃsā* based on similarity (*sādṛśya*).
"The *ḍuṇḍhu*, etc. [is the example].
Searching for them, you will perish among the thorn-filled groves of *ketakī*;
O bee, wandering about, you shall not find that which resembles the *mālatī* flower.
Thus is the shadow [of the meaning].
He explains it with the words "by the beloved" and so forth;
[he refers to] the "bee."
"Moving toward the *ketakī*" means moving toward a certain bee;
"āheti" means he speaks, and therefore it means for this reason.
"Bhṛṅgasya" means "of the story of Bhṛṅga"; that is,
when it exists as the subject matter (abhidheya).

The "locana" (the eye) is precisely what is under discussion; nor can its being out of context be understood from the vocative address, for on the contrary, that address is merely a manifestation of her innocence. Thus, by the primary denotative function (*abhidhā*), the figure of "Praise of the Irrelevant" (*aprastutapraśaṃsā*) cannot be established here.
Furthermore, once the explicit statement has been completed, the state of being an "indirect reference" (*anyāpadeśatā*) is suggested by the power of the literal meaning:

that a noble wife, full of pride in her own good fortune and resembling a *mālatī* flower with its delicate fragrance, through her devotion to sincere love, [encounters] those [men] who have attained an excess of fame through feigned cleverness, who are beset by the thorns of procuresses (*śambhalī*), and who are like a forest of *ketakī* flowers whose scent is distant.

She reproaches her beloved, who wanders from one house of courtesans to another, through an *apahnuti-dhvani* (suggestion of concealment), as in the following verse by our teacher Bhaṭṭendurāja: "He who acts as the sole essence for the dwelling of the decorative patterns of the dark, heavy leaves [of the *kālaguru* tree], upon the expansive and exceedingly beautiful expanse of the jar-like breasts of the fair-limbed woman, in that abode of nectar—[he alone is my beloved].
By the use of the particle *eva* ("only/alone"), there is an exclusion of his being anything other than the subject at hand (*prastutatva*). Thus, the suggestion of concealment is established.
One might suspect— [this is expressed by] "na ca" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from the invitation," the word "of the bee" (bhṛṅgasya) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.
The meaning is that it is due to the addressing of a bee (*bhramara*) who is not to be addressed.
"The apprehension of irrelevance" means the cognition of its being irrelevant. The syntactic connection is with the word "na ca" (and not).
Why is this so? To this he says: "On the contrary," and so forth.

*Maugdhyam* refers to the innocence (*mugdhatvam*) of that heroine; its "manifestation" (*vijṛmbhitam*) means, in effect, that which is caused by her innocence, according to the definition of an innocent girl (*mugdha*) such as "an innocent girl [is one] young in age and passion," and so on.
The word *iti* indicates the reason.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the denotation (*abhidhā*) first," and so forth:

if the account of the bee were irrelevant to the context, then the sentence would terminate solely in the sense of reproaching the beloved, and thus its completion would occur through the denotative function alone.
Since the account of the bee is also possible as being introduced in the present context, it is intended primarily [as a secondary meaning].
The meaning—that the matter consisting of the reproach of the beloved is not fully completed by the primary function (abhidhā)—is the sense [of the verse].
[This refers to the phrase] "when [the primary function] has been completed," and so forth.
The meaning is: "when the understanding of the intended sense—consisting of the bee and its kin—is accomplished by virtue of the context.
"By the force of the expressed meaning" means "by the force of the similarity of the expressed meaning."
"Anyāpadeśatā" means "being something else"; he says this with the words beginning with "yat" and so forth.
The reading is "sukumāraḥ sundaraḥ mugdhakulavadhūḥ. Regarding the word *prema*: it means love directed toward the beloved.
The connection is that he reproaches [them] by means of the reason "by way of being other. Regarding the term *kṛtaka*:
those [works] by which an excellence of renown has been acquired through artificial cleverness (*kṛtakavaidagdhyena*).
"Śambhalī" means that [the places] are filled with procuresses who are like thorns;
there is also a reading, "ḍāmbhikakaṇṭaka" (thorns of hypocrites).
"Dūre" means "far away"; the sense is that they are like those groves of *ketakī* flowers whose fragrance pervades a great distance.
"Cañcūryamāṇam" means... [moving about].
The meaning is: "moving repeatedly for the sake of enjoying that.
As for "he" (yaḥ):
he in whom there is an abundant and beautiful expanse, like the jar-like breasts of a fair-limbed woman.
In the moon, which is the abode of nectar, there is a design of leaf-patterns fashioned with black aloe-wood— meaning a "patrabhaṅga" (leaf-design);
by way of that form, or rather, by its being the "āvāsaḥ" (abode) or locus of such a design, it alone is comparable to the essence.

O beautiful one with curved limbs, this Smara, desiring to dispel the fever born from dwelling in the hearts of longing women ignited by the fire of separation, bends his wide-reaching limbs toward your eye, O lady of curved form.

Here, the concealment (*apahnava*) of Lakṣmaṇa, who resides in the center of the moon’s orb, is suggested (*dhvanyate*) by his taking on the form of the God of Love (*manmatha*), whose complexion is stained by the scorching heat arising from the hearts of women tormented by the fire of separation.
Herein lies a suggestion based on doubt (*sasandehadhvani*): because not even the name of him who dwells in the moon is mentioned;

rather, we do not know what this object might be, which displays its essence and excellence as the locus for the artistic arrangement of dark aloe-wood leaf-patterns upon the moon, which stands in the place of the full breasts of a fair-limbed woman.
Even a state of doubt is suggested:

she who previously rejected his advances, now remorseful and longing in separation, has prepared herself for the arrival of her beloved by performing rites such as adorning herself; thus, at the moment of the full moon's rising, she is brought [to him] by the mouth of a messenger.

The lover, offering flattery by saying, "The decorative leaf-designs of black aloe-wood applied to your jar-like breasts cause the arousal of love," also conveys the suggested meaning of a *prativastūpamā* (parallel simile) by implying: "This moonlight, possessing a luster dark as the petals of a blue lotus, acts in exactly the same way.

Furthermore, the word "sudhādhāmani" (the abode of nectar), though employed here as a synonym for the moon, also functions as a cause for the desire to dispel the heat, as [the lover] thinks: "He is this very one. This is according to the *Bālapriyā*.
The word "yaḥ" (which) is a reference back to the meaning of "saḥ" (that). "Viccheda" means separation from one's beloved; this very separation is the "anala," or fire.
By that [fire], the hearts of women who are longing and distressed are inflamed; he whose arising is due to the perfuming by those [hearts] is such.
"Desiring to remove the heat" means desiring to lead it away or to pacify it; this is a phrase containing a reason (*hetugarbha*). "Extended" means stretched out.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is that Smara (the God of Love) is characterized by his limbs.
He demonstrates the *dhvani* (suggested meaning) with the words beginning "here," etc. [He states:
"it is a concealment (*apahnava*)."
This is not a physical mark, but rather such a form of love (manmatha); this is the meaning of the apahnava (concealment).
The passage beginning with "yataḥ" and ending with "ācarati" is the commentary of the expounder.
"Of him" means of Lakṣmaṇa. "Was not taken" means... [as follows].
The meaning is that it has not been specifically indicated.
However, in the passage beginning with "api tu" (but rather),
the word "gṛhītam" (is grasped) is to be supplied as a supplement.
The connection is with the phrase "api tu" (but rather), meaning "it is understood as such";
that is to say, it is indicated in this manner,
such as "fair-limbed" and so forth.
The meaning is "equal to the breasts of a fair-limbed woman distinguished by their fullness.
The explanation of the term *racanāvāsa* is "as the locus of artistic arrangement (*vicchitti*).
[This refers to what] "she practices."
The meaning is "it brings about.
This is a statement of the resultant sense.
The analysis of the compound is either: "it behaves as if it were excellent," or "it becomes excellent" (*sāra*).
The word "tad" (that) means "because of such an instruction. The phrase "we do not know," and so forth, is a statement of the form of doubt.

The word *iti* means: because of the perception of doubt residing in the speaker-nāyaka, whose nature is that of one who has not reached a definitive conclusion (*anadhyavasāya*). "Sasandeha" refers to the poetic figure (alaṅkāra) of doubt.
The word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Regarding the phrase "previously" and so forth:
*praṇaya* is the request of one who is most dear.
"Anutaptām" means possessed of remorse; "bhūtām" means... [true].
The word "the heroine" (nāyikā) is to be supplied as the object; this connects with the phrase "uttering endearments" (cāṭukaṃ kurvāṇa).
The passage beginning with "belonging to you" (tvadīya) and so forth [is to be understood].
"Flattering speech" means she acts in this very manner; that is to say, she acts as an arouser of passion.
Thus, this is the path of "simile by correspondence" (*prativastūpamā*):

through the perception of the meaning of the speaker-narrator’s flattering words— that the arrangement of leaf-patterns from black aloe-wood applied to your jar-like breasts, which excites the god of love, and this luster of the moon, dark as the petal of a blue lotus, produce exactly the same effect.
The meaning is that there is a suggestion (dhvani) within the *prativastūpamā* [simile].
Regarding the phrase "the state of being a cause" (*hetutām*),
the ellipsis is to be supplied as "of the literal sense consisting in the nature of being a repository of nectar."
There is also the reading "it inflames [passion] along with the beauties.
There is also the suggestion (dhvani) of the figure of speech *hetu* (cause), in that it reveals the eye.
There is also the suggestion of the figure of speech *sahokti* (togetherness), in that the beauty of your breasts and the beauty of the moon together inflame Madana.
From the realization of the meaning, "The moon is like your breast; your breast’s expanse is like the moon," there is also the suggestion (dhvani) of *upameyopamā* (reciprocal simile).
In this way, other varieties can also be conceived here, for the speech of great poets is like a wish-fulfilling cow (*kāmadhenu*).
For it is said: Even a mere whim may bring about inconceivable results for someone, while for another, even great effort is insufficient for the slightest fruit.
The flicking of a single hair by a world-elephant shakes the earth, yet a bee, even as it descends from the sky, cannot move a mere creeper.
The state of being combined (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) or mixed (*saṅkara*) among these varieties should be considered according to their respective application.

An example of *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) as suggestion (*dhvani*) is as follows, by me alone: "Your body is the very height of the intoxication of amorous play; your two eyes are like the playful lover of the God of Love, ever-curved with artful gestures; the sequence of your playful movements of the eyebrows is a cause of transformation even at first sight; oh, the nectar of your lotus-face! Truly, O beautiful one, you alone are the singular essence of the three worlds created by the Creator."
For here, among the spring months and the intoxicants of love, there is mutual nourishment of their respective charms throughout the three worlds;
yet they are called "dear to children" because *helā* means playful sport (*līlā*).
"Effort" (*yatna*) is an activity preceded by cognition;
the phrase "it occurs in both sentences" is to be understood as the ellipsis.
He supports the stated general principle with a specific instance, beginning with "the elephant of the quarter" (*digdantī*), and so forth.
There is also the reading "the movement of the limbs of the elephant of the quarters" (digdantino 'ṅgacalanam).
Regarding the phrase "of these, however," and so forth: there is a commingling of these with the others by way of negation.
The meaning is that one should consider such matters as the commingling (*saṅkara*) of *sasandeha*, *prativastūpamā*, and *upameyopamā* through their entry into a single sentence, and so forth.
Regarding the word *kelī*:
"O beautiful lady! Your two eyes are the *kandala*—meaning the fresh sprout, that is to say, the slight manifestation—of the play (*krīḍā*) of the sporting folk."
"Kelīkandalita" means that [beauty] has sprouted as sport;
the meaning is "of that which has recently appeared.
"Vibhrama" refers to the amorous gestures of women; the "vibhrama" that produces those is "śobhā" (loveliness).
Alternatively, "dhuryam" refers to that which bears the yoke—the burden—of spring, which is characterized by the arousal of passion and so forth;
[the word] "vapuḥ" (body) is to be supplied as the object.
The meaning is that your pair of eyes becomes the very body of the recently manifested spring, performing its function of kindling desire and the like.
Likewise, "this" (*idam*) and so forth constitute a single compound.
This means that this sequence of play—the playful activity of the eyebrows—is an object of experience alone; it refers to a pair of eyebrows characterized by a successive series of playful movements.
*Bhaṅgī* is a specific kind of artistic arrangement.
By that cause, it becomes the curved and fragile bow of Kāma— alternatively, the curved bow endowed with various maneuvers (*bhaṅgī*) and characterized by sequential action (*kramika-karma*).
Or else, the word *idam* (this) is a separate term acting as an adjective for the bow.
Its meaning is "distinguished by successive actions.
Likewise, regarding that *āsava*— a specific kind of liquor— in the lotus of the mouth (*vaktrāmbujanman*),
there is here a poetic identification (*adhyavasāya*) of the nectar of the lips with the nature of *āsava*.
Even at the initial encounter, and even with a slight taste,
it becomes the cause of mental transformations such as delusion and bliss;
oh, how wonderful this is!
Therefore, you alone are the creation of the Creator; you are the essence of the three worlds, having become the very quintessence of the triple universe.
This is the truth, certain.
Here, the word "for" (hi) is connected with "is implied" (dhvanyate) and so forth.
The portion ending with "by way of nourishing" is the statement of the reason (*hetu*).
