The portion beginning with "those" (*te*) is the description of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*); these [terms] are to be construed [together].

Having thus explained the path of *alaṅkāra-dhvani*, this is said in order to demonstrate its utility: "Those poetic figures (*alaṅkāras*) which, when established as the expressed meaning (*vācya*), do not possess a formal body—these attain a supreme luster when they have entered the state of being a constituent part of *dhvani*. (DhvK 2.28)
Those figures of speech whose status as the expressed meaning is not fixed attain a supreme luster when they become subordinate elements of suggestion (dhvani). (28)
And being a constituent part of *dhvani* occurs through both modes: as the suggester (*vyañjaka*) and as the suggested (*vyaṅgya*).

In this context, it should be understood that [the figures] function as the suggested by virtue of the specific subject matter (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors. Even though they are suggested, it is only when their predominance is intended to be expressed that [they are so designated]. Locana: "By your world-transcending form, [the goddesses] have come together and abide"—here, the figure of hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) is suggested.

Since even at the first impact it is a cause of transformation, the fruition of a result that is itself transformative occurs even without the process of a succession of tastes; thus, there is also the suggestion (*dhvani*) of the figure *vibhāvanā*.
By the phrase "the preeminent bearer of the sweetness of confusion," there is also the suggestion of the figure *tulyayogitā* (parallelism).
In this way, it should be understood that all poetic figures possess the quality of being suggested.
But it is not as some have restricted it [to specific objects].

Regarding the phrase "as appropriate" (*yathāyogam*): the meaning should be applied such that in some cases the ornament (*alaṅkāra*) is the suggester (*vyañjaka*), and in others the thing itself (*vastu*). // 2.7 //

One might object: "Have not these ornaments already been mentioned by the ancients? If you now demonstrate that they are *vyaṅgya* (suggested), what is the point of this? Anticipating this doubt, he says "evam" and so forth.

For those ornaments whose embodiment consists in being expressed (*vācyatvena śarīrīkaraṇam*), which—being distinct from the primary subject that constitutes the body—are themselves bodiless like bracelets and the like; for them, the attainment of a "body" is established [through suggestion].
*Bālapriyā*: those are the intoxicants of honey and wine.
"By a body consisting of another world" means by a body in the form of eyes, in the form of eyebrows, and in the form of the nectar of the lips.
It should be understood that through the presence of the bow of Love in the form of the eyebrows, the presence of Love itself is established.
"Thus" (iti) means: by means of the cognition of the meaning of the sentence uttered by the speaker, who is desirous [of speaking].
"Hyperbole" (atiśayokti) refers to this.

The meaning is that, because of the perception of non-difference between the eyes and so forth and the spring and so forth, there is the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (poetic hyperbole) consisting of identity-in-difference.
As for "tulyayogitā" (parallelism): [it is defined as follows].

The meaning is that, by expressing the eyes as the preeminent carriers of both "bewildering beauty" (*vibhrama*) and "sweetness" (*madhu*)—intending to convey the equality between the two eyes and the spring (*madhu*)—there is what is defined by Bhāmaha and others as *tulyayogitā* (Equal Pairing), according to the principle: "even that which is inferior [is compared] with that which is superior," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "and other figures of speech likewise," he states the meaning derived from the plural number: "in this way," etc.
He states the implicit exclusion (*vyavacchedya*) with the words: "but not," etc.
"But not," [it is said]. The word "thus" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Niyata" means...
The meaning is: that for which the object—consisting of a specific type of ornament—is fixed and determined;
"the state of being suggested" (dhvanyamānatva) is to be supplied [as the predicate]. // 2.7 //
"What is the point of this? means: what is the result of demonstrating that the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) are suggested (*vyaṅgya*)? He says: [the following].
The meaning is that he demonstrates the fruit of that [practice] by means of the verse beginning with "the embodied one" (*śarīrī*).
He explains the *kārikā* with the words beginning with "of those" (*yeṣām*).
In the phrase "by way of being denotable" (*vācyatvena*), the third case ending is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
Showing the meaning of the suffix *cvi*, he explains: "making [it] into a body," and so forth. "The bringing about of bodyhood" is the meaning.

He states the reason for this established distinction: because [the meaning] can be produced with effort by a skilled poet, it is included within *dhvani*; otherwise, however, it will be demonstrated that it constitutes *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion).
Even when they function as suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) by virtue of being subordinate (*āṅgitva*),
there are two possible ways for figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*): sometimes they are suggested by a mere fact (*vastumātra*), and sometimes by another figure of speech.
In that regard— when figures of speech are manifested by the mere fact of the subject matter (vastumātra),
they certainly possess the status of being subordinate to suggestion (dhvani);
the reason for this is as follows:
...the poetic function (kāvya-vṛtti) has that [suggestion] as its basis. (Dhvanyāloka 2.29)
The reason for this is: "The function of poetry has that [suggestion] as its basis. (29)

Or rather, "locanam" means that for those [figures of speech] which, while being expressible, do not even have a fixed status as the "body" [of poetry], and are thus difficult to establish—that is to say, those figures of speech—having attained the state of being limbs of *dhvani* (the function) or of poetry by way of being the suggested form (*vyaṅgyarūpatayā*), they attain a supreme, rare "chāyā," meaning splendor or their own essential nature.
This is what is meant: just as a skilled poet, like a clever woman, may employ an ornament even if it is strained (*śliṣṭa*).
Nevertheless, its attainment of corporeality alone is achieved with difficulty, like the yellowing of saffron;
as for its attainment of selfhood, what possibility of it could there even be?
And yet, such is this suggestiveness (vyaṅgyatā) that, although it is subordinate, it bestows upon the figures of speech a superiority over those that are merely expressed (vācya).
Having kept in mind the sense that even in childhood play there is, as it were, kingship, he says: "Otherwise, however... (2.8).
Regarding the word "tatra" (therein):
it means when two courses of action are possible.
The phrase "the reason for this" is the text of the commentary (*vṛtti*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "of poetry" (*kāvyasya*) and "of the poet's activity" (*kavivyāpārasya*), [the commentary] states "of good poets" (*sukavīnām*) and so forth.
The word *vācyatve* ends in the locative case.
He explains it differently as well, taking *na* as a separate word, by saying "if, however" (*yadi vā*) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "attaining the status of a subordinate element of *dhvani*," he explains the word *dhvani* in two ways, beginning with "of the function" (*vyāpārasya*), and so forth.
To the question "In what way is it a subordinate element? he replies: "by virtue of being the suggested meaning" (*vyaṅgyatayā*).
Alternatively, in accordance with the previously mentioned explanation, he states the sense of the term "bhāva," beginning with "it has been said that... (*ataduktam*), and so forth.
"Ornament" (bhūṣaṇa) means such things as metaphors (upamā) and so forth, as well as saffron (kuṅkuma) and so forth.
"Connected" (śliṣṭa) means...
The meaning is "attached";
"closely joined" (*atiśliṣṭa*) is also a reading. "Attaining the state of a body" (*śarīrītāpatti*) means the accomplishment of being a body.
"Of this" means of the ornament consisting of the simile and so forth. "Saffron," etc. [is the meaning].
"Kuṅkumapītikā" means like a particular kind of ointment mixed with saffron;
"of ātmatā" means of the production of selfhood.
The word "asya" (of this) is to be supplied [to the previous sentence].
"What possibility [could there be]? means that the accomplishment of selfhood is something to be achieved with extreme difficulty.
He introduces the passage beginning with "otherwise" (*itarathā*) with the words "of such a nature" (*evambhūtā*), etc.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "this state of being suggested (*vyaṅgyatā*) is of such a nature.
To the question "Of what nature?", he says: "which," etc. (*yā...*).
"Like kingship": the remainder [of the sentence] is "the king's child compared to other children. (2.8)

The phrase "the commentary (*vṛtti*) text" implies that it is not a portion of the *kārikās*. This is because, as stated in the verse, "Poetry (*kāvya*) is the *vṛtti* based upon that," poetry there proceeds precisely by way of being intent upon such suggested (*vyaṅgya*) ornaments.
Otherwise, however, that would be merely a statement of those very ornaments;
furthermore, when those same ornaments function as the suggested meaning for another ornament.
... [the suggested meaning] would become a subordinate element of the sound (dhvani);
for if the predominance of the suggested (vyaṅgya) is perceived through the excellence of its beauty, [it is no longer dhvani]. (DhvK 2.30)

Furthermore, it would follow that [the suggested meaning] is a subordinate element of the sound (dhvani), if the predominance of the suggested meaning were perceived solely on account of its excellence in beauty. // 30 //

For it has been said: "The intention to emphasize the predominance of either the expressed (vācya) or the suggested (vyaṅgya) is based on the excellence of their respective beauty. Furthermore, regarding the suggestion of mere facts (vastumātra-vyaṅgyatva) by poetic figures (alaṅkāra), the scope [of this] is to be inferred from the examples shown immediately above. Thus, the function of one meaning—whether as a mere meaning or as a specific poetic figure—consists in the manifestation of another meaning that is itself a poetic figure, since it tends toward the figure that serves as its substratum.
"Otherwise" means: if it were not directed toward that [ultimate goal]. Therefore, one should not even suspect the presence of subordinated suggestion (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgyatā*) in that case.
The intended meaning (*tātparya*) is as follows:
"of those very ornaments" (*tāsāmevālaṅkṛtīnām*) is an explanatory supplement (*upaskāra*) to the verse that is about to be recited;
the word "again" (*punar*) is an explanatory supplement occurring in the middle of the verse.
"Being a limb of *dhvani*" means being a variety of *dhvani*. "The predominance of the suggested meaning" (*vyaṅgyaprādhānya*)— this is the sense.
The reason for this is "due to the excellence of beauty.
As for the word "yadi" (if):

the sense is that if [the suggested meaning] were not predominant, then the expressed ornament (*vācyālaṅkāra*) alone would be primary, and thus it would be a case of "subordinated suggestion" (*guṇībhūtavyaṅgya*).

Anticipating the objection—"Surely, an ornament (alaṅkāra) is suggested by a fact (vastu), and it is also suggested by another ornament; why then have examples for this not been shown?"—he says: "vastu" [etc.].
He summarizes this concisely: "tadevam" [etc.].
He explains [the verse] according to the reading of the kārikā, beginning with "kāvyasya" and so on.
"Of the poet's operation" means of that which consists of word and meaning. "Function" (vṛtti) [is the term used].
The meaning is "stability.
With the intention that she (the stability) has ornament as her locus, he explains [the verse] with the words beginning "ornament," etc. [He asks]:
"If there is no intent for that"?
The meaning is: "if it were not intent upon suggested figures of speech.
In the commentary, the phrase "it would be merely that sentence" refers to "that" which is intended to be poetry.
The meaning is that it is "merely a sentence" and not the soul of poetry (kāvyātman).
Therefore, one must regard it as being subordinate to that [the soul];
thus, the implication is that it is merely a constituent part of suggestion (dhvani).
The *Locana* demonstrates this intended meaning with the words "by that," and so forth.
The phrase "of those" (*tāsām*) is also connected with the expression "the state of being suggested by another ornament.
With the intention that "of those" means "of those very ornaments," the author of the *Vṛtti* stated, "of those very ornaments"; thus he says, "of those very," and so forth.
"Paṭhiṣyati," and so forth.
The meaning is that even by connecting with the verse to be stated later, it serves as an aid by removing the expectation regarding the word "kāsām" (of which).
He explains [the term] in accordance with the context: "the state of being a variety of sound" (*dhvanibhedatvam*).
The meaning is that it is a sub-variety of *dhvani*. "Only a verbal ornament" means precisely [an ornament] such as *dīpaka* and the like.
In the *kārikā*, the phrase "in the state of being suggested by another ornament" means "when there is suggestion by another ornament.
He states the essential meaning of the passage beginning with "Thus, in this way" as follows: "Of the suggested," and so forth.

When there is a manifestation [of the suggested] based on an excellence of beauty (*cārutva*), and when that [suggested] holds primacy, one should understand that this is *dhvani* consisting of a resonance (*anuraṇana*) arising from the power of the meaning (*arthaśaktyudbhava*).
Having thus explained the various divisions of *dhvani*, it is now stated in order to distinguish its manifestations:
"Where the meaning being perceived appears as something blurred, or even as a subordinate element of the expressed meaning (*vācya*), that is not the province of *dhvani*. (Dhvanyāloka 2.31)
Where the suggested meaning appears as something blurred,
or even as a subordinate element to the expressed meaning, this is not the domain of Dhvani.
Even when perceived in two ways— as clear and as unclear—
that which is perceived clearly, whether through the power of the word (*śabda-śakti*) or the power of the meaning (*artha-śakti*), alone constitutes the path of *dhvani*, and not the other.

Furthermore, even that which is perceived clearly, if it appears as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the expressed meaning (*abhidheya*), is not within the scope of this *dhvani* whose nature is resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya*).
For example:
"The lotus-pools have been trampled, the swans driven away, and yet my sister-in-law has not [been seen].

The essential meaning is that this [suggestion arising from the power of the sense] is fourfold, because the suggestor (*vyañjaka*)—whether it takes the form of a fact (*vastu*) or an ornament (*alaṅkāra*)—is itself of two kinds, and these are combined respectively. (29, 30)
Thus:

there are two primary divisions—the one where the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*) and the one where the expressed meaning is intended but has another purpose (*vivakṣitānyaparavācya*).

Of the first, there are two subdivisions: that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyantatiraskṛtavācya*) and that in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*).

The second [type of suggestion] has two divisions: that in which the sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama*) and that which consists of resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa*). The first has infinite subdivisions.
The second is twofold: rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*) and rooted in the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*).

The last [type] is threefold: that whose body is created by the bold assertion (*prauḍhokti*) of the poet, that whose body is created by the bold assertion of a speaker fashioned by the poet, and that which is possible in itself (*svataḥ-sambhavī*).

Each of these is fourfold according to the previously stated method of the distinction between the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) and the suggester (*vyañjaka*); thus, there are twelve varieties based on the power of meaning (*artha-śakti-mūla*).
Together with the first four varieties, there are sixteen primary divisions.
And these two [types of suggestion] will each be described as twofold, according to whether they are manifested by words or by sentences.

However, for that [suggestion] whose sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣyakrama*), there are thirty-five varieties, based on its being manifested by letters, words, sentences, compositions (*saṅghaṭanā*), and entire works (*prabandha*). "Distinction" (*viveka*) refers to the differentiation from those semblances of it, namely, the semblances of suggestion (*dhvanyābhāsa*).

For the sake of easy understanding for beginners, [the author] summarizes the varieties of *dhvani* already mentioned and those yet to be described, stating from the words "that whose expressed meaning is not intended" (*avivakṣitavācya*) up to the end of "thirty-five varieties.
Regarding the phrase "of the mentioned varieties":
this means the varieties consisting of *vastu* (matter) and *alaṅkāra* (ornament).

"The first four" means that there are four types: the one where the expressed meaning is completely set aside (atyantatiraskṛtavācya), the one where the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (arthāntarasaṅkramitavācya), the one where the suggested meaning has no perceptible sequence (alakṣyakramavyaṅgya), and the one consisting of resonance based on the power of words (śabdaśaktimūlānuraṇanarūpa).
"They will be described as twofold" [refers to the remaining two].
And thus, the meaning is "thirty-two.
Regarding the passage beginning with "varṇa" (phonemes) and so forth:

since the division [of poetry] was previously stated here as being manifested through words and sentences, what is intended by this [present statement] is precisely that triad of divisions which is manifested through phonemes, composition, and literary works.
Thus, there are thirty-five varieties.
Regarding the phrase "from their semblances" (tadābhāsebhyaḥ) and so forth,
it should be understood that the term "of sound" (dhvaneḥ) is connected here as well.
The first half of the verse beginning with "yatra" is explained [in the commentary] by the passage beginning with "dvividho 'pi.
The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: that which is being perceived (*pratiyamānaḥ*) is of two kinds—both the manifest (*sphuṭa*) and the unmanifest (*asphuṭa*).
Someone has thrown a flat stone into the village pond.
For in this case, the suggested element— the maiden bride’s perception of the reflection of the cloud— serves solely as a subordinate factor to the expressed meaning.

In such instances, and in other cases as well, wherever the predominance of the expressed meaning over the suggested is determined by the perception of a superior excellence of beauty in the expressed,
there the predominance of the expressed over the suggested is established through that very perception of the superior excellence of beauty in the expressed.
In that case, because the suggested meaning is perceived as a subordinate element (*aṅga*), it does not fall within the scope of *dhvani*.
For example:
"Of her who was listening to the clamor of birds flying up from the thicket of reeds..."
The limbs of Bahukā, occupied with household chores, are growing cold.
For such a subject matter is generally cited as an example of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (where the suggested meaning is subordinate).
[The Locana states: "This particular type of poetry is not within the scope of that *dhvani* which is its very soul.
The lotus-pools were not soiled, nor were the swans suddenly startled into flight."
The meaning is that it was not within range;
someone had raised a cloud over a village pond and cast it [into the water].
Thus is the shadow [of the meaning]. Others, however, say that even a father’s sister is addressed in this manner by someone who is exceedingly clever.
It is indeed a subordinate element of the expressed meaning (*vācyāṅgatva*).

For it is precisely through the expressed meaning—in the form of the transitory emotion (*vibhāva*) of astonishment—that the excellence of bewilderment is perceived; thus, the perfection of beauty arises from the expressed meaning itself.
However, the expressed meaning, for the sake of its own realization, suggests another meaning out of a desire for its own assistance.
The limbs of the young wife, occupied with household chores, grew weary as she listened to the clamor of birds flying up from the thicket of reed creepers.
Thus ends the commentary (*cchāyā*).
The word "also" (*api*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
The word "clearly" (*sphuṭa*)— [End of excerpt]
The meaning is "distinctly divided.
The term "indistinct" (*asphuṭa*) is an explanation of the phrase "that which appears as blurred.
The explanation of the latter half of the verse beginning with "vācya" is provided by the words "even though distinct" (*sphuṭo 'pi*), and so forth.

In the *Locana*, he states the meaning of the fourth quarter, "Not this [is] her mouth," (*nāsyāsau*) and so forth, which was not elucidated in the commentary (*vṛtti*): "Of such a person" (*asya*), etc.
This is a speech beginning with "The lotus" (*kamaleti*) addressed by a certain innocent young woman—astonished upon seeing a cloud reflected in a pond—to her friends or her paternal aunt.

Someone, at a village pond, has "upturned" (*uttānitam*) the cloud—that is, made it face upward; otherwise, it would not be visible beneath the water as it is seen above. However, it has been "thrown down" (*kṣiptam*).
The lotus-pools are not "malina" (dirty); rather, the shadow is "malina" because it has become soiled. The swans have suddenly flown up, having gone upwards.
And the sense is that this is not at all surprising.
He says "others," etc., to indicate that some read "pitṛṣvasa" (paternal aunt) in place of "sahasā" (suddenly).
He explains the meaning of "by someone" as "by one who is extremely skillful.
He elucidates its status as a subordinate element of the expressed meaning (*vācyāṅgatva*) with the words "by the expressed meaning itself," etc.
"For the sake of establishing one's own self and for the repose of one's own awakening" means "another object," namely,
the sight of the reflection of a cloud by a young bride. This is the meaning.
"By the desire for his own benefit," that is, as if by the very desire to perform a service for himself.
"The *vetasa* tree"— this verse is also cited in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.
He explains the nature of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinated suggestion) here with the words "In this case," and so forth.

However, where the expressed meaning, its specific nature having been determined through context and other factors, appears once again solely as a subordinate element to the suggested meaning—that is the path of this very *dhvani* consisting of resonance (*anuraṇana-rūpa-vyaṅgya*).
For example:
"Pick up the fallen flowers; do not shake the *sehālika* plant, O daughter of a plowman!
Otherwise, this discordant clamor will be heard by Samudra as the sound of a thunderbolt."
In this context, the suggested meaning (*dhvani*)— the arrival at a place suitable for the secret tryst of a lover who has been given a signal— serves to embellish the literal meaning (*vācya*).
For instance, the phrase "of her engaged in household chores" implies that she was otherwise occupied,
while "on the path" implies that she was bound by excessive shame and dependence.
"Limbs"—not even a single limb was such that it could be concealed by means of profound gravity and feigned indifference;
"knowing this," let alone the performance of household duties, they were not even able to sustain themselves.
Thus, they were clearly perceived as being occupied with household tasks.
The perfection of beauty arises from the perception of an excellence of intoxication resulting from this very expressed meaning (*vācya*).

As for the phrase "where, however": context (*prakaraṇa*) is the beginning of that [set] which includes the capacity of the proximity of other words, indicative marks (*liṅga*), and so forth; it is where the meaning has its entire nature ascertained through the understanding of those [factors].

It should be stated again; it has been expressed once more by its own words, and for that very reason, because the realization of its own nature has already been accomplished, it does not terminate in that alone—this is what is meant by "given" (*datta*). A lover who is a thief, having made a rendezvous, reaches the place suitable for dalliance, namely, a thicket of reed-canes.
This is what is being suggested (*dhvanyamāna*).
The meaning is that it is manifested by the clamor of the birds.
The phrases "another," and so forth,
as well as "excellent," and so forth, are explanations of the implied meaning.
By those two, the existence of an obstacle to the arising of a general collapse of all limbs is shown;
[this occurs] by virtue of that dissimulation (*avahittha*), which is the concealment of one's outward appearance through profound depth.
Thus, they "do not prevail."

The word "limbs" (aṅgāni) is to be supplied [from the previous verse]. By the phrase "engaged in household duties," he indicates what is understood; this is expressed by the words beginning with "household" (gṛha-). "In that way" (tathā) means by virtue of possessing an excellence of effort.
The connection is that [the sounds] are not clearly perceived in the same way during the performance of household chores;
therefore, the sense is that the mere hearing of the clamor produces an excellence of pleasure.
In the reading "yoge ca," the word division is "alakṣyamāṇāni."
"From this very denoted meaning (vācya)" means:
from the denoted object itself, characterized by the state of all its limbs being agitated, which continues precisely at the time of hearing that kind of clamor.

With the intention of including those factors designated as restrictors of the primary signification (*abhidhā*)—such as "conjunction and separation" and so forth—by the word "and so on" (*ādi*) in the phrase "context and so on," he explains: "that of which context is the first."
"By another word," and so forth;
the meaning is "of the aggregate composed of that.
"Precisely from the comprehension of that," and so forth.
The meaning is: "precisely because of ignorance of that.
Showing the connection of the word "where" (*yatra*), he explains the passage beginning with "ascertained" (*nirdhārita*) as "in whatever object," and so forth.
[He explains] "ascertained" (*niścita*).
The certainty in this context is to be understood as residing in the person to be enlightened and produced by the sentence;

for it is precisely with respect to the cognition produced by the sentence that the knowledge of the context and so forth serves as the cause. Furthermore, this is an illustration of a certainty not produced by inference.

In passages such as "uccinvī" (gathering), one must understand that the shaking of the *śephālikā* flower should not be performed because it produces undesirable results such as the anger of one's father-in-law; this refers to the certainty residing in the heroine or others, which is to be communicated and produced by words and so forth.
The phrase "of universal nature" (*samastasvabhāva*) is an explanation of the specific term.
He states "to be expressed again," containing a reason, with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*), and so on.
Thus, here, while a female friend is sporting with her husband who is not a master of discipline, her eye is drawn outward by the sound of bracelets heard from outside;
and since such a [suggestion] attains the status of a subordinate element (*aṅga*) within what is being perceived, it follows that this is the domain of *dhvani*.

By clearly stating this—which is based on the intended meaning of the suggested sense—it is implied that when the suggested sense is subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), the basis for its classification is exactly the opposite.
"Pick only the fallen flowers; do not shake the *śephālikā* bush, O daughter-in-law of Hālaka!
Your father-in-law has heard the sound of your bangles, which portends a bitter consequence for you."
Such is the shadow [of the meaning].
For the father-in-law, while guarding the *śophālikā* creeper with great effort, becomes angry by pulling and shaking it;
therefore, in this case, one should understand that there is a "ripening at an improper time" (*viṣamaparipākatva*).
Otherwise, there would be an implication of the suggested meaning by one's own statement alone.
And here, the interpretation must be made in accordance with the words "kassa vā ṇa hoi roso" (To whom would anger not arise?).
This [suggested sense] must be taken into account for the comprehension and attainment of the expressed meaning (*vācyārtha*).
Otherwise, the intended meaning cannot be obtained;
that is to say, by virtue of being established through its own nature (*svataḥsiddhatayā*), that meaning would simply be inexpressible. [Objection:

But in this way, has not the status of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*) as an embellishment (*upaskāra*) been stated on the contrary? [Response: This is merely a clarification of the word *eva* (only), beginning with "its own" (*svām*) and so forth.
"Only that much" means "only the literal meaning.
The explanation of the phrase beginning with "as a subordinate element of the suggested meaning" is the passage beginning with "of the suggested," and so forth.
"Sa" means that poem;
he states its purpose with the words "by this," and so forth.
They gather the *śephālikā*.
Regarding this, Amara states: "The *śephālikā* is indeed the *suvarhā*."
The plowman is one who draws the plow; his daughter-in-law is the wife of his son.
He states the reason for the prohibition against shaking [the tree] with the words beginning "this":
"this" refers to that which is being heard by me.

That sound of bracelets was heard by the father-in-law; it was "of uneven ripening," meaning its ripening or transformation was uneven and produced undesirable results. The word "might be" (bhavet) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
By stating "unequal fruition" (*viṣamavipāka*), he dispels the doubt that [the verse] might imply what is yet to be explained; this is done with the words beginning "since" (*yataḥ*).
The sense is that a commentary must be provided, meaning that the various types of suggested meanings (*vyaṅgya*) should be understood according to their different objects.

In this regard, the *Vṛtti* demonstrates—by means of the words "here" (*atra*) and so forth—that even when some suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) serves as a subordinate element (*aṅga*) to the expressed meaning (*vācya*), the status of being *dhvani* is established by taking into account another suggested meaning.
[The phrase] "by the lord of immodesty" (*avinayapati*) refers to the lover (*jāra*).
[The word] "friend" (*sakhi*)... [is used].
The meaning is "the heroine.

He explains the passage "for the comprehension of the expressed meaning" (*vācyārthapratipattaye*), which is to be considered here, with the words beginning "of the expressed meaning" (*vācyārthasya*).
This refers to the expressed meaning of the verses beginning with "uccinvatī."
"Lābhāya" means for the sake of the accomplishment of enlightenment free from longing, or for the sake of enlightenment together with its fruit; such is the meaning.
The explanation of the word "this" (etad) is: "this is the suggested meaning" (etad-vyaṅgyam).
The meaning is that the suggested meaning consists of the awakening of the heroine by means of her friend.
[The word] "to be expected" (apekṣaṇīyam) [is used].
The meaning is that it must be regarded as a cooperative factor (*sahakārin*).

That is to say, while there is the cognition—either as a directly expressed object (*vācyārtha*) or as something implied (*vyaṅgya*)—that "the friend of the heroine who is to be awakened is awakening me," or for those with aesthetic sensitivity (*sahṛdaya*), the cognition that "the friend is awakening the heroine who is enjoying herself," this [cognition] is what constitutes the cooperative factor for the attainment of the expressed meaning. This is the sense.
He establishes the systematic arrangement [of the argument] with the words "otherwise," and so forth.
"Otherwise" means in the absence of dependence on the manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
"Would not be obtained" means...
To the question "Why?", he says: "By virtue of being established by itself," etc.;
that is, because they are known by themselves through the heroine and others.
Thus, it is indeed inexpressible.
The meaning is "due to its fruitlessness.
"That purpose" means the purpose [expressed by] the words "do not shake the śephālikā," and so forth.
The phrase "of that which is to be expressed" (vyaṅgya) means "of that which has been stated.
Furthermore, the text "it is to be expressed again" (punarvācya) is made clear by the female friend according to the explanation already given.
This must be taken into account for the comprehension of the expressed meaning (vācyārtha).

And since a meaning that is intended to be expressed is stated with the intent of concealing its deviation [from the literal], it once again serves as a subordinate element to the suggested sense; thus, it is included within this type of *dhvani* where the suggested sense takes the form of a resonance (*anuraṇana*).

Having thus established the distinction between *dhvani* and its semblance (*tadābhāsa*) regarding that in which the expressed meaning is intended (*vivakṣitavācya*), he now speaks in order to perform the same for that in which the expressed meaning is not intended (*avivakṣitavācya*):
"A composition that falters in its progress due to either lack of proficiency or incapacity..."
And that [suggestion] is not to be known as the object of the sound (śabda) by the wise; it is the domain of resonance (dhvani).
Furthermore, that instance where a word falters in its delivery due to a lack of proficiency or incapacity is not to be understood by the wise as the domain of *dhvani*. (32)
Anticipating this objection, [the author] says: "And when it is apprehended," which means "when it has been expressed by a word. // 31 //
The locative case in "tadābhāsaviveke" (in the discrimination of that appearance) is used in the sense of a cause (*hetau*);

that is to say, it refers to the occasion characterized by the introduction of the discrimination of that appearance. In response to the expectation of whose appearance it is, he says: "of the intended denotatum" (*vivakṣitavācyasya*).
But when the clear exposition has been set forth, the phrase "it has been introduced" is inappropriate;
for the distinction from its semblance occurs at the conclusion of what was intended to be expressed,
and not now while it is being introduced.
Nor does it persist in subsequent time;
"because its movement is faltering" means [this applies] to a word that is figurative or derivative.
Lack of proficiency (*avyutpatti*) is the engagement with a composition based on a focus such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
For example: "He who constantly sports in the space of the hearts of mature women—whose familiarity is abundant due to the continuous flow of swaying love—is the very ground of good fortune.
In this instance, the word *preṅkhat* ("swaying") is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) because of the poet's delight in alliteration.
The metaphorical usage "cittākāśa" (mind-space), although employed by the poet, does not culminate in any beautiful purpose that is suggested (*dhvanyamāna*).
"Incapacity" (*aśakti*) refers to the inability to complete the metrical foot or other such deficiencies. [The author] explains the phrase "pratipanne" (when understood) as "expressed by the word."
In the commentary, "of that" means "of the expressed meaning.
"In the absence of discipline," and so forth.
The concealment of misconduct, such as theft or sexual intercourse, means the absence of public disclosure through force, reputation, and so forth;
the meaning is "with that as the primary intent.
This refers to its being a subordinate element of the suggested sense (*vyaṅgyāṅgatvam*).
The meaning is that [the word "bracelet"] serves as a subordinate element (aṅga) to the suggested sense (vyaṅgya), such as "do not make the sound of a bracelet. // 31 //
"Appearing as that" means "the discernment of that appearance. However, regarding the clear explanation, he says: [as follows].
The meaning is that if one were to explain *prastute* as "having begun" or "in the context of the subject at hand," then the word *tat* (that) would be inappropriate.
To the question "Why?", he says: "For, upon the completion of another [work]," and so forth.
He shows that by the term *avyutpatti* (lack of proficiency), its effect is intended, by stating: "alliteration and so forth."
The meaning is that the engagement in poetry occurs through that intention (*tātparya*) which is based on alliteration and the like.
Regarding the word *preṅkhat*: it refers to that which is swaying or fickle; as it has been said, "The love of women is fickle due to its longing for an ever-increasing collection of virtues."
"In that which has abundant familiarity with the continuous binding— that is, the firm stabilization— of love":
the word "characteristic" (*lākṣaṇika*) implies the sense of "unstable," as is understood from the context.
Regarding the term "secondary" (*gauṇa*):
the sense is that [the mind] is equal to space by virtue of its lack of perceptibility and so forth; this is the intended meaning.
He explains the word "incapacity" (*aśakti*) with the words beginning "ceased," etc. (*vṛtta*...).
Furthermore, the composition of a word that is figurative due to a faltering progression, or which is unetymological or incapable [of its intended meaning], is not the province of *dhvani*;
for—
in all its varieties— there is a manifestation with clarity.
When that [suggested meaning] is the principal element (*aṅgin*) of what is suggested, that is the complete definition of *dhvani*.
In all these varieties, the manifestation of the suggested meaning—which has become the primary element—with clarity is the definition of *dhvani* in its complete form. (33)

As stated in the *Locana*: "By you, falling into the ocean—the preeminent abode for the collection of families of uneven [poisonous] snakes—you have created a state where the self is unstable within a wall-like vessel that is tossed about by moving waves."
In this context, the first term ending in "pravara" is metaphorically applied to the moon;
it is used in the sense of a "receptacle" (*bhājana*) and as "consisting of walls" (*kuḍyamaya*) in its unstable state.
This does not possess any particular beauty,
except for the purpose of completing the meter;
and as for the word "sa" (he).

In the first Uddyota, regarding the statement that "poets proceed with linguistic usage in accordance with established convention," the example beginning with "he speaks of a bed of lotus leaves" was cited as being metaphorical (bhākta).
The meaning of the word "ca" (and) is that this [metaphorical usage] is not only within the scope of Dhvani, but is also something else.

With the intention of restating the very nature of Dhvani—which has already been stated—as the cause for distinguishing it from its semblances (tadābhāsa), the author of the Vṛtti provides the following supplement: "Since... (yataḥ).
Regarding the term "illumination" (*avabhāsana*):
according to the principle that "bringing forth an entity" implies "bringing forth a substance," that which is manifested is the *vyaṅgya* (the suggested).
The definition of *dhvani* is the complete essential nature (*svarūpa*) of *dhvani*.
Alternatively, illumination is knowledge; that is the definition and the means of valid cognition for sound,
and it is complete because it makes known the complete nature of sound.

Alternatively, "poison" (viṣam) refers to knowledge itself, as it is dear to the ignorant. "Viṣama" means one who possesses arrows (kāṇḍa) or shafts numbering an uneven count; [the term refers] to that Kāmadeva, whose conquest of the family is well-known.
O foremost and chief among those [who have conquered the family], O Moon—this is the meaning.

In the reading "kuraṅga," it refers to you falling and having fallen into the ocean; the phrase "in that whose middle portion—the vessel—is shaken by the deer-like creeper" (*latākuraṅgena mṛgeṇa vidhūrṇitaṃ bhājanaṃ madhyabhāgo yasya*) is an epithet of yourself.
In the reading "taraṅga," it is an epithet of the ocean.
In that which consists of a wall, in that which is immovable;
in one's own body;
[the term] "moving."
"And it moves" is the meaning.
"Produced" means brought forth.
The term "metaphorically designated" (upacarita) is also connected with the two subsequent sentences.
He says that the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase *sa ca* serves to collect what was stated in the first chapter, beginning with "In the first chapter," etc.;
and [the phrase] "That is not," etc.,
means that mere [sound] is not the object of the resonance (*dhvani*).
"Another also" means that even the aforementioned manner, beginning with "due to a lack of proficiency," [applies].
He explains the passage beginning with "manifestation" as follows: "of entities," and so forth.
The meaning is that by the word "illumination" (avabhāsana), the suggested sense (vyaṅgya) which is being illuminated is indicated;
the connection is with the phrase "the full essential nature" (pūrṇaṃ svarūpam).

Now, one might object that in this way the syntactical connection of the words "of the suggested sense" and "which has become a subordinate element" (aṅgībhūtasya) is difficult to establish; therefore, he says "illumination," and so forth.
It is the cognition [of an object] in its clarity.
Following the etymological derivation that "it is characterized" (*lakṣyate*) or "known" (*jñāyate*) by means of this, he says: "the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇam*).
It is not the natural sense of the word *lakṣaṇa* (characteristic) to have the meaning of "means of valid cognition."
With the intention that this term has as its sole purpose the expression of a unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*), he says "Alternatively," and so forth.

He states "Knowledge itself," and so forth, because the definition and the knowledge stand in a relationship of the delimited and the delimiting; thus, they are referred to here by superimposing identity upon them.
And that [definition] has precisely the aforementioned object as its domain.
Thus ends the second Uddyota in the Dhvanyāloka composed by the venerable teacher Rājānaka Ānandavardhana.
The *Locana* is a definition of *dhvani*, since a definition is that which is delimited by cognition.

By the use of the particle *eva* (*only*) in the commentary, it is indicated that anything other than that [definition] possesses only the nature of an appearance; thus, the very purpose initiated—namely, the state of being the cause for the discrimination of those appearances—is successfully accomplished. May there be auspiciousness!
I, Abhinavagupta, bow to that Paśyantī, by whom this entire universe is manifested as a mere outpouring of her own abundant splendor through the differentiation of existence.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Dhvani-saṅketa*, titled *Sahṛdayālokāloca*, illuminated by the illustrious and preeminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Abhinavagupta.
"Because it is to be determined by the cognition of the definiendum (lakṣya)" means that it must be ascertained through the cognition of that which is to be defined.
For, by means of the cognition of a cow and so forth, the definition of a cow and so forth is determined.
"By the word 'eva' (only)" means by the word "eva" [indicating] that it refers exclusively to the subject already mentioned.
"Abundant" (prājyam) means...
By which Supreme Sovereignty (parameśvarī), in the form of Māyā, this abundant and extensive world is drawn forth as the subject of the nominative case;
its manifestation is mere appearance (pratīti-tanmātra), and not substantially real— this is the intended meaning.

"By distinction" means by way of being different from Brahman; or alternatively, "by the distinction from the existent" (*sadbhedena*) is a single compound word, meaning "by way of being distinct from the existent Brahman.
"Is threaded" (*āsūtryate*) means it is revealed.
The connection [of the words] is: "I, Abhinavagupta, salute her who beholds this world.
Thus all is auspicious.
Thus ends the second Uddyota in the *Bālapriyā*, a commentary on the *Dhvanyāloka*, composed by the scholar-king Rāmaśāraka, the ornament of the learned.
